buffett.name: Warren Buffett
buffett.what: Chairman's letters to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders, 1995 to 2024
buffett.unitsLede: Each year: what the letter is most worth reading for, its one short line, the ideas it contributes, and your own notes.
buffett.scope: Buffett wrote the annual letters through the 2024 letter. The 2025 letter, published in February 2026, was written by Greg Abel and is outside this section. A 2026 letter has not been published yet. Buffett's short farewell note of November 2025 is optional reading in week 12.
buffett.readHow: Open Berkshire's letters page and pick the year. In each report, start reading at “To the Shareholders of Berkshire Hathaway Inc.”

start.lede: Buffett ran Berkshire Hathaway for six decades and wrote to its owners every year. The letters are free, plainly written, and among the best education in investing there is.
start.para: This section covers his thirty letters from 1995 to 2024. Expect about an hour a week for twelve weeks: one theme here, then two or three of his letters in full.
steps: Read the idea that underlies everything
Chapter 1: A share is a slice of a business. About ten minutes.
Read your first letter
1996 is the best single letter for an individual investor. Read the summary here, then the letter itself.
Try ten flashcards
Flashcards bring ideas back just before you would forget them.
Write your first rule
Tap “+ rule” beside any idea, or write one in My investing rules.

glossary: The cash a business will hand its owners over its remaining life, valued today. Always an estimate, best held as a range.
The gap between that value and the price you pay. It protects you when your estimate is wrong.
Whatever stops competitors from taking a business's profits: a brand, low costs, a network, a licence.
Benjamin Graham's imaginary partner who offers to buy or sell every day at prices set by his mood. Use his offers; never take his advice.
The businesses you genuinely understand well enough to value. Knowing its edge matters more than its size.
Profit a company keeps and reinvests instead of paying out. What it earns on that money decides the next decade.
A company buying its own shares. Sensible only with spare cash and a price below value.
Money an insurer holds between collecting premiums and paying claims, invested in the meantime.
Profit after the spending needed just to keep the business where it is.
Assets minus liabilities in the accounts. Buffett's yardstick for decades, retired in 2018.

units.title: The 1995 letter
units.summary: Why most acquisitions fail. Retailing against one-decision businesses. The full purchase of GEICO.

units.title: The 1996 letter
units.summary: The best single letter on how an individual should choose shares: circle of competence, the Inevitables, inactivity.

units.title: The 1997 letter
units.summary: The hamburger quiz. Ted Williams and the fat pitch. What it costs to pay with shares.

units.title: The 1998 letter
units.summary: General Re. Options as a cost. Accounting games named. The McDonald's confession.

units.title: The 1999 letter
units.summary: His worst relative year. Why no technology shares. Rules for buybacks. Look-through earnings.

units.title: The 2000 letter
units.summary: Aesop's formula for value. Investment against speculation. The bubble examined.

units.title: The 2001 letter
units.summary: After September 11: three underwriting rules, the Noah rule, the tide going out.

units.title: The 2002 letter
units.summary: Derivatives. What directors are for. Three accounting warning signs.

units.title: The 2003 letter
units.summary: The base-year trick. Lending in manufactured housing. Directors' independence. Index funds.

units.title: The 2004 letter
units.summary: Three ways investors beat themselves. National Indemnity shrinking on purpose.

units.title: The 2005 letter
units.summary: The Gotrocks family and frictional costs. Widening the moat. How pay ratchets up.

units.title: The 2006 letter
units.summary: The fading moat of newspapers. Two-and-twenty fees. Walter Schloss.

units.title: The 2007 letter
units.summary: Great, good and gruesome businesses. See's in numbers. Dexter's true cost.

units.title: The 2008 letter
units.summary: The crisis. Price against value. Models and their limits. His own errors that year.

units.title: The 2009 letter
units.summary: The list of things Berkshire does not do. Issuing shares for the railroad. Liquidity.

units.title: The 2010 letter
units.summary: Leverage and liquidity: the clearest statement of why he avoids debt.

units.title: The 2011 letter
units.summary: Three kinds of asset and the gold cube. The IBM buyback paradox. Four insurance disciplines.

units.title: The 2012 letter
units.summary: Dividends explained with a worked example. The order of capital allocation.

units.title: The 2013 letter
units.summary: The farm and the New York property. Advice for the non-professional. His will.

units.title: The 2014 letter
units.summary: Fifty-year review: bargains to quality, the conglomerate form, volatility against risk.

units.title: The 2015 letter
units.summary: Productivity and prosperity. The case against adjusted earnings. Small odds over long periods.

units.title: The 2016 letter
units.summary: The logic of buybacks. The ten-year bet. Two kinds of fear.

units.title: The 2017 letter
units.summary: Deal prices and cheap debt. Berkshire's four crashes. The bet's final lessons.

units.title: The 2018 letter
units.summary: Forest and trees. Book value retired. The $114.75 example.

units.title: The 2019 letter
units.summary: The power of retained earnings. What boards get wrong. Conflicted advice.

units.title: The 2020 letter
units.summary: The Precision Castparts confession. Conglomerates. Buybacks at Apple.

units.title: The 2021 letter
units.summary: Business-pickers. The four giants. Why so much cash.

units.title: The 2022 letter
units.summary: Coca-Cola and American Express dividends over three decades. A dozen decisions. Munger's sayings.

units.title: The 2023 letter
units.summary: Munger the architect. Writing for an absent owner. The one rule. Japan. Errors in rail and utilities.

units.title: The 2024 letter
units.summary: Mistakes and thumb-sucking. Cash against businesses. His last annual letter.

themes.title: A share is a slice of a business
themes.idea: You are buying a claim on what a company will earn. The price on the screen is an offer from a stranger, and it carries no information about the business.
ask: For each holding: could I describe what this company will probably earn five years from now, and why, without mentioning its share price?
If the exchange shut for three years tomorrow, which holdings would I be content to keep?

themes.title: Moats: what makes a business worth owning
themes.idea: A great business earns a high return on the money inside it, and can keep doing so because something stops competitors from taking it away.
ask: What exactly stops a well-funded competitor from taking this company's customers? Has that barrier grown or shrunk in three years?
Of each extra unit of profit, how much must go back in just to stay in place?
themes.caption: Schematic, after the 2007 letter. Outline: capital the business must hold to grow. Solid: what it earns on that capital.

themes.title: Price, value and the margin of safety
themes.idea: Value is the cash a business will hand its owners over time. Price is what you pay for that. The gap between the two is your return and your protection.
ask: What return does today's price imply if the business simply does what it has done before? What has to go right for more?
Is my estimate a range? How wide is it, and would I still buy at the bottom of it?
themes.caption: After the 2000 letter. The price paid must sit clearly below the low end of the range.

themes.title: Mr. Market and temperament
themes.idea: Prices swing far more than values do. The swings are there to be used or ignored. They are never instructions.
ask: If my largest holding fell 50% next month with no change in the business, what exactly would I do? Write it down now.
Which of my recent trades were responses to price, and which to a change in the business?
themes.caption: Falls in Berkshire Hathaway's own share price, as listed in the 2017 letter.

themes.title: Activity, costs and patience
themes.idea: The return from owning good businesses is earned by sitting. Almost everything an investor does beyond that subtracts from it.
ask: Add up last year's brokerage, impact cost and short-term tax. What share of my gain did motion consume?
How many decisions in my whole career produced most of the result? What was I doing in the months around them?
themes.caption: The ten-year bet, 2008 to 2017: average annual gain (2017 letter). Fund D was wound up after nine years.

themes.title: Risk, debt and survival
themes.idea: Risk is the chance of losing capital for good. Price swings are something else. Stay in a position where no single event can end the game.
ask: What single event would do permanent damage to my finances? What have I built against it, as opposed to merely predicted?
Which of my positions would hurt together in the same bad year?
themes.caption: Illustrative figures. Any run of good years, multiplied by one zero (after the 2010 letter).

themes.title: Circle of competence
themes.idea: You do not need to understand many businesses. You need to know exactly which ones you do understand, and stay there.
ask: Which holdings sit inside the circle, on its edge, or outside? Does position size follow that order?
Where have I mistaken familiarity with a product for understanding of the business?
themes.caption: After the 1996 letter: know where the edge of your circle is.

themes.title: Capital allocation: what happens to retained profit
themes.idea: Over a decade, what management does with the profit it keeps counts for more than the profit itself.
ask: Over five years, how much profit did this company retain, and how much extra profit did that retained money produce?
When did management last buy back or issue shares, and at what price against value?
themes.caption: Order of preference for each unit of profit, after the 2012 letter. Move right only when the step before cannot earn a good return.

themes.title: Acquisitions: a test for any company that buys others
themes.idea: Most deals help the seller and the adviser. Use his filters to judge every serial acquirer you own.
ask: Does this company's acquisition record pass his six filters? What did it pay with, cash or shares?
After its last three deals, did return on capital rise or fall?

themes.title: Managers, pay and boards
themes.idea: He looks for people who run a company as if it were their family's only asset, and for pay and boards that keep them that way.
ask: Does this promoter own a large stake bought or held with personal money, and how has minority capital been treated in past deals?
Does the annual report speak plainly about what went wrong last year?

themes.title: Accounting: read like an owner
themes.idea: Reported numbers are where analysis starts. His letters are a thirty-year course in where they mislead.
ask: What is this company's profit after real maintenance spending and after counting share-based pay?
Which number in the accounts depends most on management's own estimate, and what happens if it is 20% wrong?

themes.title: Insurance: float and the discipline of saying no
themes.idea: Every letter returns to insurance. The ideas carry over to any business that takes money today against a promise to pay later, such as lenders.
ask: For any lender or insurer I own: has it ever chosen to shrink when pricing was poor?
How fast is it growing against the industry, and what would have to be true for that growth to be safely priced?

themes.title: Mistakes: his own list
themes.idea: Read what he took from each one. His costly errors fall into four groups: misjudging how long an advantage would last, paying with undervalued shares, paying an optimistic price, and waiting too long once the facts changed. Market crashes do not appear on the list. The other half of the picture came in 2022: about one good decision every five years has carried the record.
ask: Which of his four groups do my own worst errors fall into? Is there a fifth that is mine alone?
What is the oldest known problem in my portfolio that I have not acted on?

themes.title: Productive assets, inflation and the long view
themes.idea: Wealth compounds in things that produce: businesses, farms, property. Claims on money and objects that produce nothing do not compound.
ask: He writes about America. The portable idea is to own productive assets in an economy with rule of law and rising productivity. How does my own allocation look against that test?
What in my balance sheet depends on someone later paying a higher price, with nothing produced in between?
themes.caption: $114.75 invested in 1942, value in early 2019 (2018 letter). Bars drawn to scale.

t1n1.text: He buys on a view of how the company will do over many years. He holds no view on where the share price or the market goes next, and does not act as if he had one.

t1n2.text: In 1986 he bought a Nebraska farm, in 1993 a retail property in New York, knowing little about farming or real estate. He asked only two things: what will this asset earn over the years, and is the price sensible against that? Neither came with a daily quote, and he never missed having one.

t1n3.text: If you can enjoy a weekend without checking the price of something you own, you can do the same on a weekday. Results on the ground decide the outcome; the price catches up later.

t1n4.lead: Count the earnings you never see.
t1n4.text: Your real income from a holding includes your share of the profit the company keeps. Accounts show only the dividend. At a business that reinvests well, the retained part is the more valuable half.

t1n5.text: Over months, price measures how liked a share is. Over years, it measures what the business is worth. This is Graham's idea, and he repeats it thirty years on because nothing has replaced it.

t1n6.lead: Two doors into the same room.
t1n6.text: Buying a whole company and buying 2% of a listed one are the same act of judgement. The listed route has two advantages: shares are sometimes offered at foolish prices, and a mistake can be sold in a day.

t1n7.lead: Part of a gem beats all of a pebble.
t1n7.text: A small piece of an outstanding business is worth more than full control of an average one, and it is far less work.

t1n8.text: A rising market flatters everyone. The test is whether you beat a cheap index after costs and tax over several years, using a benchmark chosen in advance and never swapped after a bad stretch.

t2n1.text: Great: pays a very high rate and needs few new deposits to grow. Good: pays a fair rate, but only on large new deposits. Gruesome: grows fast, demands ever more money and pays little on it. He names See's Candies, FlightSafety and airlines as the three.

t2n2.text: Bought in 1972 for $25 million, when it earned under $5 million before tax on $8 million of capital. By 2007 it earned $82 million on $40 million. Along the way it sent $1.35 billion to the parent after keeping only $32 million for itself. That cash bought other businesses.

t2n3.lead: The word that matters is enduring.
t2n3.text: A moat that must be rebuilt every few years is not a moat, which rules out industries prone to rapid change. And if results depend on one superstar, the star is great, not the business.

t2n4.text: A handful of companies will almost certainly dominate their fields for decades. A larger group will probably do so. Leaders in fast-moving industries belong to neither group. Even with an Inevitable you can overpay, and the usual way they get hurt is management drifting away from the core.

t2n5.lead: Is the moat wider this year?
t2n5.text: He asks managers to strengthen the competitive position every year, even at the cost of current profit. Earnings bought by squeezing customers or skimping on the brand are a withdrawal from the moat.

t2n6.text: Where customers buy mainly on price, the operator with the lowest costs keeps taking share. GEICO is his thirty-year example.

t2n7.text: A retailer has to be clever every single day, because rivals copy each good idea at once. Other businesses run for decades on one right decision made long ago. He prefers the second kind.

t2n8.text: Newspapers were close to a local monopoly. Once readers and advertisers had alternatives, capable managers could only slow the decline. When industry economics and management pull in opposite directions, economics wins.

t2n9.lead: Growth is a number, not a virtue.
t2n9.text: Growth that needs capital earning a poor return destroys value. Seeing that an industry will grow is easy. Working out who will keep the profit is the hard part, and when he cannot do that he passes.

t2n10.text: With too much cash for small gems, he bought a railroad and utilities: huge capital needs, steady returns on very large sums. In 2023 he said the railroad must spend more than its depreciation just to stand still, and that utility regulation had turned out worse than he assumed.

t3n1.text: A bird in the hand against birds in the bush. To value anything you need three answers: how sure are you the birds are there, when will they appear and how many, and what does a risk-free bond pay meanwhile? Growth is one input among several, and it can subtract value.

t3n2.text: Intrinsic value is an estimate. If the honest range is too wide to act on, move to something else. A rough figure that is about right beats an exact one that is wrong.

t3n3.lead: The two numbers are different things.
t3n3.text: What you pay and what you get are separate questions. In the crisis he restated the aim: a good business at a fair price, ahead of a poor one at a low price.

t3n4.lead: Wonderful at fair beats fair at wonderful.
t3n4.text: He began with statistically cheap, mediocre companies. Munger persuaded him that such bargains do not scale and seldom last. This is the largest single change in his method, and he credits it entirely to his partner.

t3n5.lead: Great companies at full prices earn ordinary returns.
t3n5.text: Buy first-class businesses at rich valuations and you earn roughly their profit growth, nothing extra. A high price removes the margin of safety even when the business is superb.

t3n6.text: He stayed out of shares unless he saw a high probability of at least 10% a year before tax. Idle cash was the accepted alternative.

t3n7.text: Shareholders together cannot earn more than businesses earn. Any return forecast has to fit economic growth plus inflation plus dividends, less costs. He ran this sum against the optimism of 1999 and against pension-fund assumptions in 2007.

t3n8.lead: Value it as if it had no debt.
t3n8.text: Cheap borrowing can make a poor purchase look fine per share. He prices every business on an all-equity basis, then decides.

t3n9.text: As capital grows, the list of ideas that can move the total shrinks. A small investor has a real edge here, and it erodes with every doubling.

t4n1.text: If you will be eating burgers for life and do not raise cattle, you should want beef to get cheaper. If you will be a net buyer of shares for years, the same logic applies. Only someone about to sell gains from high prices.

t4n2.lead: If you must time, time against the crowd.
t4n2.text: His advice to those who insist on timing: be cautious when others are eager, and eager only when others are afraid.

t4n3.text: Fear across the market helps you, because it produces bargains. Fear inside you hurts you. An investor who keeps costs low and sits with large, soundly financed businesses will almost certainly do well.

t4n4.lead: Berkshire itself has halved, more than once.
t4n4.text: He printed his own stock's four worst falls (chart below) as the case against borrowing to own shares. Nobody can say how far a price may drop in the short run, and debt forces a decision at the worst moment. Without debt, your mind stays clear.

t4n5.text: In a boom everyone plans to leave just before midnight. The trouble is that nobody in the ballroom can see a clock.

t4n6.lead: Bubbles move wealth; they do not create it.
t4n6.text: A company that loses money over its lifetime has destroyed value, whatever its market value was at the peak. The gains of promoters came out of the pockets of late buyers.

t4n7.lead: Being out is the bigger risk.
t4n7.text: The danger of sitting out of the game is far larger than the danger of staying in it. He does not step in and out on forecasts.

t4n8.lead: Bad news is the buyer's friend.
t4n8.text: Pessimism lowers prices. Large opportunities are rare, and when one arrives he acts in size.

t4n9.text: He spends no time on forecasts of the economy or the market, his own or anyone else's. Beyond the wasted hours, they crowd out the handful of facts about a business that decide the result.

t4n10.lead: Expect to trail in a boom.
t4n10.text: A quality-first approach lags when markets roar and leads when they are flat or falling. Know this ahead of time so a strong year for others does not push you into changing method.

t5n1.text: Newton gave physics three laws of motion and then lost a fortune in the South Sea Bubble. Buffett supplies the missing law: for investors as a group, the more they move, the less they keep.

t5n2.text: Imagine one family owns every business in the country. Its wealth grows by what the businesses earn. Then helpers arrive: brokers to trade between cousins, managers to choose the brokers, consultants to choose the managers, and finally hedge funds with a share of profits. Each layer is paid out of the same earnings. He guessed these frictional costs might reach a fifth of all corporate profit.

t5n3.text: High costs from trading and fees. Decisions made on tips and fashion in place of valuation. And stop-start timing: getting in after a long rise and out after a long fall.

t5n4.text: Ted Williams cut the strike zone into cells and swung only at balls in his best one. An investor has it easier, because there are no called strikes. Standing with the bat on your shoulder costs nothing.

t5n5.text: When you own pieces of excellent businesses, inactivity is the intelligent course. Nobody sells a wonderful subsidiary because of a rate forecast, so why sell a minority stake in one?

t5n6.lead: The movies would have paid better.
t5n6.text: After selling McDonald's and trimming other holdings, he told shareholders they would have done better had he spent market hours at the cinema.

t5n7.text: He takes the higher, bumpier return over the lower, steadier one. Most managers choose the reverse because smooth is easier to explain.

t5n8.text: Looking back over 58 years he counted about twelve really good decisions, roughly one every five years. The record rests on those, plus avoiding ruin in between.

t5n9.text: A plain index fund against five funds-of-funds chosen by professionals, over 2008 to 2017. The index fund won by a wide margin (chart below). The managers were not stupid. Layers of fees were the difference.

t5n10.lead: One per cent is not small.
t5n10.text: On his 77-year example, an annual fee of 1% would have cut the ending sum in half.

t5n11.lead: Idle cash is the lesser evil.
t5n11.text: Cash earning little is uncomfortable. A purchase made to relieve the discomfort is worse.

t6n1.text: Among everything that changed at Berkshire over six decades, he names one investment rule that has not and will not: do not put capital at risk of permanent loss.

t6n2.text: Risk is the probability of ending your holding period with less purchasing power. Over a day or a year, shares are riskier than cash. Over decades, cash and bonds are the riskier choice. The horizon decides which is safe.

t6n3.text: By trading actively, trying to time moves, diversifying too little, paying high fees and borrowing. Each can turn a good long-run asset into a poor result.

t6n4.text: A long run of fine numbers multiplied by a single zero is zero. Leverage wins most of the time, which is why it is addictive, and the rare loss is total.

t6n5.text: Keep so much liquidity that any conceivable cash need is small beside it. This costs return in ordinary years. It buys sleep, survival and the means to purchase when others must sell.

t6n6.text: Only when conditions turn do you learn who was running without protection. Calm years hide weak practice.

t6n7.text: He had foreseen the risk of a mega-catastrophe and done too little about it. Forecasting the flood earns nothing. The ark does.

t6n8.text: Judge a risk by what could happen. A quiet record says little about a danger that has not struck yet.

t6n9.text: Many small, unrelated risks are safe to carry. One concentrated exposure, or several that turn out to move together, is not.

t6n10.text: Models built on past data give precise answers and false comfort when the conditions that produced the data have changed. He warns in particular against handing risk decisions to people with formulas.

t6n11.text: Hidden leverage, chains of counterparties, and profits booked on models years before any cash arrives. He wound down General Re's book and admitted he took too long.

t6n12.text: A one-in-thirty chance each year becomes about 97% over a century. A risk you would dismiss in any single year is close to certain across an investing life.

t6n13.text: When safe yields are poor, the temptation is to accept weaker credit or longer maturities. He holds Treasury bills and waits.

t7n1.text: The size of the circle matters little. Knowing where it ends matters a great deal. You only ever have to value the companies you choose to value.

t7n2.text: He did not think the industry was bad. He could not tell which companies would hold a durable advantage ten years out. In 1999 that discipline cost him his worst year against the index, and he gave his own stock-picking a D. He kept the rule.

t7n3.lead: Exciting is not the same as knowable.
t7n3.text: The first item on his list of things Berkshire does not do: buy into businesses whose future he cannot assess, however thrilling the product.

t7n4.text: A plan that needs several separate things to go right has a low chance of success even if each step looks likely. He learned it from a zinc-recovery project. Simple propositions survive contact with reality better.

t7n5.text: If you cannot make a rough estimate of earnings five years ahead, move on. Nobody can call you out for not swinging.

t7n6.text: An investor who admits to knowing nothing about individual companies and buys a cheap index fund over time will beat most professionals. Trouble starts in between, with knowing a little and acting on a lot.

t7n7.text: Apple entered the portfolio in 2016 and within five years was one of Berkshire's four giants. He treats it as a consumer franchise with loyal users and large buybacks, which is ground he knows.

t7n8.text: Among the Munger sayings he passed on: the world changes, and your views must change with it. Staying inside the circle does not mean freezing it.

t8n1.text: First, reinvest in existing businesses where that widens the moat. Second, buy other businesses. Third, repurchase shares when they sell well below value. Dividends come when none of these can earn a good return.

t8n2.text: He worked an example: owners who keep everything reinvested and sell a small slice each year can end with more cash and more capital than under a payout, provided retained money earns well. Each owner also sets his own level of income.

t8n3.text: The company has more cash than the business needs, and the shares trade below a conservative estimate of value. With both, buying back is the surest use of money. Without the second, it destroys value for those who stay.

t8n4.text: If you own a company that keeps buying its own shares, and you are not selling, you should hope the price stays low for years. Each repurchase then lifts your share of the business by more.

t8n5.text: Apple's repurchases raised Berkshire's percentage stake year after year without Berkshire buying a share.

t8n6.lead: Issuing shares is selling the family silver.
t8n6.text: Paying for an acquisition with stock means handing over a slice of everything you already own. He paid for Dexter Shoe in shares; by 2007 those shares were worth $3.5 billion, for a purchase of about $400 million.

t8n7.text: Edgar Lawrence Smith set out to show bonds beat shares and found the opposite, because companies keep part of their profit and compound it. Retained earnings are the engine. Everything else is commentary.

t8n8.lead: Deferred tax is an interest-free loan.
t8n8.text: Tax owed on unrealised gains stays invested and working until the day you sell. Each sale ends that loan.

t8n9.text: A fixed-price option gains value when a manager simply retains earnings, with no skill involved. Watch how pay is set where profits pile up.

t9n1.text: The seller picks the moment and writes the forecast. He treats sellers' projections as entertainment. Most acquisitions damage the buyer's shareholders.

t9n2.text: Every proposed purchase has to beat the alternative of simply buying shares in the best listed companies. Many managements never run that comparison.

t9n3.text: Large enough to matter. Consistent earning power already shown. Good returns on equity with little debt. Management in place. A simple business. A stated price. No turnarounds, no auctions, no hostile bids.

t9n4.text: Owners who care what happens to their company after the sale prefer a buyer with no exit plan and no debt-loading. That reputation took decades to build and wins deals money alone could not.

t9n5.text: Once a chief executive wants a deal, the forecasts and the promised synergies will be found to support it. In 2017 he sat out because prices for decent businesses had reached records, pushed by cheap debt.

t9n6.text: An adviser paid only if the deal closes will favour closing. He proposed hiring a second adviser paid only if the deal fails.

t9n7.text: Surprises arrive after the ceremony. Most of his have worked out, and the good ones grow to become most of the value while the poor ones shrink in importance.

t9n8.text: The $11 billion after-tax write-down on Precision Castparts was his error alone. He was too hopeful about its normal level of profit and so paid too much. Nobody misled him.

t9n9.text: Some of his best purchases closed after one meeting with no formal checks. That works only when you know exactly who you are dealing with.

t9n10.text: Small additions to businesses run by tested people carry the least risk. They extend talent already proven.

t10n1.text: Good returns on the tangible capital the business needs, managers who are both able and honest, and a sensible price.

t10n2.text: His managers are told to run the business as if they owned all of it, it were the only asset their family would ever have, and it could not be sold for a century.

t10n3.lead: Choose carefully, then leave them alone.
t10n3.text: He hires with great care and manages very little. Capital allocation and the choice of chief executive stay at the centre. Everything else is delegated.

t10n4.lead: Pay for what the manager controls.
t10n4.text: Bonuses tied to the results of the manager's own unit. A share price moves for reasons outside any one person's control and makes a poor yardstick.

t10n5.lead: Options are a cost; bought shares are commitment.
t10n5.text: Accounting long treated options as free. He counts them as pay and deducts them when valuing a company. He prefers managers who buy shares with their own money and carry the downside too.

t10n6.lead: Beware the chief executive who forecasts growth.
t10n6.text: Very few large companies sustain 15% a year. A leader who promises it will eventually be tempted to manufacture it.

t10n7.lead: The company that always makes its number.
t10n7.text: Business is too uneven for that. Consistently meeting expectations is evidence of management of the figures.

t10n8.text: Business sense, an owner's outlook, and shares bought with personal money. When the fee is a large part of a director's income, independence is hard to keep. The core job is choosing and overseeing the chief executive.

t10n9.text: Pay committees compare with peers, nobody wants to be below average, and so the average climbs every year.

t10n10.text: Spin travels inward: tell the public a flattering story for long enough and you start to believe it. He writes each letter as he would want to be written to if a relative ran the business and he were the absent owner.

t10n11.text: Munger's term for putting off the correction of a mistake. He calls delay the cardinal sin, worse than the original error. He adds that he never looks at where a candidate went to school.

t11n1.text: It is a worse cost than most, because the cash goes out first and the benefit arrives later. He is scathing about measures that leave it out.

t11n2.text: Share-based pay is a cost. Restructuring that recurs every few years is a cost. Figures that strip them out flatter management.

t11n3.lead: Standing still costs more than the books say.
t11n3.text: For capital-heavy businesses, real maintenance spending runs above the depreciation charge. Owner earnings are lower than reported profit.

t11n4.text: Large one-time charges and reserves set up at acquisitions can be fed back into later years to smooth profit. He named the practice and declined to use it.

t11n5.lead: Not all amortisation is a cost.
t11n5.text: Writing down software is a true expense. Writing down purchased customer lists or goodwill often is not, because the asset may be growing in value. Separate the two before judging earnings.

t11n6.text: A growth table that starts in a terrible year or ends in a wonderful one can make ordinary performance look brilliant. Check the endpoints.

t11n7.text: Since unrealised gains on shares began flowing through profit, reported net income swings wildly and says little. He directs readers to operating earnings.

t11n8.text: After three decades as his yardstick, he dropped book value. It understates operating businesses, and buybacks above book reduce it while raising value per share.

t11n9.text: Weak accounting choices, footnotes you cannot follow, and management that broadcasts profit forecasts. If you cannot understand a note, he assumes that was intended.

t11n10.text: An insurer's profit depends on its own estimate of future claims. Such estimates are usually too low. The same caution applies to any business where today's profit rests on a guess about tomorrow's losses.

t11n11.text: He drafted them for audit committees. The first: had the auditor alone prepared these accounts, what would have been done differently?

t12n1.text: Premiums arrive now and claims are paid later. Meanwhile the insurer invests money it holds and does not own. If premiums cover claims and expenses, the float is free, or better than free.

t12n2.text: How much is there, what does it cost, and what is the long-run outlook for both? Size alone tells you nothing.

t12n3.text: Understand every exposure. Assess the likelihood and cost of loss conservatively. Set a price that leaves a profit. Walk away if that price is not available.

t12n4.lead: The fourth is where most fail.
t12n4.text: National Indemnity let its volume shrink for years when prices were poor, and promised no layoffs so that staff would not write bad business to keep their jobs. Most insurers cannot bear to watch competitors take the business.

t12n5.text: A badly priced contract takes a moment to sign and can take decades to pay for.

t12n6.text: In long-dated promises, bad surprises far outnumber good ones. Reserve and price with that in mind.

t12n7.lead: Profit that is not profit yet.
t12n7.text: Under-priced catastrophe cover can look like easy money for years before one event takes it all back. Judge such a business over a long span.

t12n8.lead: A weak reinsurer is no protection.
t12n8.text: Cheap cover from a party that may not pay is expensive. The same holds for any guarantee.

t12n9.text: Accounts show float as a debt due. In practice it is replaced as it is paid out, so its economic burden is far lower than the stated figure, as long as underwriting holds.

t12n10.text: The true cost of some policies is not known for decades. Optimism has no place in pricing them.

t14n1.text: Claims on currency, such as deposits and bonds, look safe and lose purchasing power quietly. Assets that produce nothing depend on a later buyer paying more. Productive assets keep yielding whatever happens to the currency. He chooses the third by a wide margin.

t14n2.text: All the world's gold, about 170,000 tonnes, would make a cube 68 feet a side. At that year's price it equalled all the farmland in America plus sixteen Exxon Mobils, with about $1 trillion left over. A century on, the farms and companies will have produced enormous output. The cube will be the same cube.

t14n3.text: His first share purchase, in 1942, cost $114.75. Put into a no-fee index fund with dividends reinvested, that sum would have reached $606,811 by early 2019. In gold it would have been about $4,200.

t14n4.text: The ideal asset can raise its prices with the currency and needs little fresh capital to do so. Farms, property and businesses such as See's pass both tests.

t14n5.text: He holds very large amounts of Treasury bills so that Berkshire can never be forced. In his last letter he also wrote that he will never prefer cash-equivalents to ownership of good businesses. Both statements hold together.

t14n6.text: Productivity gains have raised living standards for two centuries, and he expects that to continue. He says much of Berkshire's record came from this, as distinct from his own skill.

t14n7.text: Stakes in five trading houses, bought from 2019 and largely funded by borrowing in yen, so the currency risk is neutral. Simple businesses, low prices, sensible managements. The position was disclosed on his ninetieth birthday, a late lesson in looking abroad.

quotes.label: 2021 letter
quotes.text: Charlie and I are not stock-pickers; we are business-pickers.

quotes.label: 2013 letter
quotes.text: Games are won by players who focus on the playing field

quotes.label: 2008 letter
quotes.text: Price is what you pay; value is what you get.

quotes.label: 1997 letter
quotes.text: nothing recedes like success

quotes.label: 2004 letter
quotes.text: be fearful when others are greedy and greedy only when others are fearful

quotes.label: 2000 letter
quotes.text: speculation is most dangerous when it looks easiest

quotes.label: 2012 letter
quotes.text: We do better when the wind is in our face.

quotes.label: 2009 letter
quotes.text: When it's raining gold, reach for a bucket, not a thimble.

quotes.label: 2005 letter
quotes.text: For investors as a whole, returns decrease as motion increases.

quotes.label: 1996 letter
quotes.text: don't even think about owning it for ten minutes

quotes.label: 2017 letter
quotes.text: Performance comes, performance goes. Fees never falter.

quotes.label: 1998 letter
quotes.text: we prefer a lumpy 15% return to a smooth 12%

quotes.label: 2023 letter
quotes.text: Never risk permanent loss of capital.

quotes.label: 2014 letter
quotes.text: Volatility is far from synonymous with risk.

quotes.label: 2001 letter
quotes.text: Predicting rain doesn't count; building arks does.

quotes.label: 2002 letter
quotes.text: derivatives are financial weapons of mass destruction

quotes.label: 2010 letter
quotes.text: credit is like oxygen

quotes.label: 1999 letter
quotes.text: Over time, bad relative numbers will produce unsatisfactory absolute results.

quotes.label: 2016 letter
quotes.text: What is smart at one price is stupid at another.

quotes.label: 2019 letter
quotes.text: Don't ask the barber whether you need a haircut.

quotes.label: 1995 letter
quotes.text: A bad reinsurance contract is like hell

quotes.label: 2011 letter
quotes.text: You can fondle the cube, but it will not respond.

quotes.label: 2015 letter
quotes.text: The babies being born in America today are the luckiest crop in history.

quotes.label: 2020 letter
quotes.text: Never bet against America.

quotes.label: 2024 letter
quotes.text: Mistakes fade away; winners can forever blossom.

quotes.label: 2022 letter
quotes.text: The weeds wither away in significance as the flowers bloom.

mistakes.did: Sold his early GEICO stake; took Gillette preferred when the common was available.
mistakes.lesson: Selling a great business early is expensive. A clever structure earned less than plain ownership.
Seniority in the capital structure does not protect you when the business economics are broken.

mistakes.did: Sold McDonald's and trimmed other holdings.
mistakes.lesson: Activity cost money. Shareholders would have done better had he done nothing.

mistakes.did: Worst year against the index; graded his own stock-picking a D.
mistakes.lesson: Take the blame in plain words, and keep the method.

mistakes.did: Dexter Shoe: the moat vanished to imports, and he paid in Berkshire shares.
mistakes.lesson: Two errors at once: misjudged durability, and paid with a currency that became far more valuable.

mistakes.did: Did not sell richly priced holdings in the bubble; too slow closing General Re's derivatives book.
mistakes.lesson: Talking about over-valuation is not acting on it. Exits get harder with delay.

mistakes.did: Bought ConocoPhillips near the top of the oil price; lost most of a stake in two Irish banks.
mistakes.lesson: A good company bought on a commodity peak is still a poor purchase.

mistakes.did: A GEICO credit-card venture he pushed for.
mistakes.lesson: Staying inside the circle applies to the chairman's own ideas as well.

mistakes.did: Energy Future Holdings bonds, bought without consulting Munger.
mistakes.lesson: A bet resting on one commodity price. Talk to your sceptic before, not after.

mistakes.did: Held Tesco after his doubts grew. Also retold 1964: took control of the textile mill out of pique over an eighth of a dollar.
mistakes.lesson: Sell when the thesis breaks. Pride is an expensive adviser.

mistakes.did: Paid too much for Precision Castparts; $11 billion write-down.
mistakes.lesson: A wonderful business and able managers do not rescue an optimistic price.

mistakes.did: Misjudged regulatory returns in utilities; the railroad needs more capital than depreciation shows.
mistakes.lesson: Capital-heavy businesses are only as good as the return the system allows.

mistakes.did: Errors in judging people, and delay in correcting them.
mistakes.lesson: A decent batting average is all one can hope for. The sin is waiting.

changed: He began by buying mediocre companies at very low prices. Munger moved him to excellent companies at fair prices. The shift happened before 1995, and he retells it in 2014 and 2023 as the decision that built Berkshire.
See's was the ideal: high returns, little capital. By 2009 he had more cash than such businesses could absorb, so he bought a railroad and utilities and accepted moderate returns on very large sums.
From avoiding technology to owning Apple.
In 1999 he would not buy what he could not forecast. From 2016 Apple became a core holding, seen as a consumer franchise.
From book value to operating earnings.
Book value was his scorecard until 2018, when he retired it as no longer meaningful.
From no buybacks to large ones.
Considered and not done in 1999. A price rule of 110% of book in 2011, raised to 120% in 2012, replaced by judgement in 2018, then used heavily in 2020 and 2021.
The first overseas acquisition came in 2006. The Japanese stakes followed from 2019.
Hints in 1996, a clear statement in 2003, the instruction in his own will in 2013, and the ten-year bet as proof in 2016 and 2017.
The later letters spend more space on his errors. In 2024 he counted how often he had used the words mistake and error.
constant: A share is part of a business.
Price and value are different; insist on a margin between them.
No leverage that could force your hand. Large cash reserves always.
Never issue shares for less than they are worth.
Trust able, honest managers and leave them alone.
Write to owners plainly, bad news first.
Costs and activity are the investor's enemy.
Patience: few decisions, held a long time.

buffett.about: Only Warren Buffett's annual letters to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders, 1995 to 2024, starting from “To the Shareholders of Berkshire Hathaway Inc.” Nothing else is drawn on.
buffett.handbookTitle: Buffett's letters, 1995 to 2024: a study handbook

munger.name: Charlie Munger
munger.what: Talks and letters on thinking, living and investing, 1982 to 2014
munger.unitsLede: Each source: what it is most worth reading for, its one short line, the ideas it contributes, and your own notes.
munger.scope: Munger wrote no yearly letter like Buffett's. This section uses the eleven talks collected in Poor Charlie's Almanack, his letters to Wesco Financial and Blue Chip Stamps shareholders, and his 2014 essay for Berkshire. Remarks reported from meetings are left out, because no official transcripts exist and many circulating quotes are wrong.
munger.readHow: The talks are free to read in the publisher's online edition of Poor Charlie's Almanack. The letters link to published copies.

start.lede: Charlie Munger was Buffett's partner and Berkshire's vice chairman from 1978 until his death in November 2023, at 99. He trained as a lawyer, and his talks are as much about how to think and live as about money.
start.para: This section covers the eleven talks in Poor Charlie's Almanack, his shareholder letters and his 2014 essay. Expect about an hour a week for twelve weeks: one theme here, then the talk or letter it draws on.
steps: Read the idea that underlies everything
Chapter 1: A latticework of models. About ten minutes.
Read your first talk
His 1986 graduation speech is short, funny and a good way in. Read the summary here, then the talk itself.
Try ten flashcards
Flashcards include all 25 of his causes of misjudgment.
Write your first rule
Tap “+ rule” beside any idea, or write one in My investing rules.

glossary: Practical judgment built from the big ideas of many fields, used together on real problems.
The connected set of those big ideas you think with. Facts are hung on it so they can be used.
The error of forcing every problem into the one model you know.
Solving a problem backwards: ask what would cause failure, then avoid it.
The area where you really know enough to judge. Knowing its edge matters more than its size.
Drifting towards conclusions that serve your own pay, often without noticing.
An extreme result produced when several psychological forces push the same way at once.
His third basket for ideas, beside yes and no. You never have to decide on those.
Judging any use of money against the next-best use available.
His word for wealth quietly lost to wasteful investment fees, modelled on Galbraith's 'bezzle'.

themes.title: A latticework of models
themes.idea: Isolated facts do not stick and do not help. Hang them on a frame built from the big ideas of many fields, then use whichever ideas fit the problem.
ask: Which three disciplines outside your own work do you understand well enough to actually use?
Think of your last important decision. Which single model did you lean on, and what would a second model have told you?
themes.caption: Illustrative. A few of the disciplines he drew on, each linked to the others.

themes.title: Invert, always invert
themes.idea: Many problems that resist a direct attack give way when turned round. Ask what would guarantee failure, and then avoid it.
ask: Write down five sure ways to damage your finances over the next ten years. Are you doing a little of any of them now?
Pick one goal for this year. What three things would make it impossible, and which can you remove this month?
themes.caption: After HS 1986 and Practical 1996.

themes.title: Incentives
themes.idea: To predict what people will do, look first at what they are rewarded for. He put this first in his list of 25 human tendencies.
ask: In each relationship you have with an adviser, broker or fund, what exactly is the other side paid for?
Where in your own routine does the reward come before the hard part? How would Granny's rule change it?

themes.title: The psychology of misjudgment
themes.idea: He built a list of 25 mental tendencies that lead sensible people into error, and used it as a checklist. The danger peaks when several act at once.
ask: Take one decision you made in the last year. Which of the 25 tendencies were acting on you?
Where have three or more tendencies been pushing you the same way at once?
themes.caption: Illustrative. Several tendencies pushing the same way produce an extreme result (PHM 2005).

themes.title: The inner life: envy, resentment, self-pity
themes.idea: Much of his life advice is about thoughts to refuse. A few emotions do more damage than bad luck, and they are under your control.
ask: Whose success do you watch most closely? What does watching it do to your decisions?
Is there a grudge or a regret you replay? What would change if you put it down this week?

themes.title: Reliability, trust and deserving
themes.idea: He thought most of what people want in life is earned by being someone others can rely on. Trust that is deserved is the strongest arrangement there is.
ask: Who relies on you, and in what ways do you sometimes let them down?
Of the people you trust with money, which have earned it by their record, and which by a good first meeting?
themes.caption: After USC Law 2007: a seamless web of deserved trust.

themes.title: Learning for life
themes.idea: He saw lifelong learning as a duty, and as the main reason ordinary people overtake cleverer ones over a working life.
ask: What did you learn this month that changed a view you held? If nothing, what does that tell you?
Which belief of yours most needs a Darwin list of facts against it?
themes.caption: Illustrative. Small, steady gains in understanding add up over a working life (after USC Law 2007).

themes.title: Objectivity and the edge of what you know
themes.idea: Knowing the limits of your competence is worth more than its size. Self-regard and strong ideology are the usual ways people step over the edge without noticing.
ask: Which of your current views could you not argue against convincingly? Hold it more loosely.
Where is the edge of your circle? Name one thing you own that sits close to it.
themes.caption: After USC 1994 and Stanford 1996: know where the edge of your circle is.

themes.title: Investing: few, great, and then sit
themes.idea: The big money comes from a handful of great businesses, bought when the odds are clearly favourable, then held for a long time.
ask: If you had only twenty slots for the rest of your life, which current holdings would earn one?
Where have you diversified into ideas you do not believe in strongly?
themes.caption: The thought experiment he relays in USC 1994. Three slots used, for illustration.

themes.title: Business models, moats and scale
themes.idea: He studied why some businesses compound for a century while others never earn their keep, and taught it through plain examples.
ask: For each holding: when the industry adopts the next cost-saving technology, does the owner keep the saving or does the customer?
Which of your businesses is a commodity described in flattering words?
themes.caption: The arithmetic of the Coca-Cola thought experiment (Practical 1996): 2.92 trillion × 4¢ ≈ $117 billion.

themes.title: Costs, consultants and febezzlement
themes.idea: Fees and frictional costs look small each year and become enormous over time. He attacked them with arithmetic and with a word he coined.
ask: Add up every cost between your money and your businesses, including taxes from turnover. What share of your gains is it?
Which of those costs buys something you could not do yourself?
themes.caption: Illustrative. The 3% cost level is his estimate (Foundations 1998); the other figures are examples.

themes.title: Accounting, honesty and candour
themes.idea: He wrote as a lawyer who distrusted flattering numbers. The test is always what an absent owner would want to be told.
ask: In each company you own, which reported number depends most on management's own estimate?
Does the annual report read as if written for an absent owner, or for the share price?
themes.caption: Illustrative, after Scandal 2000: moderate dollops are harder to notice than one large one.

themes.title: Adversity, patience and hard work
themes.idea: Setbacks are certain, and many are unfair. What decides a life is the response to them, and the steady work done in between.
ask: Recall your worst year. What did you learn that a good year could not have taught you?
Which loss are you still refusing to accept, and what is that refusal costing?
themes.caption: Illustrative path. Setbacks are certain; what follows them decides the result.

themes.title: The Berkshire system, in his words
themes.idea: In his 2014 essay, written directly to Berkshire shareholders for the first time, he explained why the company had worked.
ask: Which of the companies you own gives managers real autonomy, and how do you know it is deserved?
How much unhurried time for reading and thinking do you protect each week?
themes.caption: After BRK 2014: a small head office and many subsidiaries run with wide autonomy.

t1n1.text: If facts do not hang together on a latticework of theory, you cannot use them when you need them. Build a frame of models from several fields and attach your reading and experience to it.

t1n2.text: A person who knows one model forces every problem into its shape. Narrow training makes this error common.

t1n3.lead: Each field has a few big ideas.
t1n3.text: The truly big ideas in each discipline, learned in essence, carry most of the load. Learning those is far less work than mastering any one field.

t1n4.lead: Learn it the way pilots do.
t1n4.text: Pilots get training wide enough to cover nearly everything useful, use checklists every time, and keep skills fresh in simulators. He wanted professionals educated the same way.

t1n5.text: Give priority to the explanation from the most fundamental discipline, and credit each idea to the field it came from.

t1n6.text: Numerical fluency was one of his five helpful notions. Arithmetic shows what a goal really requires.

t1n7.text: Expect extreme outcomes from combinations of factors acting together, not from one lever.

t1n8.text: He judged bets with the elementary probability of Fermat and Pascal. Accounting helps as well, though it stops describing reality in some cases, such as a shrinking business.

t1n9.lead: Don't worship what can be counted.
t1n9.text: Almost everyone overweighs what can be numbered and neglects what cannot.

t1n10.text: Hoping that economics will behave with the precision of physics gets clever people into terrible trouble.

t1n11.text: Economics pays too little attention to second- and higher-order effects. Follow consequences further than the first step.

t2n1.text: Asked to advise school leavers, he listed sure routes to a miserable life, adding his own to three that Johnny Carson had given years before. Avoiding them is most of the work.

t2n2.text: A countryman wished he knew where he was going to die, so he would never go there. Munger treats the joke as a serious method.

t2n3.text: The mathematician Carl Jacobi advised turning problems around. Munger points to Darwin and Einstein, who made breakthroughs by thinking in reverse.

t2n4.text: Get the needed models into your head, then think each problem through both forward and backward.

t2n5.text: Settle the big, obvious questions first. With those fixed, the rest of a problem often becomes simple.

t2n6.text: When you cannot see how to reach a goal, ask what would make it impossible, and remove that.

t2n7.text: He told law graduates the same thing: turn a problem around and you often think better.

t2n8.text: He usually decided what not to do before choosing what to do. Avoiding large errors beats occasional flashes of brilliance.

t2n9.text: For investments he kept three baskets: yes, no, and too tough to understand. The third basket is large, and he felt no duty to empty it.

t3n1.text: People respond to rewards and punishments far more strongly than they expect, and their beliefs drift to fit what pays.

t3n2.text: Decent people reach conclusions that serve their own income, often without knowing it. Take special care with advice from anyone paid by the action they recommend.

t3n3.text: His example: a delivery company's night shift ran slow until workers were paid per shift and could go home once all the planes were loaded. Pay for time and you get time.

t3n4.text: He called the cash register a great moral instrument. Systems that make cheating hard keep honest people honest.

t3n5.text: Small dishonesty that is tolerated spreads, and becomes very hard to reverse. Stop it at the start.

t3n6.text: Make the pleasant thing the reward for doing the unpleasant thing first.

t3n7.text: Whoever pays the fees must control the advisers. Layers of consultants bring perverse incentives.

t3n8.text: People comply more when given reasons, even weak ones. Give real reasons, and test the reasons you are given.

t3n9.text: Avoid perverse incentive systems, and avoid working directly under someone you do not admire and do not want to be like.

t3n10.text: He traced much corporate misconduct to standard incentive systems working on people below conscious awareness. Wrongdoing that is rewarded dies hard.

t4n1.text: Talks given in 1992, 1994 and 1995 became one. He rewrote it for the book in 2005, at 81, from memory and without fresh research.

t4n2.text: He ran through his own list, tendency by tendency, to explain events that puzzled him. Do the same before an important decision.

t4n3.text: Extreme outcomes come from several tendencies pushing the same way. One of his examples is an airliner evacuation test, run in a darkened hangar with older volunteers, that ended in many injuries.

t4n4.text: People defer to whoever is in charge, even when that person is plainly wrong. In one of his examples, that deference ended in a plane crash.

t4n5.text: Not everything you know about psychology should be used to manipulate people. Anyone who sees through it will hate you for it.

t4n6.text: Under some conditions people behave like lemmings. He said this explains much foolish thinking, in markets as elsewhere.

t4n7.text: He described shares being valued partly like Rembrandt paintings: bought mostly because their prices had already risen so far.

t5n1.text: He began with Johnny Carson's prescriptions for misery: mood-altering chemicals, envy and resentment.

t5n2.text: He cites Disraeli, who learned to give up revenge as a motive, though he kept an outlet for resentment. A grudge mostly harms the person who carries it.

t5n3.text: Envy, resentment, revenge and self-pity: he named them together as disastrous ways of thinking.

t5n4.text: He said envy and jealousy are extreme in modern life. Expect them in others, and watch for them in yourself.

t5n5.text: The standard cure for overactive hostility is to train yourself to delay your response.

t5n6.text: The mind bends facts that are too painful to accept. Notice when you are doing it.

t5n7.text: Light stress can slightly improve performance; heavy stress causes dysfunction. Make big decisions when calm.

t5n8.text: You can cause great offence by being right in a way that makes someone lose face in front of others.

t5n9.text: He warned that extremely intense ideology clouds the mind.

t5n10.text: Have low expectations, keep a sense of humour, and surround yourself with the love of friends and family.

t6n1.text: First on his own list of routes to misery was being unreliable: not faithfully doing what you have promised. He said it can outweigh all your other virtues combined.

t6n2.text: In a 2006 note he repeated that reliability is essential for progress in life, and that almost anyone can learn it to great advantage.

t6n3.text: The safest way to try to get what you want is to try to deserve it.

t6n4.text: He thought no love is so right as love grounded in admiration, and that it should extend to the instructive dead.

t6n5.text: Sell only what you would buy yourself. Work only for people you respect and admire. Work only with people you enjoy.

t6n6.lead: A seamless web of deserved trust.
t6n6.text: In your own life, what you want to maximise is trust that has been earned, all the way round.

t6n7.text: A rule from his years as a lawyer, and one that applies to partners, managers and investments too.

t6n8.text: We overlook the faults of people and things we love. Love admirable people, and still check their work.

t6n9.text: A face-to-face meeting carries too much weight. Underweigh the impression and overweigh the past record.

t6n10.text: People react strongly when they are treated unfairly. Arrangements that feel unfair breed resentment that outlasts the gain.

t7n1.text: He kept seeing people rise who were not always the smartest, but who kept learning. They went to bed each night a little wiser than they were that morning.

t7n2.text: He held that acquiring wisdom is an obligation, not a hobby.

t7n3.text: Without lifetime learning you will not do well. Berkshire's skills from one decade would not have carried it through the next.

t7n4.text: Learning everything from your own experience was on his list of routes to misery. The errors of others are cheaper teachers.

t7n5.text: Admire and learn from the great minds of the past. He counted them among the right objects of love.

t7n6.text: Curiosity drives learning and protects against many other errors.

t7n7.text: Skills fade without practice. Skills practised to fluency last much longer.

t7n8.text: Ageing makes new, complex skills harder to acquire. Keep learning and practising, and learn the difficult things while you can.

t7n9.text: Darwin trained himself early to weigh seriously any evidence against his own hypotheses. Do the same with your beliefs.

t7n10.text: Pilots are made to practise in simulators so skills do not decay. Schedule your own refreshers.

t8n1.text: Everyone has a circle of competence. Play where you have an edge, and stay out of games where others clearly have it.

t8n2.text: Know what you know and what you do not. When you lack competence, say so.

t8n3.text: Work out where your talents lie and use them. Berkshire avoided high technology partly because it had no edge there.

t8n4.text: He said he and Buffett were very good at changing their prior conclusions.

t8n5.lead: Earn the right to an opinion.
t8n5.text: He did not feel entitled to an opinion until he could state the arguments against it better than its supporters could.

t8n6.text: It is in everyone. Use routines and checklists to keep yourself objective.

t8n7.text: He quoted Feynman: the first principle is not to fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.

t8n8.text: Uncertainty is uncomfortable, so the mind grabs an answer early. Slow down before a big decision.

t8n9.text: People expect better outcomes than the odds support. The antidote is habitual use of simple probability.

t8n10.text: What comes to mind easily gets too much weight. Look for the evidence that is dull but large.

t8n11.text: People copy others and defer to authority, most of all when confused or rushed. Those are the moments to slow down.

t9n1.text: He said the great bulk of their money came from the great businesses.

t9n2.lead: Bet heavily when the odds are clear.
t9n2.text: The wise ones bet heavily when the world offers them the opportunity. The rest of the time, they wait.

t9n3.text: Imagine a ticket with only 20 slots for every investment you will ever make. You would think hard and bet big on each one.

t9n4.text: Over long periods a share earns roughly what the business earns. A business earning 18% on capital for 20 or 30 years gives a fine result even bought at an expensive-looking price.

t9n5.text: The way income tax works alone gives a large edge to holding for a long time.

t9n6.text: The investment management business as a whole adds no value for all its clients combined. A select few managers can.

t9n7.text: Judge every use of money against the next-best use available.

t9n8.text: Patience means resisting the natural human bias to do something.

t9n9.text: Someone with nearly all their wealth held long-term in three fine companies is securely rich. Heavy concentration can be a rational choice.

t9n10.text: In super-cat reinsurance, huge swings in annual results, including some very unpleasant years, are inevitable. Judge it over many years.

t9n11.text: In a 2006 note he worried about institutions imitating Harvard and Yale's investing out of envy, and favoured reducing one's perceived needs over taking more risk.

t9n12.text: Among Berkshire's mistakes he named the failure to buy Walmart early.

t10n1.text: Sears's advantages of scale did not stop it losing heavily to Walmart. Bureaucracy did Sears terrible damage.

t10n2.text: In a commodity business, the advantages of great improvements flow through to customers, not to owners.

t10n3.text: Gillette began selling blades in multiple packages, with the razor handle a one-time purchase. Repeat purchases built the business.

t10n4.text: GEICO had a magnificent business submerged in a mess, but still working. Clearing the mess released its value.

t10n5.text: It is 1884 in Atlanta. You have $2 million and must build a business worth $2 trillion. How would you do it?

t10n6.text: He set the target first: 2.92 trillion eight-ounce servings in 2034. Netting 4¢ a serving would earn $117 billion. The numbers show what the business must become.

t10n7.text: A strong trademark, Pavlovian conditioning, social proof and being always available, all working together.

t10n8.text: With New Coke, the company's own executives came to the brink of destroying the most valuable trademark in the world.

t10n9.text: Some businesses produce little cash even when volume holds steady. Borrowing short and lending long, the savings and loan model, can stop working and go into reverse.

t10n10.text: He told owners plainly that his savings and loan, as it then had to be run, was no jewel. Careful operators in that business earned very modest returns.

t10n11.text: In that industry, managers were mostly not owners, and their rewards were tied to size and recent numbers.

t10n12.text: Each dollar of Wesco's book value, he wrote, gave much less intrinsic value than a dollar at Berkshire.

t10n13.text: People underrate both the competence and the morals of competitors they dislike.

t11n1.text: Large institutions hired consultants to choose managers, adding layers with perverse incentives and little clear benefit.

t11n2.text: Counting every layer, total investment costs could easily reach 3% of a foundation's net worth each year.

t11n3.lead: Half must be below the median.
t11n3.text: After the croupiers' take, exactly half of investors get a below-median result. Yet nearly every expert says he is above average.

t11n4.text: Long-Term Capital Management collapsed through overconfidence in its highly leveraged methods.

t11n5.text: He judged indexing a wiser choice for the average foundation than what it was doing.

t11n6.text: The economist J. K. Galbraith wrote of the 'bezzle', wealth that has been embezzled but not yet missed. Munger coined 'febezzle' for wealth quietly lost to wasteful investment fees.

t11n7.text: Constantly pulling money from lagging managers is folly. He put investors' real performance lag at over 5% of assets a year.

t11n8.text: Rising share prices make people feel and spend as if richer, which he warned could produce much mischief.

t12n1.text: He imagined Quant Tech, a prosperous company whose founder died in 1982, and traced how the managers who followed him ruined it by chasing reported earnings.

t12n2.text: Because share options were not counted as a cost, managers could add phony earnings to real ones.

t12n3.text: A moderate dollop of phony earnings each year is less likely to be noticed than one large one.

t12n4.text: Inflated earnings brought a Ponzi or chain-letter effect into the share price, rewarding present holders at later buyers' expense.

t12n5.text: After the scandal, the public turned hard against the professions that had made it possible.

t12n6.text: Each year they tried to tell shareholders what they would want to be told if the roles were reversed.

t12n7.text: Repetition is right where facts stay true and analytically important over many years.

t12n8.text: He labelled a large gain as highly unusual and not likely to recur.

t12n9.lead: Book profit when it is earned.
t12n9.text: Super-cat underwriting profit was recognised only after the contracts expired.

t12n10.text: He told owners to ignore a large non-cash investment gain when judging the year's earnings.

t13n1.text: Staying down after a setback was on his list of routes to misery.

t13n2.text: Life is very likely to deliver terrible, unfair blows. Some people recover and others do not. He cited Epictetus on using each setback well.

t13n3.text: He liked the word because it meant sitting down and staying there until the job is done.

t13n4.text: Losses and near misses provoke outsized reactions. The most addictive forms of gambling are built on near misses.

t13n5.text: Change that arrives in small steps escapes notice, because each step is a small contrast with the last.

t14n1.text: He credited the constructive peculiarities of Buffett, the constructive peculiarities of the Berkshire system, good luck, and the intense devotion of some shareholders and admirers.

t14n2.text: Buffett's decision to limit himself to a few kinds of activity, and keep at them for 50 years, worked like a lollapalooza. Munger compared it to Roger Federer's tennis.

t14n3.lead: Each company keeps its own systems.
t14n3.text: There is no group-wide personnel, stock option, incentive or retirement system. Subsidiaries run their own.

t14n4.text: Buffett set out to minimise the bad effects that almost always come from a large bureaucracy at headquarters.

t14n5.text: He wanted win/win results everywhere, for instance gaining loyalty by giving it.

t14n6.lead: A narrow job at the top.
t14n6.text: The chairman keeps few tasks: managing nearly all the security investments, writing a long, useful letter as he would want it as a passive shareholder, answering questions for hours, and admiring what others achieve.

t14n7.text: No other large company he knew had half these elements. Most have heavy bureaucracy and chief executives who arrive at about 59 and are soon retired by an age limit.

t14n8.text: He named Ajit Jain and Greg Abel as proven performers.

quotes.label: USC 1994
quotes.text: To the man with only a hammer, every problem looks like a nail.

quotes.label: HLS 1998
quotes.text: Broadscale problems, by definition, cross many academic disciplines.

quotes.label: HS 1986, quoting Jacobi
quotes.text: Invert, always invert.

quotes.label: PHM 2005
quotes.text: Incentives are superpowers.

quotes.label: USC Law 2007
quotes.text: Generally speaking, envy, resentment, revenge, and self-pity are disastrous modes of thought.

quotes.label: Stanford 1996
quotes.text: Don't sell anything you wouldn't buy yourself.

quotes.label: UCSB 2003, explaining why, with no economics training, he would lecture economists
quotes.text: The answer is I have a black belt in chutzpah.

quotes.label: Foundations 1998, on the view that wide diversification is a must
quotes.text: I think the orthodox view is grossly mistaken.

quotes.label: Wesco 1996
quotes.text: super-cat reinsurance is not for the faint of heart

quotes.label: Scandal 2000, the old saying he applies to compliant accountants
quotes.text: Whose bread I eat, his song I sing.

quotes.label: Blue Chip 1982
quotes.text: if the roles were reversed and we were passive investors

quotes.label: BRK 2014
quotes.text: the weirdly intense, contagious devotion of some shareholders

tendencies.name: Reward- and punishment-superresponse
tendencies.what: Incentives move people more than they expect.
tendencies.guard: Get incentives right; distrust paid advice.

tendencies.name: Liking/loving
tendencies.what: We favour those we like and overlook their faults.
tendencies.guard: Admire the right people; see them clearly.

tendencies.name: Disliking/hating
tendencies.what: We ignore the merits of those we dislike.
tendencies.guard: Judge disliked rivals fairly.

tendencies.name: Doubt-avoidance
tendencies.what: We rush to any answer to end uncertainty.
tendencies.guard: Slow down; hear both sides.

tendencies.name: Inconsistency-avoidance
tendencies.what: We cling to past conclusions and habits.
tendencies.guard: Seek evidence against yourself; stop bad habits early.

tendencies.name: Curiosity
tendencies.what: The urge to know, mostly a help.
tendencies.guard: Feed it for life.

tendencies.name: Kantian fairness
tendencies.what: We expect fair treatment and resent its absence.
tendencies.guard: Design arrangements that feel fair.

tendencies.name: Envy/jealousy
tendencies.what: Others' gains provoke conflict.
tendencies.guard: Name it in yourself; allow for it in others.

tendencies.name: Reciprocation
tendencies.what: We return favours and hostility automatically.
tendencies.guard: Delay angry replies; refuse gifts that buy judgment.

tendencies.name: Influence-from-mere-association
tendencies.what: We credit or blame whatever sits near an outcome.
tendencies.guard: Check past wins for luck; welcome bad news.

tendencies.name: Simple, pain-avoiding psychological denial
tendencies.what: We bend facts that hurt.
tendencies.guard: Face reality; avoid habits that feed denial.

tendencies.name: Excessive self-regard
tendencies.what: We overrate ourselves and what is ours.
tendencies.guard: Trust records over impressions.

tendencies.name: Overoptimism
tendencies.what: We expect better than the odds.
tendencies.guard: Use simple probability.

tendencies.name: Deprival-superreaction
tendencies.what: Losses and near misses hurt far more than gains please.
tendencies.guard: Watch for irrational fights over small losses.

tendencies.name: Social-proof
tendencies.what: We copy others, most of all when confused.
tendencies.guard: Be wary when everyone agrees and you are rushed.

tendencies.name: Contrast-misreaction
tendencies.what: We judge by nearby comparisons.
tendencies.guard: Measure against absolute worth.

tendencies.name: Stress-influence
tendencies.what: Heavy stress distorts thinking.
tendencies.guard: Decide big things when calm.

tendencies.name: Availability-misweighing
tendencies.what: Vivid, recent facts get too much weight.
tendencies.guard: Use a checklist; seek the dull, large facts.

tendencies.name: Use-it-or-lose-it
tendencies.what: Unpractised skills fade.
tendencies.guard: Practise to fluency.

tendencies.name: Drug-misinfluence
tendencies.what: Chemicals distort judgment.
tendencies.guard: Avoid them.

tendencies.name: Senescence-misinfluence
tendencies.what: Age makes new complex skills harder.
tendencies.guard: Keep learning; learn hard things early.

tendencies.name: Authority-misinfluence
tendencies.what: We obey authority even when it is wrong.
tendencies.guard: Choose leaders carefully; question orders.

tendencies.name: Twaddle
tendencies.what: Empty talk crowds out real work.
tendencies.guard: Keep it away from serious tasks.

tendencies.name: Reason-respecting
tendencies.what: We comply when given reasons, even weak ones.
tendencies.guard: Give real reasons; test the reasons you are given.

tendencies.name: Lollapalooza
tendencies.what: Several tendencies acting together cause extreme results.
tendencies.guard: Look for confluences, the source of most disasters.

plan.label: Misjudgment

map: Before you decide
Run the checklist of models. Invert: how would this fail? Which tendencies are acting on you right now?
When you invest
Few, great, mispriced. Bet heavily when the odds are clear. Then sit, and keep costs and taxes low.
With other people
Look at incentives first. Be reliable. Deserve what you want. Choose people you admire.
Inside your head
Refuse envy, resentment, revenge and self-pity. Hunt for evidence against your own views.
Every day
Learn something. Go to bed a little wiser. Keep the habit for life.

munger.about: Only Charlie Munger's own talks and letters: the eleven talks in Poor Charlie's Almanack, his letters to Wesco Financial and Blue Chip Stamps shareholders, and his 2014 essay in Berkshire's annual report.

lynch.name: Peter Lynch
lynch.what: His books, talks and interviews on finding good stocks as an ordinary investor
lynch.unitsLede: Each source: what it is most worth reading for, its one short line, the ideas it contributes, and your own notes.
lynch.scope: Lynch wrote three books, all with John Rothchild. One Up on Wall Street is split here into its three parts plus the new introduction of 2000. Three recorded talks and interviews add his own spoken words. Magazine columns and paraphrased quotes found online are left out.
lynch.readHow: The books are in print; borrow or buy them. The 1996 interview transcript is free at PBS and the 2023 interview at Yahoo Finance.

start.lede: Peter Lynch ran Fidelity's Magellan Fund from 1977 to 1990, averaging 29.2% a year, about double the S&P 500. He retired at 46 and spent the following decades teaching ordinary people to pick stocks the way he did: look around, sort, check, explain, then own.
start.para: This section covers his three books, a 1994 talk, a 1996 TV interview and a 2023 interview. Expect about an hour a week for twelve weeks: one step of his method here, then the chapter or talk it comes from.
steps: Walk his five-step path
The stock-picker's path: from spotting a company to owning it.
Play the six-kinds game
Sort twelve invented companies into his six kinds of stock.
Read your first source
His 1996 interview is free online and full of stories and figures.
Write a two-minute drill
Explain one company you know, against the clock.

glossary: A stock that rises tenfold. His baseball term: two home runs and a double.
A large, mature company growing about as fast as the economy, owned for its dividend.
A big, established company growing earnings about 10 to 12% a year.
A small, aggressive company growing 20 to 25% a year. His favourite kind.
A company whose profits rise and fall with the economy.
A battered company that might recover.
A company sitting on something valuable that the market has missed.
The P/E divided by the earnings growth rate. Around 1 is fair; well below 1 may be a bargain.
His word for a profitable company buying unrelated businesses and making itself worse.
A short spoken case for a stock: why you like it, what must happen, what could go wrong.
