themes.title: The amateur's edge
themes.idea: An ordinary person who keeps their eyes open often spots a good company years before the professionals do.
ask: Which three companies do you know better than most analysts, because of your work or daily life?
For one of them, what would you still need to check before buying?

stories.x: He started caddying at 11 at a golf club where members talked about stocks. He caddied for Fidelity's president for years, which, he said, made his job interview a formality.

themes.caption: Illustrative. The order in which a good small company tends to get noticed: by customers and staff first, by Wall Street last.

themes.title: Is it gambling? Stocks and your stomach
themes.idea: Stocks reward patient owners of good companies; the real test is your stomach, not your brain.
ask: If your portfolio fell 25% next month, what would you actually do?
Which of your money will you not need for at least five years?

stories.x: He was on his first holiday in years when the market fell 508 points in a day, and he flew home. He later said 1987 didn't frighten him much, because his companies were still doing well; 1990 was far scarier.

themes.caption: Each dot is one market decline of 10% or more in 95 years, as he counted them in 1996. The 15 darker dots were falls of 25% or more.

themes.title: Look in your own backyard
themes.idea: The best leads come from everyday life: the store you like, the product people keep buying, the trend at your job.
ask: Name a product you or your family keep buying again. Who makes it, and is that company listed?
Which trend at your job could you understand before Wall Street does?

stories.t: The pantyhose in the shopping bag
stories.x: His wife Carolyn brought home L'eggs pantyhose, sold in supermarkets. He found good hosiery was then sold mainly in department stores, and when a rival appeared he bought 48 pairs to compare. Hanes became one of his biggest holdings.
Taco Bell was one of his early picks; he was impressed by the burrito on a trip to California.

themes.caption: Illustrative. Where his best leads came from, and the step every lead still needs.

themes.title: The six kinds of stock
themes.idea: Before buying, decide which of six kinds of stock you are looking at; that tells you what to expect and when to sell.
ask: Pick a company you know. Which of the six kinds is it, and what does that tell you to expect?
What would make it move into a different kind?

stories.x: In October 1982, on Wall Street Week, he recommended Chrysler, then his biggest holding, at about $10 a share. Friends thought it was headed for bankruptcy.

themes.caption: His three growth bands, plus three kinds defined by their situation. Growth rates are his rough guides.

themes.title: The perfect stock, and the ones to avoid
themes.idea: He looked for dull, overlooked companies in boring niches, and stayed away from the hottest story in town.
ask: How many of the 13 traits does a company you like actually have?
Is anything you own “the hottest stock in the hottest industry”?

themes.title: Earnings are the engine
themes.idea: Over months the price can do anything; over years it follows the company's earnings.
ask: What, specifically, will make your company's earnings grow over the next five years?
Have you ever judged a decision only by the price? What did you miss?
themes.caption: Illustrative. Over months the price wanders above and below the company's earnings; over years it follows them.

themes.title: The famous numbers
themes.idea: A few simple numbers tell you whether a good company is also a good price.
ask: Work out the P/E-to-growth figure for one company you follow. What does it say?
Where did the growth rate come from, and how sure are you of it?
themes.caption: His rule of thumb for the P/E compared with the growth rate. A guide, not a formula.

themes.title: Balance sheet first
themes.idea: The biggest losses come from weak balance sheets; know a company's finances before you risk money on it.
ask: Which company you like could survive two bad years without raising money?
Find one number on a balance sheet you have never checked before. What does it tell you?
themes.caption: His 2023 example: two companies both losing money. Only one can wait out the bad patch.

themes.title: The two-minute drill
themes.idea: If you can't explain why you own a stock in two minutes, simply enough for a child, you don't know enough to own it.
ask: Give your two-minute drill for one company, out loud. Where did you get stuck?
What has to happen for it to succeed, and what could stop it?

stories.x: Beating the Street opens with a class of seventh graders at St. Agnes School in Massachusetts, who built a stock portfolio from companies they understood. Their lessons led him to the crayon test.

themes.caption: The three parts of his two-minute monologue.

themes.title: Ten-baggers: let the winners run
themes.idea: You only need a few big winners in a lifetime, so let them run and don't cut the flowers to water the weeds.
ask: Have you ever sold a winner early to “lock in” a gain? What happened next?
Which holding is your weed, and why are you still watering it?

stories.x: In college he put about $1,000 into Flying Tiger, an air-cargo company, because he thought air freight would grow. It rose about tenfold and helped pay for graduate school.

themes.caption: The most you can lose on a stock is 100%. A ten-bagger gains 900%.

themes.title: Don't time the market
themes.idea: Nobody can predict the economy or the next fall; study companies, not forecasts.
ask: When did a forecast last change one of your decisions? Was it right?
What will you do the next time the market falls 10%?
themes.caption: His 1996 example, 1965 to 1995: putting money in at each year's high still earned almost as much as at each year's low.

themes.title: Keep checking the story
themes.idea: Hold as long as the story holds; recheck it every few months, and sell when the story, not the price, changes.
ask: For each company you own: has the story changed since you bought it?
Which holding are you keeping only out of boredom, or only because it hasn't come back yet?

stories.x: In 2023 he said his biggest regret was not buying Apple when the shares were around $9 with no debt and $4 to $5 a share in cash.

themes.caption: Illustrative. A company's life: the right question is always which stage it is in now.

t1n1.text: He argued that any normal person can pick stocks as well as the average Wall Street expert, using what they already see at work and in the shops.

t1n2.text: Many fund managers fear looking bad more than they want to win, so they avoid small, unknown companies until everyone already knows them.

t1n3.tags: 1989 One Up I · 1993 Beating the Street
t1n3.lead: Your edge is where you work and shop.
t1n3.text: Your job, your industry and the products you use every day can show you which companies are winning before the numbers reach Wall Street.

t1n4.text: He never said to buy a stock just because you like the product or the store. You still have to study the company's earnings, finances and competition.

t1n5.text: He called this the single most important thing, and reckoned about 80% of people own stocks they couldn't explain.

t1n6.text: In 2023 he repeated that he never told people simply to put money into the market. Knowing a company is step one; reading its balance sheet is step two.

t2n1.text: Stocks are a gamble only if you pick them like lottery tickets. Behind every stock is a business, and businesses that earn more become worth more.

t2n2.text: With a bond, the best you can hope for is your money back plus interest. Over the long run, stocks with dividends returned about 11% a year, against 5 to 6% for bonds.

t2n3.text: Company profits have grown about 8% a year over time, which is why stocks rise in the long run, even after flat decades.

t2n4.lead: Bad picks are worse than cash.
t2n4.text: Over the long run, a portfolio of poorly chosen stocks won't beat money left under the mattress.

t2n5.text: Markets fall often: he counted 53 declines of 10% or more in 95 years, 15 of them of 25% or more. If you can't sit through that, don't own stocks.

t2n6.text: Buy, hold and add when the market falls, but only with money you won't need soon.

t2n7.text: If a sharp drop would keep you awake at night, he said in 2023, you shouldn't be investing in stocks.

t2n8.lead: Start with how the world works.
t2n8.text: His beginner's book opens with the history of companies and capitalism, because investing makes sense only once you see what a company is.

t3n1.text: He believed the best place to start looking for the next winner is your own backyard: home, work and the shops.

t3n2.text: A product that friends, family or colleagues keep coming back to is a clue worth following up.

t3n3.text: One of his principles: if you like the store, chances are you'll love the stock. Then check the numbers.

t3n4.text: His biggest wins often came from small companies with room to grow. In 2023 he cited Au Bon Pain, which bought St. Louis Bread for $23 million in 1993; it later sold for $7.5 billion.

t3n5.lead: A hit product is not enough.
t3n5.text: The Cabbage Patch doll was a huge hit, but it couldn't save a mediocre company with a bad balance sheet.

t3n6.text: The more companies you look at, the more bargains you find. His early winners came from industries others ignored.

t3n7.text: An individual can do well by knowing three to five companies thoroughly and buying when one becomes attractive.

t4n1.text: Every company fits one of six kinds: slow growers, stalwarts, fast growers, cyclicals, turnarounds and asset plays.

t4n2.text: Large, ageing companies growing about as fast as the economy. You own them mainly for the dividend: low risk, low gain.

t4n3.text: Big, established companies growing earnings about 10 to 12% a year: low risk, moderate gain. He expected perhaps 30 to 50% from them, and liked them for protection in recessions.

t4n4.text: Small, aggressive companies growing 20 to 25% a year. His favourites and the land of ten- to forty-baggers, but the riskiest when growth stops.

t4n5.text: Companies whose profits rise and fall with the economy. With these, timing matters more than anywhere else.

t4n6.text: Battered companies that might recover. They can make big gains, as Chrysler did in the early 1980s, but many never come back.

t4n7.text: Companies sitting on something valuable the market has missed, such as property, cash or a business inside the business.

t4n8.text: Fast growers eventually slow down and become stalwarts or slow growers, so check the label again from time to time.

t5n1.text: The perfect company has a boring, even ridiculous name and does something dull or disagreeable, so the crowd ignores it.

t5n2.text: Big institutions don't own it and analysts don't follow it. A spinoff, or a company with a depressing or rumour-ridden image, often qualifies.

t5n3.text: A no-growth industry, a protected niche and a product people have to keep buying are all good signs.

t5n4.text: When insiders buy their own shares, or the company buys back stock, management is showing confidence. Heavy insider buying makes a near-term bankruptcy very unlikely.

t5n5.text: He preferred companies that use technology to cut their costs over companies racing to sell it.

t5n6.text: The hottest stock in the hottest industry, the one everyone talks about, is the one he would avoid most.

t5n7.text: Stocks touted as the next big name rarely are, and profitable companies that buy unrelated businesses usually make themselves worse.

t5n8.text: Long shots with thrilling stories and no earnings, and companies with exciting names in hot fields, attract buyers for the wrong reasons.

t5n9.text: Half joking: all else equal, invest in the company with the fewest colour photographs in its annual report.

t6n1.lead: Short term, no link; long term, a full link.
t6n1.text: Over months or even years there is often no connection between how a company does and how its stock does. Over the long term, the connection is complete.

t6n2.text: Something has to keep the profits growing; the more you know about that something, the better.

t6n3.text: A rising price doesn't mean you were right, and a falling one doesn't mean you were wrong. Only the business can tell you that.

t6n4.text: Time is on your side when you own shares of superior companies, and against you when you own options.

t6n5.lead: Even ten years late can be early.
t6n5.text: Investors who bought Wal-Mart ten years after its 1970 listing could still have made about 30 times their money by following its expansion.

t6n6.lead: The stock doesn't know you own it.
t6n6.text: Don't fall in love with a share. Stay while the company's fundamentals hold, and leave if they break.

t7n1.lead: P/E equal to growth is fair.
t7n1.text: A fairly priced company's P/E roughly equals its earnings growth rate. A P/E well below the growth rate may be a bargain; well above it, a warning.

t7n2.lead: Half is attractive, double is dear.
t7n2.text: A P/E around half the growth rate looked very attractive to him; around twice the growth rate, very unattractive.

t7n3.text: For dividend payers, add the yield to the growth rate and divide by the P/E. Below 1 is poor, about 1.5 is okay, and 2 or better is what you want.

t7n4.text: Check how much cash the company holds against its long-term debt. Plenty of net cash cushions the bad years.

t7n5.text: The fewer institutions own it and the fewer analysts follow it, the more room there is for discovery.

t7n6.lead: Do the arithmetic, even without earnings.
t7n6.text: For a company with no profits yet, work out what it would need to earn later to justify today's price.

t7n7.text: A $3 stock can go to zero just like a $50 one. A lousy cheap stock is as risky as a lousy expensive one.

t8n1.text: Never invest in a company without understanding its finances. The biggest losses come from companies with poor balance sheets.

t8n2.text: In 2023 he compared two loss-making companies: one with $300 million of debt, one with no debt and $200 million in cash.

t8n3.text: In a downturn, a company with little debt can wait; one with heavy debt may not. That matters most for turnarounds and cyclicals.

t8n4.text: His beginner's book teaches how to read a stock table, an annual report and a balance sheet, before trusting anyone else's summary.

t8n5.text: Before buying, check the earnings prospects, financial condition, competitive position and plans for expansion.

t8n6.text: A lavish head office can signal managers who care more about themselves than about shareholders.

t9n1.text: Before buying, he talked himself through why he was interested, what had to happen for the company to succeed, and what could get in the way.

t9n2.text: If you can't explain to a ten-year-old, in two minutes or less, why you own a stock, he said, you shouldn't own it.

t9n3.text: If you couldn't draw the idea with a crayon, he wouldn't invest in it.

t9n4.lead: Each kind has its own story.
t9n4.text: For a slow grower the story is the dividend; for a fast grower, where it can still expand; for a turnaround, how it will fix itself; for an asset play, what the assets are worth.

t9n5.text: For beginners in 2023 he suggested a paper portfolio of at least ten stocks, a few written reasons for each, reviewed every three months.

t9n6.lead: “It's going up” is not a reason.
t9n6.text: Pressed, many owners admit their real reason is that the stock is rising, which is no reason at all.

t10n1.text: His baseball term for a stock that goes up tenfold: two home runs and a double.

t10n2.text: You don't need many. A handful of tenfold winners in a lifetime makes investing worthwhile.

t10n3.text: A good stock picker is right about six times in ten, so the winners must be allowed to outgrow the losers.

t10n4.text: Selling your winners and keeping your losers is like pulling out the flowers and watering the weeds. Buffett liked the image enough to use it in his 1988 letter.

t10n5.text: He did well by owning many stocks, letting winners run and adding to them, even though Magellan missed more than a hundred ten-baggers.

t10n6.lead: Look at what you own first.
t10n6.text: The best stock to buy may be one you already own; check it before hunting for something new.

t10n7.text: Whatever you pay, picking the wrong stock costs at most the same 100%. A ten-bagger gains 900%.

t11n1.text: Spend little time on economic forecasts: he joked that 13 minutes a year on economics wastes ten of them.

t11n2.text: Watch the facts in the industries you own, such as used-car prices for carmakers or new hotel building for hotel chains.

t11n3.text: In 1982 inflation was 14%, the prime rate 20% and over half his companies were losing money. The great bull market began that year.

t11n4.text: Investing every year at the year's high from 1965 to 1995 earned about 10.6% a year; at the year's low, about 11.7%.

t11n5.text: Falls happen and no one knows when. People who say they predicted one predicted many others too.

t11n6.text: Half joking, he described four stages of a market, from guests avoiding him at parties to everyone giving him tips. He did not use it to predict.

t11n7.text: Unless you sell short for a living, it rarely pays to be a pessimist about the long run.

t11n8.text: Study history to learn that markets go down, and decide in advance that a fall is a chance to buy, not a reason to run.

t12n1.text: Even a long-term owner has to keep following the company. Stories end, for example when a business saturates its market.

t12n2.text: Companies pass through stages, from start-up to fast growth to maturity. The key question is which stage yours is in.

t12n3.text: The right exit depends on the kind of stock: a stalwart after a solid rise, a fast grower when its room to expand runs out, a turnaround once it has turned around.

t12n4.text: Give up on a stock because nothing is happening and, all too often, things start to happen the day after you sell.

t12n5.text: Cheap commissions are no reason to trade. Buying three stocks a day and selling them on Friday is gambling, not investing.

t12n6.text: A part-time picker can follow eight to twelve companies, with no more than five in the portfolio at any one time.

t12n7.text: In 2000 he warned that few dot-com buyers get the full ride, because the early gains happen before most people can buy.

t12n8.text: Don't take on more than you can handle.

lynch.sourcesNote: Only Peter Lynch's own words: his three books (written with John Rothchild), his 1994 National Press Club talk, his 1996 PBS interview and his 2023 Yahoo Finance interview. Ideas are summarised in our own words. Each source gives at most one short exact line, checked against the original text or a published copy. Magellan's record is as reported by Fidelity and repeated by Lynch; it covers his 13 years only, and fund size includes new money from investors, not just gains. The sorting game uses invented companies. Facts were checked against at least two sources.
disclaimer: For education only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.

The tools (sorting game, price check, checklist, ten-bagger maths) are teaching aids built from his published rules of thumb. They are not valuation models and must not be used as the basis for a decision.

Accuracy is not guaranteed and errors are possible; treat the original sources as correct. No liability is accepted for any loss arising from use of this material. Past results do not predict future ones.

lynch.about: Only Peter Lynch's own books, his 1994 National Press Club talk, his 1996 PBS interview and his 2023 Yahoo Finance interview. Unlike Buffett and Munger, he was a public fund manager who wrote for ordinary investors, so this section is built around doing: a five-step path, hands-on tools and stories from his notebook.

scenarios.text: A century-old electricity utility. Earnings rise about 3% a year and it has raised its dividend for decades.
scenarios.why: Growth about in line with the economy, owned for the dividend.

scenarios.text: A giant soft-drink maker, known worldwide, growing earnings about 11% a year.
scenarios.why: Big, steady and growing in the low teens: a classic stalwart.

scenarios.text: A young restaurant chain with 60 outlets in one region, adding 20 a year, earnings up 25% a year.
scenarios.why: Small, aggressive and growing 20–25%, with plenty of room to expand.

scenarios.text: A steelmaker whose profits soared last year and collapsed in the recession before that.
scenarios.why: Profits follow the economy up and down.

scenarios.text: An airline that lost money for three years, has a new boss, and has cut costs and debt.
scenarios.why: A battered company trying to recover.

scenarios.text: A sleepy department store whose shares are worth less than the city-centre land it owns.
scenarios.why: The land is the hidden value the market has missed.

scenarios.text: A carmaker whose sales jump when the economy booms and slump in recessions.
scenarios.why: Car sales rise and fall with the economy.

scenarios.text: A household-products giant: toothpaste and soap, earnings up about 10% a year.
A railroad that dominated its region for 80 years; growth now matches the economy.
scenarios.why: Once a fast grower, now mature.

scenarios.text: A software firm with a single hit product, growing 30% a year from a small base.
scenarios.why: Rapid growth from a small base, the land of the ten-baggers.

scenarios.text: A firm that emerged from bankruptcy with a slimmer business and no debt.
A small conglomerate holding cash worth two-thirds of its share price, plus a profitable side business.
scenarios.why: Cash and a business inside the business: an asset play.

bolton.what: His book, interviews and articles on contrarian stock picking
bolton.scope: Bolton wrote one book of his own and contributed a chapter of lessons to Jonathan Davis's study of his career. Articles and interviews add his spoken words. Where a point comes from a journalist's summary rather than his own text, the source is named.
bolton.readHow: Both books are in print or easy to find second-hand. The Spectator article, the MoneyWeek interview and the 2025 podcast are free online.
bolton.sourcesNote: Sources: his book (2009), Jonathan Davis's study with his own lessons chapter (2004), his Spectator article (2007), interviews with MoneyWeek and Norges Bank's In Good Company podcast (2025), and press coverage of his China fund. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

start.lede: Anthony Bolton ran Fidelity Special Situations from December 1979 to December 2007, about 19.5% a year, well ahead of the UK market. His method: buy good companies the crowd has given up on, write down why you own each one, meet the managers, and sell when the reason breaks.
start.para: This page draws on his book Investing Against the Tide, a study of his methods by Jonathan Davis, his own Spectator article, and interviews up to 2025. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

glossary: An investor who deliberately goes against the crowd: buying what is unloved and selling what is loved.
The short written reason for owning a share.
The written case against your own idea: what would make it a bad investment.
A company in trouble whose shares are priced as if it will never recover.
The value of a whole company, shares plus debt minus cash, divided by profits before interest, tax and depreciation.
Cash a company has left after investing, as a percentage of its value.
Studying price charts and trading patterns, rather than the business itself.
Companies going through change: recovery, takeover, restructuring or neglect.
Borrowing money to invest more than you have. It magnifies both gains and losses.

themes.title: The contrarian's edge
themes.idea: The best bargains are usually in companies the crowd has given up on. The hard part is buying when it feels uncomfortable.
ask: Which company do most people around you dislike right now? Do they have a good reason?
Could you hold a share for two years while everyone says you are wrong?
themes.caption: He bought as the mood bottomed out and sold as it became euphoric, never on mood alone.

themes.title: Write down why you own it
themes.idea: Every share you own needs a reason you can write in a few lines, and a written case against it.
ask: Can you write in three lines why you own each of your shares?
What would have to happen for you to admit you were wrong?

themes.title: What is already in the price
themes.idea: Look for a gap between price and value, measured in several ways, then give it time to close.
ask: Which two measures would you use to value a business you know well?
How long are you prepared to wait for a cheap share to be noticed?

themes.title: Meet the managers
themes.idea: He learnt most by meeting the people who run companies, again and again, and writing everything down.
ask: What would you most want to ask the boss of a company you own?
How would you tell whether a manager is being candid?

themes.title: What makes a good company
themes.idea: Start with the quality of the business, then ask whether it will be worth more in ten years.
ask: Which company you know will clearly be worth more in ten years? Why?
What could take a company's destiny out of its own hands?

themes.title: Where the analysts are not
themes.idea: Medium and smaller companies, and those analysts have given up on, are where mispricing lives.
ask: Name a company you know that almost nobody writes about.
Why might a small company be priced less efficiently than a giant one?

themes.title: Charts as a second opinion
themes.idea: Research comes first. He used price charts to confirm it and to time his buying and selling, never on their own.
ask: What could a ten-year chart tell you that a one-year chart hides?
When might relying on charts alone mislead you?

themes.title: When to sell
themes.idea: Sell when the reason for owning breaks, when the price reaches your target, or when you find something better.
ask: Which of your holdings would you sell today if you were starting from cash?
Have you ever held a share only to get back to even?

themes.title: Know yourself
themes.idea: Temperament matters more than intelligence. Find an approach that fits your nature, then stick with it.
ask: Are you calm or anxious when your shares fall? What does that tell you about your style?
What kind of investing would you actually stick with for ten years?

themes.title: Even legends stumble
themes.idea: His China fund went badly at first. How he explained it teaches as much as his years of success.
ask: What would you check more carefully before investing in a country you don't know?
Why might borrowing to invest turn a bad year into a terrible one?

t1n1.text: When everyone likes a share, the good news is already in the price. When everyone hates it, a little good news can lift it a lot.

t1n2.text: He bought recovery shares before all the information was in, a place he called the discomfort zone.

t1n3.text: He warned that buying too early is a common mistake. Be patient with your entry, and add more only when conviction is high.

t1n4.text: In the late 1990s he refused internet shares. His fund lagged the market by almost 20% before the bubble burst and proved him right.

t1n5.text: Going against the crowd only pays when you know why the crowd is wrong. A share can be unpopular for good reasons.

t2n1.text: Know what you own and why, in words simple enough to explain to a friend.

t2n2.text: He went back to each thesis at regular intervals to check that it still held.

t2n3.text: He also wrote down what could make the share a bad investment, and worked out why he disagreed with the doubters.

t2n4.text: He made a point of listening to people with the opposite view, to stress-test his own.

t2n5.text: The price you paid says nothing about what a share is worth today.

t3n1.text: He bought where the price looked out of line with what the company was worth, then waited for the gap to close.

t3n2.text: Price to earnings, company value to cash profits, free cash flow yield, price to sales and cash returns on investment, each against history and against other companies.

t3n3.lead: The right tool for the job.
t3n3.text: For housebuilders he thought price to earnings nearly useless, because one-off land sales distort profits. Price to adjusted book value worked better.

t3n4.text: Seeing a mispricing is easier than knowing when it will correct. Some ideas took one year, some several.

t3n5.text: Share prices and profits can drift apart for a year or two. Keep testing the idea rather than giving up on it.

t4n1.text: He met two or three companies every working day and valued hearing from managers directly.

t4n2.text: He handwrote notes in every meeting and kept them all from the late 1980s onwards.

t4n3.text: He looked for managers who were candid and consistent. Like Buffett, he believed a boss who misleads shareholders may end up misleading himself.

t4n4.text: Repeated follow-up meetings, not first impressions, uncovered the occasional gem.

t4n5.text: In the 2003 Carlton–Granada merger he pressed for an independent chairman. The press nicknamed him the Quiet Assassin, a name he disliked.

t5n1.text: Begin by judging how strong the business franchise is.

t5n2.text: Ask whether the company will still be here in ten years, and be more valuable.

t5n3.text: Prefer companies in control of their own destiny, rather than at the mercy of others.

t5n4.text: Check that the people in charge understand the business strategically, operationally and financially.

t6n1.text: He leaned towards medium and smaller companies, which fewer analysts followed.

t6n2.text: He liked companies that analysts had given up on, with few or no profit forecasts.

t6n3.text: Owning many cheap, mid-sized companies meant some would be bid for. His book has a whole chapter on why it is good to have your shares bought out.

t6n4.text: His book has chapters on where to find information and on the value of good brokers: do the reading others skip.

t7n1.text: He used charts to confirm his research, not to replace it.

t7n2.text: He found charts most useful on bigger companies, to time buying and selling once the research was done.

t7n3.text: He compared checking a chart to a visit to the doctor: being too early in a share can be costly.

t7n4.text: Charts, shareholder lists and directors' dealings all helped him judge where the crowd already stood.

t8n1.text: Something breaks the thesis; the share reaches his valuation target; or he finds a better idea.

t8n2.text: Holding a loser just to win back what you lost, or to prove the original idea right, is dangerous.

t8n3.text: Even if the share now looks cheap, a broken reason is a reason to go.

t8n4.text: When a share becomes everyone's favourite, the risk has risen even if the story has not changed.

t9n1.text: He believed emotional people do not make good investors, however clever they are.

t9n2.text: Find an approach that suits your personality, and keep to it through good and bad years.

t9n3.text: He ran the fund on his own judgement rather than hugging the index, which is why it could look so different from the market.

t9n4.text: He drew on the widest possible range of facts and opinions, but the final call was always his own judgement.

t10n1.text: In 2010 he came out of retirement to launch a China fund, a market he had not invested in before.

t10n2.text: He blamed a focus on smaller companies, too much weight in consumer shares, and borrowing to invest, all of which hurt in a falling market.

t10n3.text: Accounting scandals at some Chinese companies listed in the US also hurt. Familiar methods need new checks in an unfamiliar market.

t10n4.text: He apologised to investors for poor results. By the time he retired in 2014 the trust had just about turned a profit.

smith.name: Terry Smith
smith.what: His letters, rules and books on owning the best companies and doing nothing
smith.scope: Smith writes plainly and often. The Owner's Manual and the annual letters are free on Fundsmith's website; his Financial Times columns and letters to 2020 are collected in Investing for Growth. Accounting for Growth (1992) is out of print but easy to find second-hand.
smith.readHow: Start with the Owner's Manual (about twenty pages) and the latest annual letter. Both are free.
smith.sourcesNote: Sources: the Fundsmith Owner's Manual (2010), the annual letters (2010 to 2025, figures from the 2025 letter), 'Ten golden rules of investment' (Financial Times, 2013), Accounting for Growth (1992) and Investing for Growth (2020). Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

start.lede: Terry Smith exposed creative accounting in 1992 and was sacked for refusing to withdraw his book. In 2010 he founded Fundsmith on three rules: buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing. Since launch it has returned 13.8% a year against 12.1% for world shares, though it trailed the market every year from 2021 to 2025.
start.para: This page draws on the Fundsmith Owner's Manual, his sixteen annual letters, his ten golden rules and his two books. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the letter or chapter it comes from.

glossary: Operating profit as a percentage of the money tied up in a business. His main test of quality.
Sales minus the direct cost of making them, as a percentage of sales.
Profit after running costs, before interest and tax, as a percentage of sales.
How much of the reported profit actually arrives as cash.
How many times profits cover the interest bill.
The cash a company produces after investment, as a percentage of its value.
The share of a portfolio bought and sold in a year.
All the costs of owning a fund, including dealing costs, not just the headline charge.
A fund that simply buys a whole market index rather than choosing companies.
Legal but misleading ways of making profits look bigger or smoother than they are.

units.title: Fundsmith Equity Fund Owner's Manual
units.date: Fundsmith, first published 2010 and essentially unchanged since.
units.summary: The rulebook: what the fund buys, what it never does, and why the biggest risk to your returns is you.

units.title: Annual letters to fund owners
units.date: Sixteen letters, January each year. Figures on this page are from the 2025 letter.
units.summary: Each letter gives the results, the portfolio's quality numbers, the biggest winners and losers, and plain explanations when things go wrong.

units.title: Ten golden rules of investment
units.date: Financial Times, 15 February 2013, republished by Fundsmith.
units.summary: His ten rules for private investors, from 'if you don't understand it, don't invest' to 'switch off the screen'.

units.title: Accounting for Growth
units.summary: The book that exposed how British companies of the 1980s flattered their profits, and cost him his job.

units.title: Investing for Growth
units.date: Harriman House, 2020: his letters and newspaper columns from 2010 to 2020.
units.summary: Ten years of his writing in one place, including the golden rules and his case for buying only the best companies.

themes.title: Buy good companies
themes.idea: A good company earns a high return on the money tied up in it, in cash, and keeps doing so for decades.
ask: Which company you use every day earns its money from many small, repeated purchases?
Could a well-funded rival copy that company in five years?
themes.caption: His whole method in three steps, with the 2025 numbers behind each.

themes.title: The numbers that show quality
themes.idea: Every year he publishes the same few measures for his companies beside the market's. Quality shows up in the numbers.
ask: Find the return on capital of a company you know. Is it above 17%?
Why might a company founded a century ago still be a good investment?

themes.title: Don't overpay
themes.idea: Even the best company can be a bad investment at the wrong price. He checks how much cash you get for what you pay.
ask: What would make you refuse to buy even a wonderful company?
Why is 'someone will pay more later' a weak reason to buy?

themes.title: Do nothing
themes.idea: Once you own good companies at sensible prices, the hardest and best thing is to leave them alone.
ask: How often do you check share prices? What would happen if you checked once a quarter?
Which of your past trades would you undo?

themes.title: Read the accounts
themes.idea: His first fame came from showing how companies dressed up their profits. Reported profit can mislead; cash is harder to fake.
ask: Where in a company's accounts would you look to check that profits turn into cash?
Why might managers want profits to look smoother than they are?

themes.title: You are the biggest risk
themes.idea: Most damage to investors' returns is self-inflicted: chasing fashion, trading too much, buying what they don't understand.
ask: What investment have you bought mainly because others were buying it?
Can you explain each of your investments in two sentences?

themes.title: Costs come out of your pocket
themes.idea: Fees, charges and dealing costs are certain; returns are not. Keep the certain losses small.
ask: Do you know the total yearly cost of every fund you own?
How much would 1% a year cost you over 30 years?

themes.title: Don't over-diversify
themes.idea: Twenty or so well-chosen companies give most of the safety of spreading out. More than that, and you know each one less well.
ask: How many companies could you follow properly in a year?
When does spreading money out stop reducing risk?

themes.title: Avoid poor businesses and star bosses
themes.idea: Stay away from companies that earn poor returns, and from companies that only work with a genius in charge.
ask: Which company you know would struggle if its founder left tomorrow?
Why might predictable everyday purchases make a business easier to value?

themes.title: When it doesn't work
themes.idea: From 2021 to 2025 his fund trailed the market five years running. How he explained it is a lesson in honesty and patience.
ask: How many years of trailing the market would you tolerate from a fund manager?
What is the difference between bad luck and a broken strategy?

t1n1.lead: Return on capital is the test.
t1n1.text: A good business makes a high return on the capital it uses, in cash, and can sustain it.

t1n2.text: Its advantages should be difficult for rivals to replicate.

t1n3.text: It should not need heavy borrowing to earn its returns.

t1n4.text: It should be able to reinvest its cash at high rates, so growth compounds.

t1n5.text: It should be resilient to change, especially technological change.

t2n1.text: In 2025 his companies averaged a 31% return on capital, against 17% for both the S&P 500 and the FTSE 100.

t2n2.text: Gross margin 62% against 45% and 43%; operating margin 28% against 18% and 17%.

t2n3.text: They turned 94% of their profits into cash.

t2n4.text: Median interest cover was 29 times, against 9 and 8: profits dwarf interest bills.

t2n5.text: The average company in the fund was founded in 1919.

t3n1.text: He tracks free cash flow yield, the cash a company produces against its price. At the end of 2025 his portfolio's was 3.7%, against 2.8% for the S&P 500.

t3n2.text: Buy only what you would happily own at a price you accept. Profits that depend on someone paying more later rely on a greater fool.

t3n3.text: He argues that the market tends to underestimate how long great companies keep compounding, so paying up for them can still work.

t4n1.text: Frequent trading adds costs that steadily eat into returns.

t4n2.text: In 2025 the fund's turnover was 12.7%, and voluntary dealing cost 0.008% of the fund.

t4n3.text: Most people buy after rises and sell after falls. Guessing the turns rarely works.

t4n4.text: If you own good companies at sensible prices and dislike what the price is doing, stop looking.

t5n1.text: In 1990 several big British companies went bust while reporting healthy profits. Their real problem was cash.

t5n2.lead: The book that cost his job.
t5n2.text: In 1992 he expanded his research into a book. His employer, UBS Phillips & Drew, asked him to withdraw it; he refused and was sacked.

t5n3.text: Acquisition accounting, deferred payments, exceptional items, off-balance-sheet debt, hidden liabilities, brand values, changed depreciation, capitalised costs and currency mismatches.

t5n4.text: Many of the practices he exposed were later curbed or stopped.

t5n5.text: Managers who flatter their earnings rarely change, so treat it as a lasting warning sign.

t6n1.text: His Owner's Manual warns that the greatest threat to your returns is your own behaviour.

t6n2.text: The fund will not own something because it is in fashion and might go up, because eventually it goes down, usually by a lot.

t6n3.text: If you can't explain how an investment works, don't buy it. Complexity often hides risk.

t6n4.text: Never invest just to avoid tax. Tax-driven schemes often carry high fees and weak returns.

t7n1.text: Charges from advisers, platforms and funds can swallow most of an investment's income.

t7n2.text: Fundsmith reports a total cost of investment that includes dealing costs: 1.06% a year for its main share class in 2025.

t7n3.text: A cost of 1% a year sounds small, but over decades it takes a large share of the final pot.

t8n1.text: Around 20 well-chosen shares capture most of the benefit of diversification.

t8n2.text: At the end of 2025 Fundsmith Equity held 29 companies.

t8n3.text: His Owner's Manual asks how much a manager can really know about the 80th company in a portfolio.

t9n1.text: Companies that earn weak returns on their capital destroy value over time; strong ones compound it.

t9n2.lead: A business an idiot could run.
t9n2.text: Avoid companies that depend on one brilliant or charismatic leader who may not stay.

t9n3.text: He favours businesses built on many small, predictable purchases, such as household goods and medical supplies.

t10n1.text: The fund lagged world shares in every calendar year from 2021 to 2025.

t10n2.text: It returned 0.8% while world shares rose 12.8%; even cash did better.

t10n3.text: A market led by a handful of giant technology shares, money pouring into index funds, and a weak dollar. His biggest single drag was Novo Nordisk, which cost the fund about 3 points.

t10n4.text: Over 15 years the fund remains ahead: 13.8% a year against 12.1%.

t10n5.text: A sound approach can trail for years. Decide in advance how long you will give a strategy, and judge it honestly.

keynes.name: John Maynard Keynes
keynes.what: His memos, letters and books on markets, and his record running King's College's money
keynes.handbookTitle: John Maynard Keynes: a study handbook
keynes.scope: Keynes left no book on investing. His views come from his memos and letters (printed in his Collected Writings), from The General Theory, and from the King's College archives studied by David Chambers and Elroy Dimson. Famous lines often credited to him that he never wrote are flagged.
keynes.readHow: Chapter 12 of The General Theory is free online. The 1934 letter is reproduced in Warren Buffett's 1991 letter. The research summaries are free on the Cambridge Judge Business School and CFA Institute websites.
keynes.sourcesNote: Sources: his May 1938 memo to the King's College Estates Committee, his letter to F. C. Scott of 15 August 1934, The General Theory (1936), research by Chambers, Dimson and Foo (Cambridge, 2013–14), a study of his currency trading (2016), King's College and Quote Investigator. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

start.lede: John Maynard Keynes was the most famous economist of the 20th century. He also ran King's College, Cambridge's investments for 25 years. He failed as a market forecaster in the 1920s, changed his method, and from 1922 to 1946 his fund averaged about 16% a year against 10.4% for the UK market.
start.para: This page draws on his 1938 investment memo to King's College, his 1934 letter to F. C. Scott, chapter 12 of The General Theory, and Cambridge research that rebuilt his record from the college archives. About an hour a week for ten weeks.

themes.title: The forecaster who failed
themes.idea: In the 1920s he tried to profit from the ups and downs of the economy. Even he could not time them.
ask: If one of the world's best-informed economists couldn't time markets, why might you?
What would buying too late and selling too late look like in your own history?

themes.title: From forecaster to stock picker
themes.idea: In the early 1930s he stopped forecasting the market and started choosing individual companies. His results improved dramatically.
ask: What belief about investing have you changed in the last five years?
Why might fewer trades lead to better results?

themes.title: His three principles
themes.idea: In May 1938 he summed up successful investment in three principles: careful selection, steadfast holding, balance.
ask: Which of the three principles do you find hardest?
What does the £1 note story tell you about selling cheap shares to buy them back cheaper?

themes.title: A few big bets you understand
themes.idea: He thought spreading money across many things you know little about was a mistake. Better a few large holdings you understand.
ask: How many companies do you understand well enough to bet big on?
What is the risk of concentration, and how did his third principle answer it?

themes.title: Shares over bonds, for the long run
themes.idea: He moved a centuries-old college endowment from land and bonds into shares, decades before other institutions.
ask: Why might a fund that must last for centuries prefer shares to bonds?
What does buying below break-up value protect you from?

themes.title: The beauty contest
themes.idea: He compared the stock market to a newspaper contest where you win by guessing what others will pick, not what you think is best.
ask: When did you last buy something because you thought others would want it?
How could the beauty contest create bargains for a patient investor?
themes.caption: In a market, many players stop asking what is good and start guessing what others will think.

themes.title: Convention and reputation
themes.idea: Most people assume tomorrow will look like today, and most professionals would rather be wrong with the crowd than right alone.
ask: Would you rather be wrong with the crowd or right alone? Be honest.
Who would need to trust you for you to invest unconventionally?

themes.title: Animal spirits
themes.idea: Much of what drives business and markets is not calculation but a spontaneous urge to act, which can switch off suddenly.
ask: Where do you see animal spirits running high right now?
How would you tell a casino from an enterprise in today's market?

themes.title: Holding through the falls
themes.idea: Long-term investing means sitting through sharp falls. He did, and it cost him a chairmanship.
ask: How would you feel watching your portfolio fall 25% in a few months?
What would you need to have decided in advance to hold on?

themes.title: Words he never said
themes.idea: Keynes is the most misquoted investor of all. Checking who really said what is a good habit for every investor.
ask: Which famous investing quote have you shared without checking it?
Where would you look to check who really said something?

t1n1.text: At first he believed profit could be made by holding shares in slumps and selling them in booms, which he called a credit cycle policy.

t1n2.text: Looking back in 1938, he admitted the fund had not managed to profit from moving in and out of shares as a whole.

t1n3.text: He found that people who try usually move after the turn, both in and out, and trade too often, which piles up costs and makes them jumpy.

t1n4.text: Having suffered heavy losses, he sold a fifth of his UK shares and moved into government bonds, the conventional response.

t1n5.text: In 354 currency trades he was usually right about direction but struggled with timing.

t2n1.text: From the early 1930s he moved from top-down market timing to bottom-up stock picking.

t2n2.text: His yearly turnover fell from about 55% in the 1920s to 30% in the 1930s and 14% in the 1940s.

t2n3.text: Even in his 1938 review, buying particular shares when their prices were greatly depressed had done well.

t2n4.lead: He changed his mind in writing.
t2n4.text: His 1938 memo openly drew the opposite lesson from the one he had set out to prove. Admitting it is the first step.

t3n1.text: A few investments, picked because they are cheap compared with what they are likely to be worth over the next few years, and compared with the alternatives.

t3n2.text: Own them in size and refuse to be shaken out, for years if needed, until they deliver or you can see you were wrong.

t3n3.text: Mix your risks even though each holding is big, ideally with some that tend to move the other way, as gold-mining shares often did against other shares.

t3n4.text: Selling something worth £1 for 15 shillings (75p), hoping to buy it back for 12s 6d (about 62p), is a poor trade. So is refusing to buy it at 15 shillings because it looks too good to be true.

t4n1.text: In 1934 he told a colleague it is better to invest decent amounts in a few businesses you understand and whose managers you believe in.

t4n2.lead: Two or three at a time.
t4n2.text: He reckoned that at any one moment only two or three companies earned his complete confidence.

t4n3.text: His holdings grew from about 20 to over 60, yet at times more than half the fund sat in five shares.

t4n4.text: In 1936, 66% of the fund was in mining shares.

t5n1.text: He moved King's into shares while most institutions still relied on bonds and property.

t5n2.text: For investors with very long horizons, he favoured shares over bonds.

t5n3.text: By the late 1930s his fund held less in Britain than in the US or Africa.

t5n4.text: He leaned towards cheap shares with high dividend yields. One famous buy, the mining group Union Corporation, cost 30% less than its estimated break-up value.

t6n1.text: Readers had to pick the six prettiest faces from a hundred photographs. The prize went to whoever picked closest to the average choice.

t6n2.text: So each player picks not the face he finds prettiest, but the one he thinks others will pick, and some go further still.

t6n3.text: Many professional investors focus on guessing how market opinion will shift in the coming months, not on a business's long-run worth.

t6n4.text: Prices can drift far from value for a long time. Thinking about the business, not the crowd, is what lets you profit when they meet again.

t7n1.text: Lacking real knowledge of the far future, we assume the present will continue unless we have a specific reason to expect change.

t7n2.text: He saw that for a professional's reputation, failing with everyone else is safer than succeeding alone.

t7n3.text: Because shares can be sold at any moment, their prices are revalued daily, letting short-term mood dominate.

t7n4.text: He could be unconventional because the Fellows of King's trusted him. Long-term investing needs patient backers.

t8n1.text: Many decisions to invest rest on spontaneous optimism, which he called animal spirits, rather than on careful calculation.

t8n2.text: If optimism dims, investment can collapse even with no new facts.

t8n3.text: He warned that when a nation's investment is driven by casino-like speculation, the job is likely to be done badly.

t8n4.lead: Use the mood, don't share it.
t8n4.text: His own best buys came when prices were greatly depressed: when animal spirits were at their lowest.

t9n1.text: In nine years his whole share portfolio had twice fallen 20 to 25% within a few months, and he could not escape either fall.

t9n2.text: When London shares fell sharply he stayed invested, and resigned as chairman of an insurance company whose board would not stick with his strategy.

t9n3.text: He spent no more than about half an hour each morning on it, usually before getting out of bed. You don't need to watch every price.

t9n4.text: By his death, King's had drawn level with Trinity, the wealthiest college in Cambridge.

t10n1.text: "The market can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent" has no solid source in Keynes's writings. The earliest record found is the American adviser Gary Shilling, in 1986.

t10n2.text: "When the facts change, I change my mind" is also widely credited to him, but scholars of his papers have found no primary source.

t10n3.text: His real words, in chapter 12 of The General Theory, the 1938 memo and the 1934 letter, are sharper than the invented ones. Read them.

t10n4.text: If a quote is too perfect and has no date or source, it is probably not genuine.

keynes.honest: Keynes was a supporter of eugenics throughout his life and director of the Eugenics Society from 1937 to 1944. These views, held by many of his era, are now widely condemned. We include him for his investing, where the record is strong and well documented, and state this plainly so you can judge for yourself.

lilu.name: Li Lu
lilu.what: His interview, lectures and foreword on value investing, in China and the world
lilu.scope: Li Lu writes no yearly letters. His thinking is in a handful of speeches, one long interview and a foreword, most of them free on Himalaya Capital's website, plus a book in Chinese (2020). Some talks were given in Chinese; where we rely on a translation, the source says whose. He has published no fund figures since 2009.
lilu.readHow: Start with the 2013 Columbia interview and the 2015 Peking University lecture. Both are free in English.
lilu.sourcesNote: Sources: his foreword to the Chinese edition of Poor Charlie's Almanack (2010), the Graham & Doddsville interview (2013), his Peking University lectures (2015 and 2019), his book (2020, in Chinese), his conversation at Columbia's Graham & Dodd luncheon (2026), and news reports on BYD. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

start.lede: Li Lu reached the United States in 1989 with little money and less English, heard Warren Buffett speak at Columbia in 1993, and founded Himalaya Capital in 1997. Charlie Munger later called him the only outside manager he had ever invested with. His method: treat a share as part of a business, know exactly where your knowledge ends, buy with a margin of safety, and wait for the rare great bet.
start.para: This page draws on his foreword to Poor Charlie's Almanack, a long interview with Columbia students, two lectures at Peking University, his book, and a 2026 talk at Columbia. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

glossary: Buying a share for less than the business is worth, and holding it while the business grows.
The area where you genuinely understand businesses well enough to value them.
The gap between a cautious estimate of value and the price you pay.
Benjamin Graham's picture of the market as a moody partner offering prices you may take or ignore.
Borrowing shares to sell them, hoping to buy them back later at a lower price.
A fund that only owns shares and never bets on prices falling.
A period during which investors agree not to withdraw their money.
What a business is really worth, judged from the cash it will produce.
Someone trusted to act in another person's interest, before their own.

themes.title: A share is a piece of a business
themes.idea: Value investing rests on four ideas. The first is that a share is part-ownership of a real business, so your return comes from the business growing.
ask: Pick a company you own or know. How exactly does it earn its money?
Would you still want to own it if no price were quoted for five years?

themes.title: Know where your circle ends
themes.idea: Your circle of competence should be small and clearly drawn. The skill is knowing where it ends, and what would prove you wrong.
ask: Name one industry where you are truly inside your circle, and one where you only feel you are.
What single fact would prove your favourite investment idea wrong?
themes.caption: What matters is not how big the circle is, but knowing exactly where it ends.

themes.title: The market serves you
themes.idea: Prices are there to use when they suit you. The market cannot tell you what a company is worth, and it punishes anyone who forgets that.
ask: When did a falling price last change your opinion of a business? Should it have?
What results would you need every quarter to feel calm? Is that realistic?

themes.title: Margin of safety
themes.idea: Because the future is uncertain, buy at a price far below your cautious estimate of value. He started with very cheap shares and moved, over time, to great businesses at fair prices.
ask: What is your cautious estimate of value for one company you know, and how far below it is the price?
When would you sell a share that has risen to its value?

themes.title: Research like an owner
themes.idea: Study a company as if you had just inherited it and had to run it. Talk to everyone, from the boss to the security guard.
ask: If you inherited a company you own shares in, what would you want to know first?
Who, besides the boss, could tell you the truth about a company?

themes.title: Why he gave up short selling
themes.idea: He calls short selling one of his worst mistakes. The maths, the frauds and the distraction all work against you.
ask: Why might a short seller lose money even when right about a company?
What else in your investing eats attention without adding much?

themes.title: Patient, then decisive
themes.idea: Great opportunities are rare. Wait calmly while nothing happens, then act firmly when one appears.
ask: How many truly great opportunities do you think you will see in the next ten years?
What would you need to see to act in size?

themes.title: A different road from Wall Street
themes.idea: Munger told him his problems were Wall Street's problems. He rebuilt his fund around long-term partners and a sense of duty to their savings.
ask: If someone managed your parents' savings, what would you want them never to do?
Why might a smaller fund with patient partners do better than a bigger one?

themes.title: Own a slice of the world
themes.idea: Real wealth is your share of the world's buying power. Over two centuries, owning businesses beat cash, gold and bonds by a vast margin.
ask: What share of your wealth sits in cash or gold? What has inflation done to it?
Which market or industry near you do most investors ignore?

themes.title: Mistakes, luck and compounding knowledge
themes.idea: He had a bad first year, sold winners too early and gave up shorting the hard way. He credits luck, and says knowledge compounds like money.
ask: Which of your mistakes taught you the most?
What will you know in five years that you don't know now, and how will you learn it?

t1n1.text: He sums up value investing as four ideas: a share is part of a business; the market is there to serve you; buy with a margin of safety; stay inside your circle of competence.

t1n2.lead: The lecture that changed his life.
t1n2.text: A classmate took him to hear Buffett at Columbia. He found the case clear and convincing: shares are pieces of businesses, and over time prices follow what those businesses are worth.

t1n3.text: He then spent nearly two years reading about Buffett, Berkshire and Munger before buying his first share, while his own net worth was still below zero.

t1n4.text: Once he owned a company he became curious about every part of it, and that curiosity taught him the whole industry.

t1n5.text: He likes investing in businesses because owner and company can both win. Trading against other traders is a zero-sum game.

t2n1.text: What counts is not how much you know but knowing exactly where your knowledge stops.

t2n2.lead: Say when you would be wrong.
t2n2.text: You should be able to state the conditions under which your view of a company would fail.

t2n3.text: A real circle is built over years and stays small. Most people cannot see five or ten years ahead for most companies.

t2n4.text: Intellectual honesty comes first: you are the easiest person to fool, and people tend to believe whatever suits them.

t2n5.text: From Munger he took the rule of holding no opinion until he can state the opposing case better than its supporters.

t3n1.text: Use market prices to buy and sell when they suit you; never take them as a verdict on value.

t3n2.text: Many investors want the benefits of value investing and good results every quarter. Chasing both pushes you into speculation.

t3n3.lead: The market finds your weak spots.
t3n3.text: Act outside what you understand, or let fear and greed run you, and the market will expose it sooner or later.

t3n4.text: He estimates that only about one market participant in twenty invests this way. That is why the opportunity lasts.

t4n1.text: Since value can only be estimated, buy at the lowest price you can, and study the parts of a business that bear on your margin of safety.

t4n2.text: As a student he bought a holding company whose stake in a large cable firm was alone worth about three times the whole company's market value.

t4n3.text: He sold once the margin of safety had gone. The shares kept rising for years afterwards.

t4n4.text: A beginner with little money, he first bought very cheap shares, the safest choice. In time he moved to strong businesses at reasonable prices.

t4n5.text: Early on he visited nearby companies to check that their assets were real and the business was running.

t5n1.text: He suggests picturing that the company has just become yours and you must learn everything about it.

t5n2.text: He talks to people at every level, down to security guards, and asks about hiring, pay and how staff are treated.

t5n3.text: Two identical petrol stations drew very different custom, one about four times the other. The difference was an owner who ran his with care. So ask: do managers think like owners?

t5n4.text: His ideas come from wide reading, newspapers and annual reports, and from people who run businesses, more than from other investors.

t5n5.lead: When you can't judge the boss.
t5n5.text: Management matters but is hard to assess. When he cannot judge it, he leans on the quality of the business and the price.

t6n1.text: He ran a long-short fund in his early years, then stopped shorting around 2004 and calls it one of his worst mistakes.

t6n2.text: A short can make at most 100% but can lose without limit, and you can be forced out before you are proved right.

t6n3.text: The best shorts often involve fraud, and frauds can survive long enough to squeeze you out.

t6n4.text: Constant short-side trading left no time to study his best long-term ideas.

t6n5.text: Over long periods, a growing economy works for those who own businesses, not for those betting against them.

t7n1.text: Munger read Barron's for decades and found just one big idea in it. That is how rare the best chances are.

t7n2.text: Patience and decisiveness have to live together: wait without fidgeting, then move in size.

t7n3.text: It can take around fifteen years to tell real skill from luck; short-term results are often luck.

t7n4.text: Like golf, a good hole does not guarantee the next. Judge each decision on its own merits.

t7n5.text: He was drawn to the battery and car maker by its founder's engineering record, its rise in a fierce market, and a margin of safety. Berkshire bought 10% in 2008 for about $230m and sold out by 2025 after a more than twentyfold rise.

t8n1.text: He took Munger through every company he owned or followed. Munger said his problems came from the way Wall Street thinks, and offered to invest if he would take a different path.

t8n2.text: With Munger's help he rebuilt the fund like Buffett's early partnerships: no shorting, long lock-ups for partners who stayed, and no new investors.

t8n3.text: He says a manager should treat clients' money like the lifetime savings of their own parents, and that people without that instinct should not be in the business.

t8n4.text: He criticises the common hedge fund fee of 2% a year plus 20% of profits as serving managers better than clients.

t8n5.text: He recalls Munger's ideal: a seamless web of deserved trust. Keep partners who share your approach, rather than chasing the most money.

t9n1.text: From Munger he takes the rule to look where others are not: less crowded markets, industries and countries.

t9n2.lead: Wealth is a share of the world.
t9n2.text: He measures wealth as your percentage of global buying power, not gold, cash or any currency, and keeps it by owning great businesses in growing economies.

t9n3.text: He cites US figures from 1802: a dollar in cash lost about 95% of its value, gold roughly tripled after inflation, and shares grew about a million times, roughly 6.7% a year after inflation.

t9n4.text: In his book he describes history in stages: hunting and gathering, farming, then free markets plus modern science, the stage in which businesses can compound.

t9n5.text: In 2015 he argued value investing could work in China: its markets had risen about fifteenfold from 1991 to 2014, while short-term trading still dominated.

t10n1.text: His first year ended 19% down on paper, and a large investor left the next year.

t10n2.text: He was an early investor in Capital IQ, the data company, and sold; it later became far more valuable.

t10n3.text: He treats each mistake as a lesson, and names short selling as his biggest.

t10n4.text: He credits part of his success to luck.

t10n5.text: Knowledge and trusted relationships compound like capital. Learning faster is how money, eventually, grows faster.

A student leader in the Tiananmen Square protests; leaves China and, by way of France, reaches the United States
Hears Warren Buffett speak at Columbia University, almost by chance, and starts reading everything about him
Graduates from Columbia with three degrees at once, in economics, law and business; first meets Charlie Munger
Starts his fund in January with money from a few friends; down 19% on paper in its first year
At Thanksgiving, takes Munger through every company he owns or follows; Munger offers to invest if he leaves Wall Street's habits behind
Munger becomes his partner; the fund stops short selling and asks investors for long lock-ups
Berkshire buys 10% of BYD, the battery and car maker Li Lu had brought to Munger
Helps publish Poor Charlie's Almanack in Chinese and writes its foreword
First lecture at Peking University's new value investing course
Publishes his book Civilization, Modernization, Value Investing and China, in Chinese
Berkshire completes its exit from BYD after 17 years
Fireside chat at Columbia's Graham & Dodd luncheon, aged 60

duan.name: Duan Yongping
duan.what: His talks, interviews and online answers on buying businesses and keeping a stop-doing list
duan.scope: Duan writes in Chinese, mostly short answers on Xueqiu, where readers call him Da Dao. The 2025 book collects twenty years of them and is the only collection he has approved. Most sources here are in Chinese: lessons are our own English summaries, and short quotes are in the original with our translation. His investment results are personal and unaudited.
duan.readHow: If you read Chinese, start with the Stanford talk, which is free online, then the 2025 book. Otherwise, browser translation of the free transcripts works reasonably well.
duan.sourcesNote: Sources: his talk to Chinese students at Stanford (2018), his interview with Xueqiu's founder Fang Sanwen (2025), excerpts from the book of his answers (CITIC Press, 2025), his replies on Xueqiu, an AFP interview (2017), and press reports on his Buffett lunch (2006), BBK's stop-doing list and his gifts. Lessons are in our own words; short quotes are in the original language with our translation.

start.lede: Duan Yongping built two electronics companies, Subor and BBK, whose offshoots grew into the phone makers OPPO and vivo. He stepped back in 2001, moved to California and turned to investing: a large bet on NetEase when it was in trouble, then Apple and Kweichow Moutai for many years. His rules: buying a stock is buying the company, buy only what you understand, never borrow, and keep a list of things you will not do.
start.para: This page draws on his 2018 talk at Stanford, his 2025 interview with the founder of the investor site Xueqiu, the 2025 book of his online answers, and press interviews. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

glossary: Doing what you should, honestly and without being asked; not taking advantage of others.
Staying rational and returning to fundamentals whatever is happening around you.
A written list of things a person or company will not do, whatever the short-term gain.
Valuing a company by adding up the cash it will produce in future, each year's cash shrunk back to today's money.
When a share that many have bet against rises fast, forcing them to buy back at high prices.
A contract giving someone the right to buy a share at a set price. Selling one brings in cash now, but caps your gain.
Making products for another company to sell under its brand.
What you give up by choosing one use of money over the next best one.

themes.title: Buying a stock is buying the company
themes.idea: One sentence from Buffett changed how he invested. A share is part of a company, and a company is worth the cash it will produce from now on.
ask: For one share you own, how much cash does the business produce in a year?
Are you trying to earn what a company earns, or what other traders lose?

themes.title: Only what you understand
themes.idea: Be honest about what you understand. He says he truly understands only a few companies, and his losses came when he strayed.
ask: Which companies could you explain to a child?
Have you ever lost money on something you didn't really understand?

themes.title: The stop-doing list
themes.idea: Doing the right thing mostly means refusing to do wrong things. Most people know what is wrong; they do it anyway for a short-term gain.
ask: Write down three things you will never do as an investor. Why each one?
Which of your habits do you know is wrong but keep anyway?
themes.caption: First ask whether it is the right thing. Only then ask whether it pays.

themes.title: Never borrow
themes.idea: His companies take no interest-bearing loans, and he never borrows to invest. Debt makes you faster in both directions.
ask: What would happen to your portfolio if prices halved tomorrow and you had borrowed?
Which opportunity did you miss without regret?

themes.title: Right business, right people, right price
themes.idea: Look at the business model and the culture first. Price comes last.
ask: What is the culture of a company you own? How would you find out?
Would you buy a dull, unique business over an exciting, ordinary one?

themes.title: Benfen and a calm mind
themes.idea: Benfen means doing what you should, even when nobody asked. Add a calm, ordinary mind and, he says, you have the whole secret of BBK.
ask: What does doing what you should mean in your own investing?
When did staying calm last save you from a mistake?

themes.title: Hold great companies
themes.idea: Good companies rarely need selling. He sells when the business changes or something clearly better appears.
ask: Which of your holdings would you happily own for ten years?
Have you ever sold a great company only because its price rose?

themes.title: NetEase, Apple and Moutai
themes.idea: Three bets made him famous as an investor. Each fits his rules: a business he understood, a culture he liked, a sensible price.
ask: What did all three companies have in common?
Which company near you holds more cash than the market thinks?

themes.title: The Buffett lunch and giving back
themes.idea: In 2006 he paid a record sum to lunch with Buffett, to charity. He plans to give most of his money away, and gives with conditions that make gifts last.
ask: If you gave something away, how would you make sure it lasted?
What would you ask Buffett over lunch?

themes.title: The mistakes he admits
themes.idea: He is frank about his errors. Most came when he speculated or strayed outside what he understood.
ask: Which of your losses came from speculating rather than investing?
What rule would have prevented your worst mistake?

t1n1.text: In America he first tried charts and could make no sense of them, until Buffett's line that buying a stock is buying a company made everything clear.

t1n2.text: A company is worth all the cash it will produce from now until it ends, discounted back to today.

t1n3.lead: Fewer than one in a hundred.
t1n3.text: The idea sounds simple, he says, but perhaps fewer than 1% of investors truly understand it.

t1n4.lead: The company's money, not the market's.
t1n4.text: Investors earn what their companies earn. People forever talking about bull and bear markets are really hoping to win other traders' money.

t1n5.text: He decides by comparing opportunities, not by predicting the economy.

t2n1.text: Honesty with yourself is the heart of a circle of competence: know what you know and admit what you don't.

t2n2.text: He says he understands Apple, Tencent and Moutai, only partly understands a few others, and avoids most of the rest.

t2n3.text: He admits the line between understanding and not is blurry, which is why he keeps to the few he knows best.

t2n4.text: He credits his NetEase success to knowing the games business from his Subor years.

t2n5.lead: Others may understand what you don't.
t2n5.text: Not understanding a company is no judgement on it; it simply isn't for you.

t3n1.text: Most people can tell right from wrong. They do wrong things anyway because the short-term pull is strong, like smokers who know the harm.

t3n2.text: When you realise something is a mistake, stop at once. Stopping is cheapest at the start.

t3n3.text: No selling on credit, no late payments to suppliers, no late wages, no haggling, no making products for others, no interest-bearing loans, no attacking rivals.

t3n4.text: He once refused an order for a million VCD players without even discussing price: haggling would only waste everyone's time.

t3n5.text: Many items on the list came from painful lessons; each rule saves them from a class of mistakes.

t4n1.text: BBK, OPPO and vivo take no interest-bearing loans, so they cannot die from running out of cash. He cites Munger: most failures come from borrowing too much.

t4n2.text: Borrowing speeds up gains and losses alike. Getting your feet wet is unavoidable; getting soaked can be permanent.

t4n3.text: With ample cash, every crisis became a chance to act rather than a threat.

t4n4.text: Missing some opportunities is acceptable, as long as you catch the right ones.

t4n5.text: Most of his old competitors have disappeared; he believes avoiding debt is a big part of why his companies survived.

t5n1.text: Right business, right people, right price, an order he credits to Buffett. Price matters least.

t5n2.text: He looks at two things, the business model and the corporate culture. If he dislikes either, he stops looking.

t5n3.lead: Cheap, seen from ten years out.
t5n3.text: Whether a share is expensive today is a short-term question. Look back from ten years ahead.

t5n4.text: Products no different from rivals' can only compete on price and rarely make money. He calls 'value for money' an excuse for weak products.

t5n5.text: He avoids anything that produces no cash flow, such as Bitcoin.

t6n1.text: Asked whether BBK's success came from advertising or incentives, he says no: it came from benfen plus a calm mind.

t6n2.lead: Do the right thing, and do it right.
t6n2.text: He came across Peter Drucker's line as a student; it became BBK's motto.

t6n3.text: He cites a study of top chief executives: their personalities differed in every way except one, integrity.

t6n4.text: Don't deceive customers or investors; what you say, you must do.

t6n5.text: He left Subor because its owner broke promises about shares: a problem of trust, not money.

t7n1.text: By 2018 he had never sold Apple, saying good companies don't need selling.

t7n2.text: The company's earning power changes, or a clearly better company he understands appears at a good price.

t7n3.text: He calls himself a full-position investor and dislikes idle cash, since bank interest earns less than good companies.

t7n4.text: When Moutai's shares fell by about half, he held on and kept buying.

t7n5.text: By 2025 he thought Apple's shares expensive and was trimming by selling call options.

t8n1.text: He bought heavily when the shares were in panic and the company held more cash than its market value. They rose about twentyfold in six months and more than a hundredfold in all.

t8n2.text: He later sold, saying he felt uneasy holding so much, and admits the later share price suggests he sold too soon.

t8n3.text: He began buying in 2011, seeing the shift to software and the platform, and a culture that puts users first and refuses products that add too little.

t8n4.text: A unique product whose taste does not change, loyal customers, and steady dividends and buybacks.

t9n1.text: In 2006 he paid $620,100 at Buffett's charity lunch auction, the first winner from mainland China.

t9n2.text: He said he planned to follow Buffett by giving most of his money away.

t9n3.text: In 2025 and 2026 he gave Moutai shares to education funds, on condition the shares are kept and only the dividends spent.

t9n4.text: At Zhejiang University in 2011 he told graduates: have no grand ambitions, keep a list of things you won't do, and be upright.

t9n5.text: Asked about beating Apple, he said they think about improving themselves, not about surpassing anyone.

t10n1.text: A speculative bet on Baidu ended in a short squeeze that cost him $100 to 200 million. He calls it speculation, not investing.

t10n2.text: He bought GE in 2008, sold a few years later, and says he never really grasped its business model.

t10n3.text: About $100 million put into an oil index lost more than $10 million before he sold.

t10n4.text: BBK was slow to see the shift to smartphones; losses in 2012 and 2013 drained much of its cash.

t10n5.text: He says his real investing mistakes were few and small; the big losses came from speculation.
