qiu.name: Qiu Guolu
qiu.what: His two books and talks on cheap prices, pricing power and going against the crowd
qiu.scope: Qiu writes in Chinese. His first book gathers essays and posts written mostly before 2013; the sequel draws on Gaoyi's internal discussions. Neither has an English edition. Lessons are our own English summaries; short quotes are in Chinese with our translation. His funds report returns only to their investors, so we show none we cannot check.
qiu.readHow: If you read Chinese, start with The Simplest Things in Investing: short chapters in plain language. Otherwise, the free articles linked below carry the core ideas, and browser translation works reasonably well.
qiu.sourcesNote: Sources: his books (2014, updated 2020; and 2018 with Gaoyi colleagues), a 2015 newspaper profile, interviews in 2018 and 2019, a 2017 lecture at the Gaoli value investing institute, and press reports of his 2022 letter to investors. Lessons are in our own words; short quotes are in Chinese with our translation.

start.lede: Qiu Guolu formed his approach during six years at Wedge Capital in the United States, ran investment at China Southern Asset Management from 2008, and in 2014 founded Gaoyi Asset Management, a home for several star managers that grew past 100 billion yuan. His bestselling book boils investing down to three questions: why is it cheap, why is it good, and why buy now?
start.para: This page draws on his book The Simplest Things in Investing (2014) and its sequel (2018), a 2017 lecture, interviews and his 2022 letter to investors. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

themes.title: Three questions
themes.idea: All his analysis comes down to three questions: why is it cheap, why is it good, and why buy now?
ask: Answer the three questions for one company you know. Which was hardest?
How did the company make its profits over five years: margins, turnover or borrowing?
themes.caption: Valuation is the easiest of the three to measure; quality is the hardest to judge.

themes.title: Cheapness is the hard truth
themes.idea: A low price is the investor's first protection. Even an ordinary company can pay well if bought cheaply enough.
ask: Can you name a dull company that looks cheap? Why is it cheap?
How many truly great companies can you name in your own market?

themes.title: Pricing power is the core advantage
themes.idea: A company with a real edge can raise prices without losing customers. That power comes from doing what you can repeat and others cannot copy.
ask: Which company you buy from could raise its prices tomorrow without losing you?
What does it do that nobody else can copy?

themes.title: Count the moons, not the stars
themes.idea: Look at the whole industry, not just the company. The best skies have one bright moon; the worst are crowded with stars.
ask: In one industry you know, how many moons are there?
Which firms are really competing with each other, and which only look as if they are?
themes.caption: From best to worst: one moon; a moon with bright stars; two or three moons; a sky full of stars.

themes.title: Win first, then fight
themes.idea: Crowded, fast-growing industries make poor hunting grounds. Wait until the battle is over and back the winner.
ask: Name an industry where the battle is over. Who won?
Which product you use has barely changed in thirty years?

themes.title: Take what others discard
themes.idea: Go where the crowd is not, and be careful where it is packed. But cheap can stay cheap: check why the crowd left.
ask: Which industry are fund managers crowding into now?
Why might a cheap share stay cheap for years?

themes.title: A lucky win is not a right bet
themes.idea: Judge your method, not this year's result. A sound process shows itself over five to ten years.
ask: Was your best result last year skill or luck? How would you tell?
How many bad years would make you abandon your method?

themes.title: Clients first
themes.idea: A fund firm must put compliance before growth, clients before itself, and results before size.
ask: If you ran a fund, which promise to clients would you write down first?
Why might a fund do worse as it grows bigger?

themes.title: Value investing works in China
themes.idea: He has tried most methods. For most people, he concluded, only value investing can really be learned and used, in China as anywhere.
ask: Which investing methods have you tried? Which could you actually keep using?
What would make a method work in one country but not another?

themes.title: Even legends stumble
themes.idea: After two hard years he wrote to investors about his mistakes, and what he would watch more closely.
ask: What could change an industry's pricing power overnight?
When did you last add to a falling share too early?

t1n1.text: Every analysis answers three questions: why the company is cheap, why it is good, and why now is the time to buy.

t1n2.text: Price to earnings, to book value and to sales are the most scientific measures, and the easiest to learn.

t1n3.text: Few people can spot a truly great company before the market does, and many once-great companies lost their edge.

t1n4.lead: Good industry, good company, good price.
t1n4.text: His whole approach: find good companies in good industries, then wait for a good price.

t1n5.text: Porter's five forces for the industry, DuPont analysis for how profits are made, and comparisons with peers and history for the price.

t2n1.text: He borrows a retailer's rule, Sam Walton's: you can only sell cheaply if you buy cheaply. In investing, buying cheaply matters even more.

t2n2.text: An ordinary company bought at a low enough price can still give a fine return.

t2n3.text: He reckoned that among about 2,500 Chinese listed companies perhaps ten were truly great, so most of the time price must do the work.

t2n4.lead: Wary of the next great thing.
t2n4.text: He is suspicious of stories about the next great company, and admits he struggles even to pay a fair price for great ones.

t3n1.text: A company with a real edge does something it can repeat again and again, and something others cannot copy.

t3n2.text: He cares less about how few rivals there are than about the bargaining power and irreplaceability that brings.

t3n3.text: That power is the dividing line between businesses that earn easily and those that work hard for little.

t3n4.text: Scarce resources, a strong brand, patents, a dominant position or a licence: in the end each shows up as pricing power.

t4n1.text: One dominant firm is best; then one leader with a few strong rivals; then two or three equals; worst is a sky full of small competitors.

t4n2.text: The skill is drawing the right boundary: which firms are real rivals and which belong to a different sky.

t4n3.text: Firms from other industries can enter any sky.

t4n4.text: The prize is a company whose pricing power the market has not yet noticed.

t4n5.text: Investors often pick the right industry but the wrong company.

t5n1.text: In a crowded industry it is hard to know whom to back, however fast it grows. Wait until the fighting ends and a winner emerges.

t5n2.text: In fast-moving technology, rivals simply build a new castle elsewhere. Televisions went through tubes, projection, LCD, plasma, LED and 3D in a few years; air conditioners changed far less.

t5n3.text: Coca-Cola's formula has hardly changed in a hundred years, and China too has traditional products that last for centuries.

t5n4.text: After food scandals, industry sales recovered within months and the big brands gained share, as buyers trusted known names.

t6n1.text: Every January and July he adds up the industry weights of all fund companies, then grows cautious on the crowded industries and more hopeful on the shunned ones.

t6n2.text: He lived through the 1992 rush for share certificates and the late-1990s Nasdaq boom and crash.

t6n3.text: In 2020–21 he stayed out of the crowded trade in richly valued favourite shares, which then fell about 40% from early 2021.

t6n4.text: His book warns that some cheap shares stay cheap for good reasons, and describes the kinds most likely to become traps.

t7n1.text: Winning a bet and betting right are not the same: a good process can give poor results for a while, and a bad one can get lucky.

t7n2.text: A sound method gives good results with high probability over five to ten years, not six months.

t7n3.text: He reckons a sound method beats the market in about six or seven years out of ten, a poor one in three or four.

t7n4.text: Citing Joel Greenblatt: value investing works over time precisely because it doesn't work every year.

t7n5.text: Investors who keep changing methods tend to fail; successful ones stick with one.

t8n1.text: In 2017 he wrote to all staff: when growth clashes with compliance, compliance wins; when the firm's interest clashes with clients', clients win; when size clashes with results, results win.

t8n2.text: Many Gaoyi funds lock investors in for two or three years, some for five or eight, because stable money lets managers think long term.

t8n3.text: He built Gaoyi to handle everything except investing, so its managers can concentrate on picking shares.

t8n4.text: His first job was as a strategist and quantitative analyst; his approach took shape during six years at Wedge Capital.

t9n1.text: At 19 he queued overnight for share subscription certificates and made his first stock market gains.

t9n2.text: Tips, charts, quant trading, concentrated picking, growth investing: he tried them all, and concluded that for most people only value investing can be learned and used.

t9n3.text: The 2015 profile credits him with six strong years at China Southern, using value methods in China's A-share market.

t9n4.text: The same profile sums up his habits: independent judgement, faith in common sense, a contrarian streak and patience for delayed rewards.

t9n5.text: The point of the sequel: the principles are simple; holding to them, and applying them flexibly in a noisy market full of traps, is not.

t9n6.text: He enjoys investing as a search for the truth, with new industries to learn every year.

t10n1.text: Too much in Hong Kong shares, cutting holdings too early in 2020, and too little attention to policy, especially the regulation of internet companies.

t10n2.text: After China's internet shares halved in late 2021 he added more, and they fell further.

t10n3.text: His conclusion: keep your eyes on the road, but look up at the sky too, meaning watch policy as well as companies.

t10n4.text: He kept his faith in low valuations and his refusal to chase crowded favourites.

start.lede: Zhang Lei learned investing as an intern under David Swensen at Yale's endowment, then founded Hillhouse in 2005 with $20 million from Yale. He backed Tencent early, put $300 million into JD.com in 2010, and built one of Asia's largest investment firms. His creed: think long term, research deeply, back entrepreneurs with great vision, and be a friend of time.

t1n1.text: Long-termism means putting time and conviction into things that keep creating value, learning the most effective ways of thinking, and always seeking the truth.

t1n2.text: A long horizon gives you an advantage before you begin, because so few investors can afford to wait.

t1n3.text: Yale taught him that investing is not a race for quick returns but working with the best people to build lasting organisations.

t1n4.text: Long holding periods are the result of backing companies that keep creating value, not a goal in themselves.

t1n5.text: He sums up his approach in three phrases: long-termism, walking with people of great vision, and being a friend of time.

t2n1.text: Short of money for his second year at Yale, he got an internship in Swensen's office. His first task was translating Swensen's book into Chinese.

t2n2.text: Swensen answered hundreds of his questions, on the trading floor and over squash and softball.

t2n3.text: Swensen showed him what a fiduciary is: someone who puts the interests of those who trust him first. He struggled to find a Chinese word for it.

t2n4.text: Yale backed him when he was 32 and had never managed a portfolio. Swensen's reason: work with the right people and good things tend to follow.

t2n5.text: Swensen spoke of organisations with a soul, driven by a mission. Zhang came to believe such teams innovate more and last longer.

t3n1.text: Make deep fundamental research the basis of every decision, and place a few bets rather than chase many ideas.

t3n2.text: Value investing is not maths on paper. Like a sociologist doing fieldwork, you must see how people really live and buy.

t3n3.text: His team works as generalists, and he counts himself one of the analysts.

t3n4.text: Success comes down to stripping an investment to its most basic questions.

t3n5.text: Qiu Guolu recalls Zhang convening top scientists in 2015 on cancer immunotherapy, before most Chinese investors knew the field, and backing BeiGene in eight rounds.

t4n1.text: Before investing, find out whether owners, directors and managers are long-term, intelligent and aligned with their customers' needs.

t4n2.text: Intelligence, independent thinking and honesty count for more than experience or background.

t4n3.text: Curiosity, independence and honesty, plus empathy: qualities he looks for in people.

t4n4.text: Swensen's reason for backing him became Hillhouse's motto: spend quality time with quality people.

t4n5.text: He describes Hillhouse as entrepreneurs who happen to be investors.

t5n1.text: Long-term thinking amid uncertainty; deep insight into the industry; focused execution; and strong empathy that brings people and resources together.

t5n2.text: He calls great vision Hillhouse's secret handshake with companies: founders who want to build something great make the best partners.

t5n3.text: Good entrepreneurs see ten or twenty years ahead, sometimes beyond their own lives.

t5n4.lead: Choose the person, then the project.
t5n4.text: When Swensen backed him, it was a bet on a person. Zhang applies the same logic to founders.

t6n1.text: Long-termism helps companies escape zero-sum games and keep rebuilding a dynamic moat through constant innovation.

t6n2.text: As markets grow more efficient, deeply undervalued companies become rare. Investors must find new, forward-looking drivers of value.

t6n3.text: He looks for industries being changed by technology and new ways of doing business.

t6n4.text: He invests in both new technology and traditional industries, public or private, large or small.

t7n1.text: Unlike buyout firms that plan the exit first and lean on debt and cost cuts, he backs good people and solid cash flow and lets the exit take care of itself.

t7n2.text: In 2017 Hillhouse led the $6.8 billion purchase of the shoe retailer Belle, aiming to use technology for online sales, stock control and better service in shops.

t7n3.text: With freedom to invest in public shares, venture and private equity, he focuses on the substance of a deal, not its form.

t7n4.text: In 2010 he put $300 million into JD.com in one go, backed by years of studying retail around the world.

t8n1.text: Things fire can burn, such as money and houses, are not what matters. What matters is what fire cannot burn: knowledge, ability and values.

t8n2.text: Don't reason by analogy. Peel back the surface to see what a thing really is, then build up from there.

t8n3.text: He has given generously to Yale and, inspired by Swensen, founded an institute to teach long-term investing.

t8n4.text: Swensen saw teaching as one of his most important duties; Zhang took that as the clearest sign of a long-term mind.

t9n1.text: In 2019 a Hillhouse fund paid 41.66 billion yuan, partly borrowed, for 15% of Gree Electric and became its biggest shareholder.

t9n2.text: By early 2026 Gree's shares were nearly 20% below the purchase price, a paper loss partly offset by about 15 billion yuan of dividends.

t9n3.text: In 2026 Hillhouse planned to sell about 2% of Gree to repay bank loans from the deal.

t9n4.text: By 2020, Swensen said, Hillhouse had made about $2.4 billion of gains for Yale.

t10n1.text: HHLR, Hillhouse's public-markets unit, owned 5.85% of the solar company LONGi. In March 2023 it lent out shares, taking its stake below 5%, the level above which sales must be announced.

t10n2.text: When the loan ended, its stake was only 4.98%, implying it had sold about 0.9% of the company without an announcement.

t10n3.text: In November 2023 the regulator opened an investigation for suspected breaches of share-transfer rules, and the exchanges soon closed the loophole.

t10n4.text: In April 2024 HHLR began buying the shares back, promising to hand any gain to LONGi. We have found no published final penalty decision.

sp.text: In November 2023 China's securities regulator opened an investigation into HHLR, the public-markets unit of Hillhouse. HHLR owned 5.85% of the solar company LONGi. In March 2023 it lent out shares, taking its stake below 5%, the level above which sales must be announced; when the loan ended its stake was only 4.98%, implying it had sold about 0.9% of the company without an announcement. graham.name: Benjamin Graham
graham.what: His books, last interview and Senate testimony on value, safety and Mr Market
graham.scope: Graham's books are long and were revised several times; we use the 1973 edition of The Intelligent Investor. The often-repeated claim that he earned 20% a year for decades is not supported by the best study of his fund, so we show the measured figures instead.
graham.readHow: Start with chapters 8 and 20 of The Intelligent Investor, on Mr Market and the margin of safety. Then read his short 1976 interview, free online.
graham.sourcesNote: Sources: Security Analysis (1934), The Intelligent Investor (1973 edition), his Senate testimony (1955), his 1976 interview with the Financial Analysts Journal, Kahn and Milne's study for the CFA Institute (1977), and Buffett's 1984 talk and 1987 letter. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

start.lede: Benjamin Graham taught Warren Buffett, wrote Security Analysis (1934) and The Intelligent Investor (1949), and is called the father of value investing. The 1929 crash nearly ruined him, and he spent the rest of his life working out how an ordinary person could invest without being ruined. His answers: know the difference between investing and speculating, treat the market as a moody partner, and always insist on a margin of safety.
start.para: This page draws on his two books, his last interview (1976), his testimony to the US Senate (1955), a study of his record by his former assistant, and Buffett's writing about him. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

glossary: Buying in the hope that the price will rise, without a margin of safety in value.
The gap between a cautious estimate of value and the price you pay.
Graham's picture of the market as a moody partner offering prices you may take or ignore.
Current assets divided by current liabilities.
Current assets minus all liabilities, with nothing for factories or brands.
A company's assets minus its liabilities, as shown in its accounts.
The share price divided by the profit per share.
Selling some of what has risen and buying what has fallen, to return to a set mix.

themes.title: Mr Market
themes.idea: Picture a partner who offers every day to buy your share or sell you his, at a price that depends on his mood. You may take his offer or ignore it.
ask: When did Mr Market last offer you a silly price, high or low?
Would you check a share's price every day if you owned the whole business?

themes.title: Margin of safety
themes.idea: Pay well below what something is worth. The gap protects you from your own mistakes, bad luck and the unknown.
ask: What is your cautious estimate of one company's value? How far below it is the price?
What could go wrong that your margin would have to absorb?

themes.title: Know which investor you are
themes.idea: He split investors in two. Defensive investors want safety and little effort; enterprising ones will put in time and skill. Mixing the two is the danger.
ask: Honestly, how many hours a month do you give to investing?
Which investor are you, and does your portfolio match?

themes.title: Seven tests for the defensive investor
themes.idea: For investors who want safety, he set seven plain tests: size, strong finances, steady earnings, dividends, growth, and moderate prices against earnings and assets.
ask: Try the tests on one company you know. Which does it fail?
Why might a great company fail these tests?

themes.title: Buying below working capital
themes.idea: His favourite bargain: shares selling for less than the company's current assets minus all its debts, giving nothing at all for factories or brands.
ask: Why might a company sell for less than its cash and stock in hand?
What could make such a bargain a trap?

themes.title: Simple rules, many stocks
themes.idea: Late in life he decided that detailed analysis rarely paid any more. Better to buy groups of cheap shares by simple rules, and to sell by rules too.
ask: Do you have a rule for selling, or only for buying?
How would a group of 30 cheap shares behave differently from one?

themes.title: Stocks and bonds: the 25–75 rule
themes.idea: Keep at least a quarter of your money in shares and at least a quarter in bonds, always. Rebalance as markets move.
ask: What share of your savings is in shares today? Would you keep it there after a 40% fall?
When did you last rebalance?
themes.caption: Never less than 25% in either; lean towards bonds when prices are high, towards shares when they are low.

themes.title: The market catches up with value
themes.idea: Prices can stray far from value for a long time. But, as he told the Senate, the market eventually catches up.
ask: How long would you wait for a cheap share to reach its value?
Why might the market be slow to notice value?
themes.caption: In the short run prices follow the crowd's votes; over time they follow the weight of value.

themes.title: Loss, luck and generosity
themes.idea: The crash taught him caution, GEICO taught him how much luck matters, and his friends remembered his generosity.
ask: What did your worst loss teach you?
Have you ever mistaken one lucky win for skill?

t1n1.text: After thorough analysis, an investment promises safety of the money you put in and an adequate return. Whatever fails that test is speculative.

t1n2.text: A share has one investment side, the business growing over decades, and one speculative side, prices swinging with hope, fear and greed.

t1n3.text: He did not forbid speculation; he asked that you do it knowingly, with money you can afford to lose, and keep it apart from your investments.

t1n4.text: The investor's main problem is usually himself: his moods, not the market.

t2n1.text: Mr Market turns up daily with a price. Some days he is euphoric and asks too much; some days gloomy and sells too cheap.

t2n2.text: You are never obliged to trade. His offers are there to use when they suit you.

t2n3.text: For a true investor, price swings mean one thing: a chance to buy wisely after sharp falls and sell wisely after big rises. Otherwise, forget the market.

t2n4.text: Buffett wrote that this picture of Mr Market describes the attitude to price swings he finds most useful for investing.

t3n1.text: He called the margin of safety the central concept of investment, the closing chapter of his book.

t3n2.text: In his last interview: every purchase, and the price paid, should be justified by a margin of safety in value terms.

t3n3.text: Buffett summed up Graham's school as buying a dollar of value for 40 cents, then waiting.

t3n4.text: A margin of safety works on average, not every time, which is why he spread his money across many holdings.

t4n1.text: A defensive investor wants freedom from bother and serious mistakes. Simple rules and a balanced portfolio suit him.

t4n2.text: An enterprising investor is willing to spend real time and care to earn more than average, and must have the knowledge to do it.

t4n3.text: The difference is the work you will do, not how much risk you will take.

t4n4.text: A sound, if unspectacular, result needs little effort. Doing better than that takes much more work and some wisdom.

t5n1.text: A large company, with current assets at least twice current liabilities and long-term debt no larger than working capital.

t5n2.text: Earnings in each of the past ten years, dividends paid without a break for twenty, and earnings up at least a third over ten years.

t5n3.text: No more than 15 times average earnings of the past three years, and no more than 1.5 times book value, or a product of the two no higher than 22.5.

t5n4.text: Few companies pass all seven. The tests are meant to keep a defensive investor away from trouble, not to find the next great growth story.

t6n1.text: Buy shares priced below net current asset value: current assets minus every liability, with fixed assets counted as zero.

t6n2.text: He said this method had earned about 20% a year over more than 30 years.

t6n3.text: Such bargains grew scarce in the boom years, then returned after the 1973 to 1974 crash: in January 1976 he counted over 300, about a tenth of listed shares.

t6n4.text: He applied it to a spread of such shares, not one or two, so that the winners outweighed the disappointments.

t7n1.text: Elaborate research rewarded investors forty years earlier; by 1976 he thought it rarely justified its cost.

t7n2.text: Buy groups of shares at no more than seven times the past year's earnings. He said tests of this kind showed 15% a year or better from 1925 to 1975.

t7n3.text: Set a profit target of 50% to 100%, and sell anything that has not reached it within two or three years.

t7n4.text: Institutions are limited to some 300 to 400 huge companies; an individual can choose from about 3,000.

t8n1.text: Hold no less than 25% in shares and no less than 25% in bonds or their equivalent; a 50–50 split is a sensible default.

t8n2.text: After a big rise in shares, move some into bonds; after a fall, do the reverse.

t8n3.text: He suggested bond holdings averaging seven or eight years to maturity.

t8n4.text: A fixed rule stops you buying more just because prices rose and selling just because they fell.

t9n1.text: Asked by a senator how a cheap share ever reaches its value, he called it one of the mysteries of the business, but said experience shows it does.

t9n2.text: In 1984 Buffett showed nine investors from Graham's school beating the market over long periods with different stocks.

t9n3.text: Buffett's point: if the winners all come from one small village of thinking, the method matters, not chance.

t9n4.text: Graham doubted most professionals could beat the averages, and thought clients should expect roughly index results.

t10n1.text: From 1929 to 1932 his account fell about 70%. He blamed his own borrowing, not the crash.

t10n2.text: From 1945 to 1956, leaving out GEICO, Graham-Newman earned 17.4% a year against 18.3% for the S&P 500, with far smaller swings.

t10n3.text: GEICO, bought against his own rule of wide diversification, made more than all his other decisions together. He drew the lesson himself in his book.

t10n4.text: He quietly helped refugees from Nazi Germany, read Greek and Latin, and translated a Spanish novel into English.

sp.title: Try his seven tests on a company

tests.label: Adequate size
tests.help: A large, established company. His 1973 line: at least $100 million of yearly sales for an industrial firm.

tests.label: Strong finances: current ratio
tests.help: Current assets ÷ current liabilities. Passes at 2 or more.

tests.label: Strong finances: debt below working capital
tests.help: Debt due after a year is no larger than current assets minus current liabilities.

tests.label: A profit every year for 10 years
tests.help: No loss in any of the past ten years.

tests.label: Dividends for 20 years
tests.help: Paid without a break for at least twenty years.

tests.label: Earnings up a third in 10 years
tests.help: Compare three-year averages at the start and the end.

tests.label: Price to book value
tests.help: Passes at 1.5 or below, or if P/E × P/B is 22.5 or less.

sp.note: His 1973 tests for defensive investors in US industrial companies, as a study aid. Numbers are for learning, not a recommendation; he expected few companies to pass.

sp.title: A quick price check
sp.text: Tests 6 and 7 together cap the price at the square root of 22.5 × earnings per share × book value per share. People now call this the Graham number. Enter a company's figures to see it.
sp.note: Use average earnings over three years, as he did. A loss-making company has no Graham number.

sp.text: Graham called himself a defensive investor's teacher first. These tests protect; they do not promise big gains.

fisher.name: Philip Fisher
fisher.what: His books and own story on finding outstanding companies and holding them for decades
fisher.scope: Fisher published no audited record of his results, so we show none. His books are short and still in print together in one volume; his own story is in Developing an Investment Philosophy (1980).
fisher.readHow: Start with the first three chapters of Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits: the scuttlebutt method and the fifteen points.
fisher.sourcesNote: Sources: Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits (1958), Paths to Wealth through Common Stocks (1960), Conservative Investors Sleep Well (1975), Developing an Investment Philosophy (1980), his New York Times obituary (2004) and Forbes's 1969 profile of Buffett. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

start.lede: Philip Fisher ran his own investment firm in San Francisco from 1931 until he retired at 91. Where Graham looked for cheap shares, Fisher looked for outstanding companies, found out everything about them by talking to the people around them, and then held on, in Motorola's case for nearly fifty years. Buffett once said he was 15% Fisher.
start.para: This page draws on his four books, written between 1958 and 1980, his obituary, and Buffett's comments. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

glossary: Information gathered informally from people who deal with a company.
A share in a company expected to grow sales and profits much faster than average.
Profit as a share of sales.
Spending on new products and processes.
When a company issues new shares, each existing share owns less of it.
Spreading money across many holdings to reduce the harm of any one mistake.
A company that can make its product more cheaply than its rivals.
Part of a company's profit paid out to shareholders.

units.summary: His main book: the scuttlebutt method, the fifteen points, when to buy and sell, dividends, and ten don'ts for investors.

themes.title: Scuttlebutt
themes.idea: Find out about a company from the people around it: customers, suppliers, competitors, former employees and scientists. Only then visit the managers.
ask: Who, outside a company you own, could tell you how good it really is?
What would its customers say about it?
themes.caption: Ask the people around a company before you ask the company itself.

themes.title: The fifteen points
themes.idea: He listed fifteen questions an outstanding company should answer well. A company need not pass all, but must pass most.
ask: Which three of the fifteen points matter most to you?
Can you answer them for a company you own?

themes.title: Ability and integrity
themes.idea: Two traits in the people who run a company are essential: business ability, and honesty. Without both, he would not invest.
ask: How would you find out whether a management is honest?
When did a company you follow last report bad news plainly?

themes.title: Growth that lasts
themes.idea: Look for companies that can keep growing for years, because they keep developing new products. Fortunes come from seeing big changes early.
ask: Which change in the world today will lift a whole group of companies?
What will a company you own sell in ten years?

themes.title: Conservative investors sleep well
themes.idea: A conservative investment keeps your purchasing power with the least risk. He defined it in four dimensions.
ask: Which company you know is the lowest-cost producer in its industry?
Would you sleep well owning it in a crash?

themes.title: When to sell: almost never
themes.idea: If you bought the right company, the time to sell is almost never. He gave three reasons to sell, and dismissed the rest.
ask: Have you sold a great company only because it rose? What happened next?
Which of his three reasons applies to anything you own today?

themes.title: Own the best, not the most
themes.idea: Over-diversifying into companies you don't know well is riskier than owning a few you know thoroughly.
ask: How many companies can you truly follow?
Which holding would you drop if you could only keep five?

themes.title: Don't follow the crowd
themes.idea: Prices swing with fashion. Look years ahead, buy when fear runs high, and judge price by tomorrow's earnings, not today's.
ask: What does the crowd dislike right now? Is it right?
What would a company you like earn in three years?

themes.title: Dividends matter less
themes.idea: He thought investors made too much fuss about dividends. A company that can reinvest profits well usually serves owners better by doing so.
ask: Would you rather a company paid you 3% or reinvested it at 20%?
Does a company you own have a clear dividend policy?

themes.title: Lessons from his own mistakes
themes.idea: He saw the 1929 crash coming and still lost money. He started his firm in the Depression with almost nothing, and built his method from mistakes.
ask: When did you know you were right and still lose money?
What standard would you set for someone managing your money?

t1n1.text: He found the business grapevine remarkably informative: put together many small views and a clear picture forms.

t1n2.text: Ask five companies in an industry about the strengths and weaknesses of the other four, and you will learn a great deal about all five.

t1n3.text: Meet management only after the scuttlebutt, so you know which questions matter.

t1n4.text: Buffett said that from Fisher he learned the value of the scuttlebutt approach.

t1n5.text: His habit began at business school, visiting companies each week with a professor.

t2n1.text: Products or services with enough market to lift sales sizably for years, and a management determined to find the next ones.

t2n2.text: Effective research for its size, and a sales organisation better than average.

t2n3.text: A worthwhile profit margin, and a plan to keep or improve it.

t2n4.text: Good relations with staff and among executives, depth of management, and sound cost controls.

t2n5.text: A company that fails one or two points can still be outstanding; one that fails many is not.

t3n1.text: He learned early that the people running a company need two things: business ability and integrity.

t3n2.text: His last point asks whether management has unquestionable integrity. Managers are far closer to the assets than shareholders are.

t3n3.text: Beware managers who talk freely when things go well but clam up when trouble comes.

t3n4.text: Ask whether growth will need so many new shares that existing owners gain little.

t4n1.text: Ask what the company will sell once today's products are fully exploited.

t4n2.text: Now and then a deep change, in technology or in society, lifts or sinks a whole group of companies at once.

t4n3.text: The big gains go to those who see what such a change means before everyone else does.

t4n4.text: He bought Motorola in 1955, when it was still a radio maker, and held it for the rest of his life.

t5n1.text: To be truly conservative, a company must be the lowest-cost producer, or close to it, and strong in marketing, research and finance.

t5n2.text: Second, the people: able and honest managers.

t5n3.text: Third, a business whose nature lets it earn better than average returns.

t5n4.text: Fourth, the price: a great company can still be a poor buy if the market already prices it for perfection.

t6n1.text: You made a mistake: the company is not what you thought.

t6n2.text: The company has changed and no longer passes the fifteen points as it did.

t6n3.text: A clearly better opportunity appears; he thought this should be rare.

t6n4.text: A big rise in price, or fear of a market fall, is not a reason to sell an outstanding company.

t7n1.text: Owning too many companies means owning ones you cannot follow properly.

t7n2.text: Spread enough that one mistake cannot cripple you, then take care to own the best, not the most.

t7n3.text: He held a small number of companies for very long periods, Motorola above all.

t7n4.text: In 1969 Buffett described himself as 85% Graham and 15% Fisher: cheapness from one, quality from the other.

t8n1.text: Don't be afraid of buying when war fears push prices down.

t8n2.text: With a true growth company, waiting for a perfect price can cost more than paying a fair one.

t8n3.text: He came to see that a company's price against its earnings a few years out matters far more than today's figure.

t8n4.text: Good moments to buy often come when a passing problem makes the market think less of an outstanding company than it deserves.

t9n1.text: He devoted a chapter to what he saw as excessive attention to dividends.

t9n2.text: A fast-growing company that reinvests profits at high returns may do far more for owners than one that pays them out.

t9n3.text: What matters is a dividend policy that is clear and consistent, so owners know what to expect.

t10n1.text: He later called his first job, as a bank's securities analyst, intellectually dishonest, and resolved to work differently.

t10n2.text: In August 1929 he warned his bank of the worst bear market in 25 years, then bought shares he thought cheap and lost money in the crash.

t10n3.text: He opened his firm with costs of $25 a month and made $3 a month in the first year.

t10n4.text: He told clients to fire him if he had not produced worthwhile results within three years.

items: Its market can lift sales sizably for years

All fifteen. Rare: check the last point twice, then the price.
Most points passed: a candidate for deeper scuttlebutt.

items: the company was never what you thought.
it no longer passes the points as it did.

items: just because it trades off the main exchange.
means the growth is already priced in.

templeton.name: John Templeton
templeton.what: His rules, his famous trades and his search for bargains all over the world
templeton.scope: Templeton was born and built his career in the United States; in the 1960s he gave up US citizenship, became British and later lived in the Bahamas. He wrote mostly about life and faith, and less about investing, so his 16 rules are the main source in his own words.
templeton.readHow: Start with his 16 rules for investment success, free as a short brochure from Franklin Templeton.
templeton.sourcesNote: Sources: his 16 rules (World Monitor, 1993), obituaries in the Washington Post, the Irish Times and by AP (2008), Morningstar and interactive investor profiles, Financial Advisor magazine, an LGT study of his method, and Investing the Templeton Way (2008). Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

start.lede: John Templeton grew up in a small town in Tennessee, won a Rhodes scholarship, and in 1939 borrowed $10,000 to buy every cheap share he could as war broke out. His Templeton Growth Fund, started in 1954, looked for bargains across the world long before that was usual. His creed: buy at the point of maximum pessimism, search everywhere, stay humble, and never think you know it all.
start.para: This page draws on his 16 rules for investment success (1993), obituaries, his great-niece's book about his methods, and reports of his trades. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

glossary: His own name for his style: buying shares far below what they are worth.
Your return after tax and inflation.
Borrowing shares to sell them, hoping to buy them back later at a lower price.
A period after a share's first listing when insiders may not sell.
A company's first sale of shares to the public.
A pooled fund that invests many people's money together.
Spreading money across many holdings to reduce the harm of any one mistake.

themes.title: Buy at maximum pessimism
themes.idea: Shares only become bargains when people sell them, and people sell when they are gloomy. So the best time to buy is when almost everyone else is pessimistic.
ask: What are people most gloomy about right now?
Have you ever bought something everyone else was selling?
themes.caption: He bought when the mood was darkest and sold when it was brightest.

themes.title: The 1939 basket
themes.idea: As war broke out in Europe, he borrowed $10,000 and bought 100 shares in each of 104 companies trading at $1 or less. Nearly all of them made money.
ask: Why did buying all 104 make more sense than picking five?
Would you borrow to invest? What could go wrong?
themes.caption: 104 companies: 34 in bankruptcy, but only 4 ended worthless.

themes.title: Search the whole world
themes.idea: He looked for bargains in every country, not just at home. That was rare in the 1950s, and it gave him far more choices.
ask: Which markets do you never look at? Why?
What could you learn from investors in another country?

themes.title: Bargains among quality
themes.idea: Cheap is not enough. He looked for good businesses, with strong market positions and capable managers, at low prices.
ask: Is a company you like cheap because it is bad, or because people are scared?
What might it earn in five years?

themes.title: Value, not forecasts
themes.idea: Buy individual companies on their own merits, not on what you think the economy or the market will do.
ask: When did an economic forecast last change what you bought? Was it right?
What do you know about a company's earnings that the market may be ignoring?

themes.title: Diversify, and keep watching
themes.idea: There is safety in numbers. Spread your money by industry, by risk and by country, and keep checking what you own.
ask: How much of your money depends on one country or one industry?
When did you last check why you own each holding?

themes.title: Don't panic
themes.idea: When markets crash, don't sell in fear. And don't be gloomy too often: over time, optimism has paid.
ask: What did you do in the last big market fall?
What would you do if your shares fell 30% tomorrow?

themes.title: Selling into euphoria
themes.idea: The mirror of buying at maximum pessimism is selling at maximum optimism. In 2000, aged 87, he bet heavily against overpriced technology shares.
ask: What looks absurdly priced today?
Why is betting on a fall riskier than buying?

themes.title: Humility
themes.idea: Invest, don't speculate. Learn from mistakes, accept there is no free lunch, and never think you know it all.
ask: What mistake have you repeated more than once?
Where are you most sure of yourself? Should you be?

themes.title: Distance, thrift and giving
themes.idea: He did his best work far from Wall Street, lived frugally, and gave much of his fortune to the study of the spiritual side of life.
ask: Would you invest better further from the daily news?
What would you do with a fortune once you had enough?

t1n1.text: Buy when others are despondently selling, and sell when they are greedily buying. Following the crowd means buying what is already expensive.

t1n2.text: The only way a share gets cheap is that people sell it, and the usual reason they sell is pessimism.

t1n3.text: A line widely credited to him describes a bull market's life: born on pessimism, growing on scepticism, maturing on optimism, dying on euphoria.

t1n4.text: He kept a wish list of quality companies, with orders ready to buy if prices collapsed, so fear could not stop him acting.

t2n1.text: In 1939 he bought 100 shares in each of 104 companies selling at $1 or less, including 34 in bankruptcy.

t2n2.text: Just four of the 104 let him down; after repaying the loan he had a handsome profit.

t2n3.text: He reasoned that in wartime, things that were in surplus and unprofitable become scarce and profitable.

t2n4.text: He borrowed the money, a big risk for a young man; he spread it across 104 companies so no single failure could sink him.

t3n1.text: He launched the Templeton Growth Fund in 1954, incorporated in Canada, and it searched for bargains across the world.

t3n2.text: He bought large holdings in Japan while its economy was still recovering from the war, and sold them in the boom years of the 1980s.

t3n3.text: Diversify by country as well as industry: more markets mean more chances to find something cheap.

t3n4.text: After Oxford he spent seven months travelling the world with a friend, on very little money, before starting work in New York.

t4n1.text: Search for bargains among quality companies: a strong market position, capable management and enough capital.

t4n2.text: He judged price against estimated earnings about five years ahead, and avoided shares above roughly 12 to 14 times.

t4n3.text: He held shares for about four years on average.

t4n4.text: From 1978, when Ford looked headed for bankruptcy, he bought and kept buying as the shares fell further. By 1987 they were worth many times his price.

t5n1.text: Buy value, not market trends or the economic outlook. Individual shares can move against the market.

t5n2.text: Study a company carefully before you buy, or hire wise experts to do it for you.

t5n3.text: No type of investment is always best. Stay open to shares, bonds and cash, and hold cash when bargains are scarce.

t6n1.text: Diversify by industry, by risk and by country, so that one setback cannot ruin you.

t6n2.text: Monitor your investments: markets change, companies rise and fall, and no share should be bought and forgotten.

t6n3.text: Aim for the best total return after tax and inflation; anything else is not a real return.

t7n1.text: In a crash, don't sell just because everyone else is. Sell only if you find something clearly more attractive.

t7n2.text: He warned against investors who think this time is different when it is really a repeat of the past.

t7n3.text: His last rule: do not be fearful or negative too often. Over decades, shares have risen despite many falls.

t8n1.text: He said technology shares had reached 100 times earnings, or 20 times sales where there were no earnings.

t8n2.text: He bet against dozens of newly listed technology shares that had soared, timed for just before insiders were free to sell.

t8n3.text: According to his great-niece, he put about $185 million into these bets and made about $90 million.

t8n4.text: He usually bought; betting on falls was something he did only when prices looked truly absurd.

t9n1.text: Frequent trading and speculation tend to lose money in costs and mistimed moves.

t9n2.text: Study your errors, forgive yourself, and don't try to win losses back with bigger risks.

t9n3.text: Don't invest on tips or sentiment; there is no free lunch.

t9n4.text: An active Presbyterian, he began meetings with a prayer, which he believed clears the mind and reduces mistakes.

t9n5.text: An investor who has all the answers doesn't even understand all the questions.

t10n1.text: His record improved after he moved away from Wall Street to the Bahamas in 1968, where he worked largely by fax.

t10n2.text: He paid part of his way through Yale with poker winnings after the Depression hit his father, and in the Bahamas he drove old cars.

t10n3.text: In 1972 he created the Templeton Prize, meant as a Nobel-style award for progress in religion.

t10n4.text: He was knighted in 1987 for his philanthropy, and set up the John Templeton Foundation the same year.

quotes.text: It was insane, and I took advantage of the temporary insanity.

items: Prices have fallen hard, the news is grim and people are selling to escape.
This is the point he looked for: buy, carefully, among quality companies.
Prices are recovering, but most people doubt it will last.
Keep holding; bargains are getting rarer but still exist.
Rising prices feel normal and good news is everywhere.
Be selective. Fewer bargains; check each holding is still cheap.
Everyone is talking about shares, and 'this time is different' is in the air.
Time to sell what is overpriced. In 2000 he even bet on falls.

bogle.name: John Bogle
bogle.what: His books, speeches and life on low costs, index funds and investing for the long run
bogle.scope: Bogle wrote twelve books; we use The Little Book of Common Sense Investing (2007, revised 2017) as the main one. Vanguard's own funds are mentioned for history only, not as a recommendation.
bogle.readHow: Start with The Little Book of Common Sense Investing. It is short, and each chapter makes one point.
bogle.sourcesNote: Sources: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing (2007), Vanguard's 2019 announcement of his death, obituaries by the Associated Press, the Telegraph and Morningstar, a trade-press obituary, and Buffett's letter for 2016. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

start.lede: John Bogle, called Jack, founded Vanguard in 1974 and in 1976 launched the first index fund for ordinary investors. Critics called it Bogle's folly. His idea was simple: most investors cannot beat the market after costs, so own the whole market as cheaply as possible and hold it. Warren Buffett later said that if anyone deserves a statue for helping American investors, it is Bogle.
start.para: This page draws on his best-known book, a landmark speech, obituaries from Vanguard, the Associated Press, the Telegraph and Morningstar, and Buffett's 2016 letter. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

glossary: A fund that simply owns all the shares in a market index, such as the S&P 500, instead of picking.
A fund's yearly running costs, as a percentage of the money invested.
Picking investments in an attempt to beat the market.
How much of a fund's holdings it sells and replaces in a year.
A legal and moral duty to act in someone else's best interest.
A pooled fund that invests many people's money together.
Earning returns on past returns, so growth speeds up over time.

themes.title: Buy the haystack
themes.idea: Instead of searching for the few stocks or funds that will beat the market, buy the whole market through a low-cost index fund, and hold it.
ask: How many of your holdings have beaten the market after all costs?
What would you gain, and lose, by owning the whole market?
themes.caption: Picking the few winning stocks is hard. Owning all of them guarantees you hold the winners.

themes.title: Costs matter
themes.idea: Returns are uncertain; costs are certain. Every fee and commission comes straight out of what you earn, and over decades the damage compounds.
ask: What do you pay each year, in total, to invest?
How much would that cost add up to over 30 years?
themes.caption: The same market return, two different yearly fees: the gap widens every year.

themes.title: The simple arithmetic
themes.idea: All investors together own the market. So, before costs, they earn the market's return; after costs, they must earn less. Beating the market is a loser's game for most.
ask: Why can't most investors beat the average they make up?
Who is on the other side of your trades?

themes.title: Bogle's folly
themes.idea: His first index fund was mocked and nearly failed to launch. He stood behind it for years until the idea won.
ask: What idea do you hold that most people laugh at?
How long would you stick with it?

themes.title: Owned by its investors
themes.idea: After losing his job in 1974, he built Vanguard differently: the fund company is owned by its funds, and so by their investors, not by outside shareholders.
ask: Whose interests come first at the companies that manage your money?
How would you know?

themes.title: Time is your friend
themes.idea: Buy, hold, and stay the course. Trading in and out, and chasing what has done well, is how investors lose the market's return.
ask: When did you last sell in fear, or buy in excitement?
What would make you abandon a 30-year plan?

themes.title: Yesterday's winners, tomorrow's losers
themes.idea: Funds that topped the charts rarely stay on top. Chasing past performance means buying high and paying for luck.
ask: Did you ever buy a fund because of last year's return? How did it do?
How would you tell skill from luck?

themes.title: Taxes and trading
themes.idea: Trading costs money twice: in commissions and in taxes. Low turnover keeps more of the return working for you.
ask: How often do you trade? What did it cost last year, including tax?
What would happen if you traded half as often?

themes.title: A duty of trust
themes.idea: He believed managing other people's money is a duty, not just a business, and spent his later years saying so.
ask: Does the firm that manages your money act like a professional or a salesman?
What would a duty of trust mean in your own work?

themes.title: A statue, a heart, and enough
themes.idea: He took far less from his work than he could have, survived years of heart disease, and was honoured by Buffett as the person who did most for American investors.
ask: How much is enough for you?
What would you do with your work if money were not the goal?

t1n1.text: Don't hunt for the needle; buy the whole haystack. An index fund owns every company, so it is sure to own the winners.

t1n2.text: Successful investing is simple, he wrote, but it takes discipline and patience to stick with it.

t1n3.text: The book's subtitle promised only your fair share of the market's return, which most investors fail to get.

t1n4.text: Index funds already existed for big institutions; his was the first one ordinary savers could buy.

t2n1.text: He set the magic of compounding returns against the tyranny of compounding costs. Over long periods costs can eat a large part of your gains.

t2n2.lead: You get what you don't pay for.
t2n2.text: In most things you get what you pay for; in fund investing, he argued, the money you don't pay in fees is what you keep.

t2n3.text: One chapter tells investors simply to focus on the lowest-cost funds.

t2n4.text: His obituaries describe a career spent pushing for lower fees for ordinary investors.

t3n1.text: As a group, investors earn exactly the market's return before costs, and less after them. Someone's gain over the average is someone else's loss.

t3n2.text: Trying to beat the market is a loser's game for most, he wrote: the more the managers and brokers take, the less investors make.

t3n3.text: Buffett bet that an S&P 500 index fund would beat five funds of hedge funds over ten years. By 2016, $1 million in the index fund had gained $854,000; the hedge funds, $220,000.

t3n4.text: Buffett told both large and small investors to stick with low-cost index funds.

t4n1.text: First Index Investment Trust launched on 31 August 1976 with only about $11 million (sources say $11 million to $11.4 million).

t4n2.text: Rivals called it Bogle's folly and said it aimed only for average results.

t4n3.text: Vanguard says he stood behind the idea, in the face of sceptics, until it was widely accepted.

t4n4.text: The fund became the Vanguard 500 Index Fund and a huge success.

t5n1.text: He lost his job running Wellington after the falling stock market of the early 1970s and a quarrel with his partners.

t5n2.text: In most fund companies an outside management firm runs the funds for its own profit. At Vanguard the funds own the manager.

t5n3.text: Morningstar called Vanguard the first, and still the only, mutually owned fund family.

t5n4.text: He named it after Nelson's flagship at the Battle of the Nile.

t6n1.text: His simplest strategy: buy and hold all of a nation's listed businesses, at very low cost, for good.

t6n2.text: In the long run, he argued, the returns of businesses, their dividends and earnings growth, matter more than the market's moods.

t6n3.text: He saw the two great enemies of investors as expenses and emotions.

t6n4.text: Followers who share his buy-and-hold approach call themselves Bogleheads.

t7n1.text: A chapter titled Yesterday's Winners, Tomorrow's Losers shows how top funds tend to sink back towards the average.

t7n2.text: He warned that a hot record is often luck, and luck does not repeat.

t7n3.text: Many funds that once looked good were later closed or merged out of existence.

t7n4.text: Even advisers picking funds for you face the same problem, he wrote, so be wary of paying for selection.

t8n1.text: One chapter's title tells investors not to pay the tax authorities any more than they should.

t8n2.text: Funds that trade a lot pass on costs and taxes that an index fund, which rarely sells, largely avoids.

t8n3.text: He was wary of exchange-traded funds when they were used for frequent trading rather than holding.

t9n1.text: He told the fund industry it must change its pricing, products and promotion, and hold itself to higher standards of trust and fiduciary duty.

t9n2.text: He argued fund management should behave like a profession rather than a mere industry.

t9n3.text: Morningstar wrote that admirers and critics alike agreed he was a man of irreproachable integrity.

t10n1.text: Buffett wrote that if a statue is ever built for the person who did most for American investors, it should be of Bogle.

t10n2.text: Buffett noted that Bogle's low-cost funds earned him only a tiny share of the wealth that flowed to managers who charged far more.

t10n3.text: He received a heart transplant in 1996, a month after handing Vanguard to John Brennan.

t10n4.text: In 2012 he said his one regret was not having more to give away.

marks.name: Howard Marks
marks.what: His memos and books on risk, cycles and thinking differently from the crowd
marks.scope: Marks is still working and writing; facts are as of late 2026. Oaktree's funds are mentioned for history only; this page says nothing about investing with any firm.
marks.readHow: Start with his first memo, The Route to Performance (1990), three pages long, then the book The Most Important Thing (2011).
marks.sourcesNote: Sources: his memos The Route to Performance (1990), You Can't Predict. You Can Prepare. (2001), Taking the Temperature (2023) and The Best of (2025); his books The Most Important Thing (2011) and Mastering the Market Cycle (2018); a Goldman Sachs talk; and a CFA Institute report of a 2019 talk. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

start.lede: Howard Marks co-founded Oaktree Capital in 1995 and is best known for his memos to clients, which he has written since 1990. Buffett says they are the first thing he opens. Marks's message: you cannot predict the future, but you can know where you stand in the cycle, avoid big losses, and think differently from the crowd.
start.para: This page draws on his memos, which are free on Oaktree's website, his two books, and his talks. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

glossary: Thinking about what others think, and what is already reflected in the price.
Bonds and loans of companies in, or close to, financial trouble.
A bond from a riskier company that pays more interest; also called a junk bond.
The repeated rise and fall of economies, profits, credit and moods.
A ranking out of 100: the 4th percentile means better than 96% of the group.
What an asset is really worth, based on what it will earn.
How much and how fast a price moves up and down.

themes.title: Second-level thinking
themes.idea: To do better than others you must think differently, and better. First-level thinking asks whether something is good; second-level thinking asks what is already in the price.
ask: What does everyone believe about a company you own?
Is that belief already in the price?
themes.caption: First-level: it's a good company, buy. Second-level: everyone thinks so, so it's overpriced.

themes.title: Risk means losing money
themes.idea: For Marks, risk is not the jiggling of prices. It is the chance of a permanent loss, and it is hardest to see when times are good.
ask: What could make one of your investments lose money for good?
When did you last feel risk didn't matter?

themes.title: It's what you pay
themes.idea: There is no such thing as a good or bad asset in itself, only a good or bad price. A great company bought too dear can be a poor investment.
ask: Which great company would you refuse to buy at today's price?
Which unloved asset might be cheap enough to be safe?

themes.title: The pendulum
themes.idea: Investor psychology swings like a pendulum between greed and fear, optimism and despair. It spends little time at the sensible midpoint.
ask: Where is the pendulum today: greed or fear?
How did you feel at the last extreme?
themes.caption: Investor moods swing from greed to fear and back, spending little time in the sensible middle.

themes.title: You can't predict. You can prepare.
themes.idea: Nobody can forecast the economy or the market reliably. But you can know roughly where you are in the cycle and prepare for what usually follows.
ask: What are you assuming will happen next? What if it doesn't?
How would you prepare for a 40% fall without predicting one?

themes.title: Take the temperature
themes.idea: Watch how people around you behave. When everyone is eager and careless, be careful; when everyone is frightened, look for bargains.
ask: What do people around you say about the market this month?
Are you feeling it too?

themes.title: bubble.com
themes.idea: In January 2000, near the peak of the technology bubble, he warned that internet and telecom shares had become a bubble. It burst within weeks.
ask: What looks like a bubble today? What would prove you wrong?
How would you act on a warning without betting everything on it?

themes.title: Buying in the panic
themes.idea: Being prepared paid off in late 2008. When panic was at its worst, Oaktree had money ready and spent it.
ask: Do you keep money ready for a panic?
What would you buy if prices halved tomorrow?

themes.title: Avoid the losers
themes.idea: Superior results over time come less from big wins than from avoiding big losses. His very first memo made the point.
ask: What was your worst year? What would avoiding it have meant for your total?
Do you aim to win big or to avoid losing big?

themes.title: Writing to think, and saying 'I don't know'
themes.idea: His memos are how he thinks. He is candid about uncertainty and avoids flat predictions.
ask: Would writing down your reasons change your decisions?
When did you last say 'I don't know' about the market?

t1n1.text: His book opens with second-level thinking: a simple, obvious view cannot beat the market, because everyone already holds it.

t1n2.text: If you think like everyone else you will act like them and get the same results; you have to think differently from the norm.

t1n3.text: A first-level thinker says a company is good, so buy. A second-level thinker asks whether everyone agrees, and whether the price already reflects it.

t1n4.text: He warns that second-level thinking is hard work and that easy formulas are a sign of first-level thinking.

t2n1.text: The most important risk is the chance of losing money, not short-term volatility.

t2n2.text: He devotes three chapters to risk: understanding it, recognising it and controlling it.

t2n3.text: Easy markets teach investors that risk doesn't matter, just before it does.

t2n4.text: Riskier assets must appear to offer higher returns, but that is a promise, not a guarantee.

t3n1.text: He gives separate chapters to value and to the relationship between price and value.

t3n2.text: A high-quality asset bought at too high a price can be risky; a low-quality one bought cheaply can be safe.

t3n3.text: His answer to when to buy is simple: when the price is below intrinsic value.

t4n1.text: His book has a chapter on awareness of the pendulum.

t4n2.text: Moods overshoot in both directions; the extremes are where mistakes, and opportunities, are made.

t4n3.text: His second book traces the cycles in the economy, in profits, in attitudes to risk, in credit and in investor psychology.

t5n1.text: He dismisses economic forecasts, which he thinks add no value, but believes deeply in cycles.

t5n2.text: The key is to know where you are, even if you cannot know exactly where you are going.

t5n3.text: He took the memo's title from an insurance company's advertising slogan.

t5n4.text: Since we never know what will happen, consider the likely scenarios and prepare for them.

t6n1.text: He judges the market by its psychology: is it buoyant and greedy, or depressed and fearful?

t6n2.text: A strong move one way is more likely to be followed by a correction than to grow to the sky.

t6n3.text: Beware optimism so strong that no price seems too high, and look for despair so deep that any sale seems good.

t6n4.text: Stand apart from the crowd, and act when you see something illogical.

t7n1.text: His January 2000 memo, bubble.com, warned of a bubble in technology, internet and telecom shares as it peaked.

t7n2.text: Oaktree owned little technology at the time.

t7n3.text: From 2004 to 2007 he grew steadily more cautious, selling assets and raising the bar for new investments before the crisis.

t8n1.text: Oaktree had raised a large fund for distressed debt before the crisis, so it could buy when others were forced to sell.

t8n2.text: From mid-September to the end of 2008 his partner Bruce Karsh's team invested about $400 million a week, about $6 billion.

t8n3.text: In 2020 he again bought as markets fell, accepting it might not be the lowest point.

t8n4.text: Extreme pessimism, in his view, is when risk is lowest and bargains are best.

t9n1.text: A pension fund he met was never in the top quarter in any of 14 years, yet ranked in the top 4% over the whole period.

t9n2.text: It never had a disastrous year, never falling below the middle of its peers.

t9n3.text: He argued that bold moves aimed at great performance are as likely to be wrong as right.

t9n4.text: He later said the memo set out what became a core part of Oaktree's investment philosophy.

t10n1.text: He has written memos to clients since 1990, and they are posted publicly on Oaktree's website.

t10n2.text: He says he never tells clients anything as flatly negative as to get out of the market.

t10n3.text: When asked something he can't answer, he says he doesn't know.

t10n4.text: Buffett has written that Marks's memos are the first thing he opens in his mail.

klarman.name: Seth Klarman
klarman.what: His book and interviews on margin of safety, avoiding loss and patience
klarman.scope: Klarman is still working, and Baupost is private; its returns are not published, so the figure we show is the reported one. His letters to clients are private and are not used here.
klarman.readHow: If you can find it, read Margin of Safety, chapters 5 and 6. Otherwise, start with his 2026 interview on Masters in Business.
klarman.sourcesNote: Sources: Margin of Safety (1991) and a summary of it, his 2026 Masters in Business interview, the Ivey Business School and Harvard profiles, and a 2018 report on the book. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

start.lede: Seth Klarman has run the Baupost Group in Boston since 1982, when four families hired him at 25 to manage about $27 million. In 1991 he wrote Margin of Safety, which sold few copies, went out of print and became a cult classic. His creed is Graham's, pushed further: avoid losing money first, value things cautiously, and wait for the market to offer a big discount.
start.para: This page draws on his 1991 book, a long 2026 interview, a university profile and reports on the book's strange history. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

themes.title: Avoid loss first
themes.idea: Klarman puts avoiding loss ahead of everything. A big loss takes a long time to recover from, so protecting money comes before chasing returns.
ask: Which of your holdings could fall 70% and stay down?
Would you survive that?

themes.title: Margin of safety
themes.idea: Valuation is never precise, the future is unknowable and people make mistakes. So buy only at a price far enough below value to absorb all three.
ask: How big a discount do you insist on before you buy?
What mistakes would that discount have to absorb?

themes.title: Investors and speculators
themes.idea: Investors buy businesses below their value; speculators bet on which way prices will move. Wall Street, he argues, mostly serves the speculators.
ask: Which of your trades were bets on price rather than value?
Who earns money from your activity?

themes.title: The performance derby
themes.idea: Many professional investors are judged every quarter against an index. That pushes them to follow the crowd, which creates chances for investors who don't have to.
ask: Do you judge yourself against an index or against your own goals?
What would you do differently if no one compared you each quarter?

themes.title: Value it three ways
themes.idea: No single method gives the true value. He discusses several, from future cash flows to break-up value to what similar companies fetch, and urges conservatism.
ask: What would a company you own fetch if it were broken up and sold?
How different are your three estimates?
themes.caption: Three ways to value a business; a cautious investor leans on the lowest.

themes.title: Look where others aren't
themes.idea: Bargains are most common in complicated, unpopular or forced-sale situations that most investors avoid.
ask: Which investments do most people avoid because they're complicated?
Who might be forced to sell right now?
themes.caption: Bargains hide where the crowd cannot or will not look.

themes.title: Cheap isn't enough
themes.idea: A cheap share can stay cheap for years. He looks for a catalyst, an event that can close the gap between price and value.
ask: What event could make the market see value in a share you own?
How long would you wait for it?

themes.title: Patience and cash
themes.idea: When there is nothing good to buy, hold cash rather than take more risk. But he admits that holding too much cash for too long was a mistake.
ask: How much cash do you hold, and why?
What does waiting cost you?

themes.title: Fear is useful
themes.idea: Klarman sees fear as protective. Being worried keeps you prepared; the danger is when everyone feels safe.
ask: When do you feel most confident about markets? Is that a warning?
Could anything force you to sell?

themes.title: A book that landed with a thud
themes.idea: His one book sold poorly, went out of print and became one of the most sought-after investing books in the world. His career began with two mentors and four families.
ask: Who were your mentors, and what did they teach you?
Would you write down your method for everyone to read?

t1n1.text: The book argues that avoiding loss should be every investor's first goal.

t1n2.text: The book's own subtitle describes its strategies as risk-averse.

t1n3.text: He tests each holding against severe scenarios, asking whether it would survive a collapse like 1933.

t1n4.text: Protecting the downside lets you keep buying when weaker investors are forced to sell.

t2n1.text: A margin of safety is needed because valuation is imprecise, the future is unpredictable and investors are human.

t2n2.text: He took the title from Graham, who made the margin of safety the central idea of The Intelligent Investor.

t2n3.text: Do the work to estimate value, assume you are wrong and cut the estimate, then wait for that lower price.

t2n4.text: Value investing with a margin of safety has tended to hold up well when markets fall.

t3n1.text: The book's first part covers speculators and unsuccessful investors and how they go wrong.

t3n2.text: He argues that Wall Street makes money from activity and fees, so its interests often work against investors.

t3n3.text: Separate price movements from the reality of the business behind them.

t3n4.text: Once you adopt a value approach, he wrote, other kinds of investing start to look like gambling.

t4n1.text: A chapter on the institutional performance derby argues that short-term relative performance contests hurt clients.

t4n2.text: Rules and habits that limit institutions can push prices away from value.

t4n3.text: Baupost judges itself on absolute returns, aiming to beat inflation by a wide margin rather than beat an index.

t5n1.text: The book discusses valuing a business by the present value of its future cash, by its liquidation or break-up value, and by stock market comparisons.

t5n2.text: Since no one can predict when values will rise or fall, value conservatively, giving real weight to worst-case liquidation value.

t5n3.text: Value is better thought of as a range than a precise figure, so leave room for error.

t6n1.text: The book discusses bankruptcies and financially distressed companies, thrift conversions and other neglected areas.

t6n2.text: He still looks in complicated corners such as distressed debt, real estate and private deals, where competition is thin.

t6n3.text: When others must sell, for rules or lack of cash, prices can fall well below value.

t6n4.text: He relies on studying individual investments, not big economic forecasts.

t7n1.text: In 2026 he said simply buying cheap things is not a strategy on its own.

t7n2.text: Baupost wants an identifiable event that can drive a turnaround within a year or two.

t7n3.text: One chapter on where to look starts with catalysts, alongside market inefficiencies and institutional constraints.

t8n1.text: He has said that, rather than take more risk, Baupost holds cash when opportunities are scarce.

t8n2.text: Cash is meant to be spent when bargains appear, not kept forever.

t8n3.text: He now says Baupost almost certainly held too much cash for too long, and has made its holdings more liquid so it needs less.

t8n4.text: He says he should have paid more attention to venture capital.

t9n1.text: He has said Baupost is a fan of fear: better to be scared than sorry.

t9n2.text: In 2026 he described the market as feeling stretched, expensive and speculative.

t9n3.text: Avoiding situations where you must sell at the worst time is essential.

t10n1.text: He learned the trade working for Max Heine and Michael Price at Mutual Shares.

t10n2.text: Baupost began in 1982 with about $27 million from four families who had sold businesses; he was 25.

t10n3.text: The book sold about 5,000 copies at $25. Used copies later sold for more than $1,000.

t10n4.text: In 2018 a $9.99 e-book briefly appeared on Amazon and sold thousands before vanishing.

t10n5.text: He edited the 2023 edition of Graham and Dodd's Security Analysis.

schloss.name: Walter Schloss
schloss.what: His one-page note, his record and his quiet way of beating the market for 47 years
schloss.scope: Schloss wrote little; his 1994 note is the main source in his own words. Sources give slightly different figures for his long-term record, so we show the range.
schloss.readHow: Read his one-page 1994 note, Factors Needed to Make Money in the Stock Market, then Buffett's 2006 letter where he writes about Schloss.
schloss.sourcesNote: Sources: his 1994 note of 16 factors, Buffett's 1984 talk and 2006 letter, an Outstanding Investor Digest interview (1989), obituaries in InvestmentNews/Bloomberg (2012) and Morningstar profiles. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

start.lede: Walter Schloss never went to college. He started as a Wall Street runner at 18, learned from Benjamin Graham at evening classes and worked for him before starting his own partnership in 1955. For 47 years he bought cheap shares by simple rules, owned around a hundred at a time, never visited managements and beat the market by a wide margin. Buffett called him one of the good guys of Wall Street.
start.para: This page draws on his 1994 note of 16 factors, Buffett's 1984 talk and 2006 letter, a 1989 interview, and obituaries. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.
