themes.title: Price comes first
themes.idea: His first factor: price, compared with value, is the most important thing. A share is part of a business, not a piece of paper.
ask: Do you know what a company you own is worth, roughly?
Would you buy the whole business at today's price?

themes.title: Assets over earnings
themes.idea: He preferred buying assets at a discount to buying earnings. Earnings can change fast; assets usually change slowly.
ask: What is the book value of a company you own? Is the price above or below it?
How much debt does it carry?
themes.caption: Book value usually moves slowly; earnings can swing wildly from year to year.

themes.title: Buy near the lows
themes.idea: He liked shares trading near the bottom of their range of recent years, and he was patient once he had bought.
ask: Where is a share you like in its range of the past five years?
How long are you prepared to wait?

themes.title: Own many, buy in steps
themes.idea: He spread his money across around a hundred shares and bought and sold gradually rather than all at once.
ask: How many holdings do you have? Could you follow a hundred?
Do you buy all at once, or in steps?
themes.caption: Buy a little at a time as the price falls; sell a little at a time as it rises.

themes.title: Public numbers only
themes.idea: He never visited managements or chased inside information. He read the published numbers, sent for annual reports and decided for himself.
ask: Could you make your decisions from published reports alone?
What do company meetings really add?

themes.title: Keep emotions out
themes.idea: Fear and greed are the worst emotions for an investor. Have your own method, follow it calmly, and don't be swayed by tips or crowds.
ask: When did a tip last make you buy? How did it go?
Can you write your method in one paragraph?

themes.title: Don't sell too soon
themes.idea: Many investors sell after a quick gain. He re-checked the company's value first, and watched the level of the whole market.
ask: What made you sell your last winner?
Was the company worth more than the price you sold at?

themes.title: Compounding, shares and leverage
themes.idea: Let returns compound, prefer shares to bonds over the long run, and be careful with borrowed money.
ask: How long will your money take to double at your expected return?
How much of your investing uses borrowed money?

themes.title: Paid only when partners gained
themes.idea: He charged no management fee. He took a share of profits only, and kept his costs tiny.
ask: How do the people managing your money get paid?
Are they paid when you lose?

themes.title: A quiet life on Wall Street
themes.idea: He came in as a teenage runner, learned from Graham, served in the war and ran his partnership for 47 years with his son. Buffett used his record to show that skill, not luck, can beat the market.
ask: What could you achieve with simple rules followed for decades?
Could you keep your method that long?

t1n1.text: Price, set against value, is the most important factor of all.

t1n2.text: Try to work out what the company is worth, remembering that a share is a piece of a business.

t1n3.text: Buffett said Schloss simply buys businesses selling for less than they are worth, and that's all he does.

t1n4.text: He picked shares by simple statistical methods learned while working for Graham.

t2n1.text: Use book value as the starting point for estimating what a business is worth.

t2n2.text: Make sure debt is well below the shareholders' equity.

t2n3.text: Earnings can change dramatically in a short time; you need to know far more about a company to buy its earnings.

t2n4.text: Unlike most analysts, he paid little attention to earnings growth or to management.

t3n1.text: He found it helpful to buy near the low of the past few years.

t3n2.text: A share that has fallen from 125 to 60 may look cheap, but if it was 20 three years ago, it may still be vulnerable.

t3n3.text: Stocks don't go up immediately; give them time.

t4n1.text: Buffett noted that Schloss owned well over 100 stocks at a time.

t4n2.text: Buy on a scale and sell on a scale: in steps, not all at once.

t4n3.text: A few big winners did not explain his success; it came from many modest ones.

t5n1.text: Buffett wrote that Walter and Edwin never came within a mile of inside information and used outside information only sparingly.

t5n2.text: He looked up the numbers in the manuals and sent for the annual reports.

t5n3.text: He worked without a secretary, clerk or bookkeeper; his only associate was his son.

t6n1.text: Try not to let emotions affect your judgment; fear and greed are the worst of them.

t6n2.text: Don't buy on tips or for a quick move, and don't sell on bad news.

t6n3.text: Don't be afraid to stand alone, but look hard for weaknesses in your own thinking.

t6n4.text: Have a method of investing and stick to it once you have decided.

t7n1.text: A 50% gain is not by itself a reason to sell; re-check the company's value against its book value first.

t7n2.text: Before selling, ask whether yields are low, prices high and people very optimistic.

t7n3.text: Listen to people you respect, but remember it's your money and the decision is yours.

t8n1.text: At 12% a year, money doubles in about six years: divide 72 by your return.

t8n2.text: Bonds limit your gains and inflation eats their value, so he preferred shares.

t8n3.text: Be careful with borrowed money; it can go against you.

t8n4.text: It is harder to keep money than to make it, and a big loss is hard to recover.

t9n1.text: He charged no management fee, taking a 25% share of the profits instead.

sampat.name: Chandrakant Sampat
sampat.what: His interviews and the notes of those he taught, on cash flow, durability and patience
sampat.scope: Sampat left no books or letters, and his returns were never published. So this page relies on his interviews and on notes kept by people close to him, and says so wherever it does.
sampat.readHow: Start with the January 2000 investor round table, where he speaks at length, then Rohan Shah's notes of his sayings in Outlook Business (2015).
sampat.sourcesNote: Sources: an investor round table (Capital Ideas Online, 2000), a Business Standard interview (2003), a profile collecting his quotes, obituaries in Business Standard and The Economic Times (2015), and tributes in Outlook Business by Rohan Shah and Chetan Parikh (2015). Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

start.lede: Chandrakant Sampat is called India's original value investor. He left his family's business in the 1950s to buy shares, made his fortune owning the Indian arms of global consumer companies when few others saw their worth, and taught a generation, including Parag Parikh and Radhakishan Damani. He wrote no books and gave few interviews; he jogged, read, lived simply and kept to a handful of strict rules.
start.para: This page draws on his rare interviews (2000 and 2003), obituaries in Business Standard and The Economic Times, and tributes by two people who knew him well. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

glossary: The Mumbai street of the Bombay Stock Exchange; shorthand for India's stock market.
The Foreign Exchange Regulation Act of 1973, which pushed many foreign companies to cut their stakes in Indian units.
The government office that approved and priced new share issues in India before 1992.
Operating profit as a share of the money tied up in the business.
Cash a business generates after paying for the investment it needs.
Capital expenditure: spending on plants, machines and other long-lived assets.
Fast-moving consumer goods: everyday items like soap, razors and food.
Ten million rupees; ₹1 lakh is one hundred thousand.

themes.title: Own businesses, don't build factories
themes.idea: He left his family's business in the 1950s, drawn to shares. Buying a slice of a good listed business, he believed, beats the struggle of building one from scratch.
ask: Would you rather build a business or own a slice of the best one?
Which Indian businesses could you never build, but could own?

themes.title: The FERA windfall
themes.idea: In the 1970s, India's Foreign Exchange Regulation Act forced many foreign companies to sell shares to Indian investors, often cheaply. Sampat bought the best of them and held for decades.
ask: Where today are sellers forced to sell for reasons that have nothing to do with value?
What rule change could create the next windfall?
themes.caption: Under FERA, many foreign companies had to sell shares to Indians, often below what they were worth.

themes.title: Cash flow and durability
themes.idea: For Sampat a good investment had to throw off cash, year after year, and last. He judged businesses by their cash, not their story.
ask: How much cash did a company you own actually produce last year?
Will it still exist, and earn, in 30 years?

themes.title: Buy at the lows
themes.idea: Find good companies with good managements, then wait until their share price sinks to an eight- or ten-year low. Buy from pessimists; sell to optimists.
ask: Which good company is near a multi-year low today? Why?
Could you wait years for your price?

themes.title: Simple, with little debt
themes.idea: He wanted businesses simple enough for anyone to understand, carrying little debt and needing little new money to grow.
ask: Can you explain a company you own to a child in two sentences?
How much new money does it need each year just to grow?

themes.title: Muscle, fat or cancer
themes.idea: Not all growth is good. He sorted it into muscle, fat and cancer, and warned that nothing grows exponentially for long.
ask: Which kind of growth does a company you own have?
What happens to its returns if growth slows?
themes.caption: Muscle: sales, profit and cash rise together. Fat: sales grow, profit doesn't. Cancer: growth that eats the business.

themes.title: Technology and creative destruction
themes.idea: He believed new technology destroys old businesses ever faster. That made him wary of fashionable shares and focused on durability.
ask: What new technology could make a company you own obsolete?
Which businesses get stronger as technology changes?

themes.title: Integrity: humility plus courage
themes.idea: Sampat defined integrity as humility plus courage, and lived it. His four touchstone values were high enlightenment, high integrity, low expectation and hard work.
ask: Would you write publicly to a board you disagreed with?
Which of his four touchstone values is hardest for you?

themes.title: How many things can you do without?
themes.idea: One of India's richest investors lived simply, jogged daily and asked how little he needed, not how much he could have.
ask: What could you do without, starting this week?
When did you last question something everyone takes for granted?

themes.title: A teacher, and his blind spot
themes.idea: He shaped some of India's best investors. But his caution in later years also cost him, which he would have wanted us to learn from too.
ask: When has being right too early cost you?
How do you keep caution from turning into paralysis?

t1n1.text: He began in the mid-1950s, when the Controller of Capital Issues still oversaw new share issues, after leaving his family's business.

t1n2.text: When a young Parag Parikh's plan to make toothpaste tubes was rejected, Sampat told him to buy shares in good businesses instead: share the growth, skip the factory.

t1n3.text: In those days, closing a business in India could drag on endlessly. A share could simply be sold.

t1n4.text: He read The Economist and Fortune closely, keeping an eye on business far beyond India.

t2n1.text: FERA required foreign companies to dilute their holdings at prices below their real value. He made a killing.

t2n2.text: He bought Hindustan Lever when its shares were priced in the teens.

t2n3.text: Later he bought Gillette's Indian arm at ₹16 a share, when it was still called Indian Shaving Products.

t2n4.text: He held his consumer companies for decades; a profile names Hindustan Lever and Nestlé among his picks.

t3n1.text: He looked for positive cash flow, cash flow that lasts, and barriers that keep rivals out.

t3n2.text: A business qualifies as a good investment only if it generates cash and shows durability.

t3n3.text: He favoured high return on capital employed, a long record of dividends and little need for capital spending. Few companies passed.

t3n4.text: He warned people to beware of those he called spreadsheet specialists.

t4n1.text: Pick up good companies with good managements when the share price is at an eight- or ten-year low.

t4n2.text: If you must act sooner, buy good companies about 40% below their 52-week high.

t4n3.text: Buy from pessimists, sell to optimists, and be patient in between.

t4n4.text: He preferred a P/E of 15 or less, but said to focus on the quality and longevity of the business, and not to be rigid about the number.

t5n1.text: He bought only businesses that even a fool could understand, with very little debt.

t5n2.text: A great business needs little extra capital to grow; a weak one needs capital forever.

t5n3.text: He was strongly influenced by the management thinker Peter Drucker.

t6n1.text: Good growth is muscle, bad growth is fat, and some growth ultimately kills, like cancer.

t6n2.text: Gillette was his example: the number of razors sold grows slowly, but the value of each sale grows a lot.

t6n3.text: He compared nature to a miserly accountant that punishes even the smallest extravagance. Businesses, he implied, are no different.

t6n4.text: In 2000 he told the software enthusiasts that nothing grows exponentially for long.

t7n1.text: At the height of the technology boom he argued that Indian software firms lacked free cash flow.

t7n2.text: In 2003 he said faster technology would shorten the lives of companies and the business cycle.

t7n3.text: He drew on Joseph Schumpeter, the economist who described how innovation keeps destroying old businesses.

t8n1.text: Integrity, he said, is humility plus courage.

t8n2.text: A friend described his ethics as complete harmony between what he thought, said and did.

t8n3.text: In 2006 he wrote an open letter to the directors of Wyeth India over the transfer of a drug's marketing rights.

t8n4.text: He drew on the Bhagavad Gita and Jain scriptures, as well as on Drucker and Schumpeter.

t9n1.text: Parag Parikh said Sampat's philosophy was how many things you can do without.

t9n2.text: For years he jogged about seven kilometres a day, from Haji Ali to Marine Drive.

t9n3.text: He objected to excessive consumption, debt, money-printing and short-termism.

t9n4.text: Take the best ideas from great thinkers in every field, connect them yourself, and take nothing and nobody for granted.

t10n1.text: Parag Parikh said he always walked away wiser after sitting with Sampat.

t10n2.text: In his last years he stayed out of the market, worried that cheap money had inflated prices, and missed a strong rally in shares like Hindustan Unilever and Nestlé.

t10n3.text: A friend wrote that he foresaw a credit-driven bubble but may have misjudged when it would end.

t10n4.text: In 2003 he feared fast-changing technology could spell doom for capital markets within a few years. That did not happen.

parikh.name: Parag Parikh
parikh.what: His books, talks and the fund he built on behavioural finance, patience and honesty
parikh.scope: Parikh's returns as a broker and portfolio manager were not published in full, so we show none. His fund continues today; it is mentioned for history only, not as a recommendation.
parikh.readHow: Start with Stocks to Riches (2005). It is short, plain and full of Indian examples.
parikh.sourcesNote: Sources: Stocks to Riches (2005) and Value Investing and Behavioural Finance (2009), his views at a Morningstar conference (2014), interviews and obituaries in Cafemutual, Value Research, Moneylife and Business Standard (2015), and PPFAS's own tribute and books pages. Lessons are in our own words; exact quotes are short and checked.

start.lede: Parag Parikh started as a sub-broker on Dalal Street in 1979; later his wife and mother sold some of their jewellery to help him grow. He became India's pioneer of behavioural finance: the study of why investors make the same mistakes again and again. In 2013 he launched a mutual fund with just one scheme, put his own money in it, and later closed his broking business to avoid conflicts. He died in 2015 in Omaha, after attending Berkshire Hathaway's annual meeting.
start.para: This page draws on his two books, his talks, interviews and the tributes written after his death. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

glossary: The study of how emotions and mental shortcuts shape investors' decisions.
An agent who dealt through a registered stockbroker, often a first step into broking.
Asset management company: the firm that runs a mutual fund.
Portfolio management service: a manager running a separate portfolio for each wealthy client.
Doing what everyone else does because they are doing it.
Feeling a loss about twice as strongly as an equal gain.
Treating money differently depending on where it came from, such as a bonus.
Valuing something more just because you own it.
The Securities and Exchange Board of India, the market regulator.

themes.title: From toothpaste tubes to shares
themes.idea: As a young man he wanted to make toothpaste tubes. Chandrakant Sampat told him to buy shares in good businesses instead. He started as a sub-broker, with his family's help.
ask: Who changed the direction of your working life?
What would you risk to start on your own?

themes.title: Study the mind, not just the accounts
themes.idea: He believed investor behaviour moves markets as much as company results. Understanding emotions, yours and others', is half the job.
ask: What emotion drove your last trade?
Whose mistakes might you be profiting from, or making?

themes.title: Leave the herd
themes.idea: Greed and fear make Indian markets swing. He urged investors to buy when others are fearful, and paid a price for it in the technology boom.
ask: When did you last follow the crowd? How did it end?
What is everyone buying right now?
themes.caption: The crowd runs one way; the patient investor walks the other.

themes.title: Mistakes with Indian faces
themes.idea: His books name the traps: loss aversion, sunk costs, the endowment effect, mental accounting, decision paralysis. He showed them in Indian investors and Indian markets.
ask: Which of these mistakes do you make most?
What rule could protect you from it?

themes.title: The law of the farm
themes.idea: Value investing is boring. You plant, you wait for years, you harvest. He called it the law of the farm.
ask: How long have you held your oldest share? Why?
Do you keep a watchlist of businesses to buy when cheap?
themes.caption: Plant, tend, wait. There is no shortcut to a harvest.

themes.title: What a good business looks like
themes.idea: He looked for four things: honest management that treats minority shareholders well, a simple business, a strong moat and pricing power.
ask: Does a company you own have pricing power? How do you know?
How does its management treat minority shareholders?

themes.title: Skin in the game
themes.idea: He insisted that those who manage money should invest alongside their clients, and he removed every conflict he could, even at a cost.
ask: Does the person managing your money invest in the same thing?
What conflict of interest do you tolerate today?

themes.title: One fund, not a grocery shop
themes.idea: While fund houses launched scheme after scheme, he launched one. One clear way of investing, he argued, serves investors better.
ask: How many mutual fund schemes do you hold? Why so many?
Would you be happier with one you understand?

themes.title: Standing up to the system
themes.idea: He was outspoken about the failings of India's finance industry, and argued with the regulator when he thought a rule would hurt competition.
ask: Which industry practice do you think is unfair to investors?
Would you speak up about it publicly?

themes.title: A firm built to outlast him
themes.idea: He died suddenly in 2015, in Omaha, after Warren Buffett's annual meeting. The firm he built, run on his principles, carried on without him.
ask: Would your work carry on if you stopped tomorrow?
What would you want your clients to remember?

t1n1.text: When his manufacturing idea was rejected as unviable, Sampat pointed him to listed businesses: share the growth without running the factory.

t1n2.text: He started as a sub-broker in 1979, aiming to become a full broker. When he needed capital, his wife and mother sold some of their jewellery to help.

t1n3.text: His firm was one of the first Indian brokerages to set up a formal equity research desk.

t1n4.text: He said that whenever he sat with Sampat, he walked away wiser.

t2n1.text: Stocks to Riches set out to discover what makes investors tick, and what keeps the stock market alive.

t2n2.text: Investors can profit from the mental and emotional mistakes of others, if they avoid their own.

t2n3.text: His two books applied behavioural finance to Indian investors and Indian market history.

t3n1.text: His second book argues that successful investing means restraining and channelling emotions like greed and fear.

t3n2.text: In the technology boom he suffered not because he owned such shares, but because he kept telling clients to sell them.

t3n3.text: As prices kept rising he admitted he was unsure whether he or the world was sane, but he held to his principles.

t4n1.text: Stocks to Riches covers speculation, loss aversion, the sunk cost fallacy, the endowment effect, decision paralysis, mental accounting and mental shortcuts.

t4n2.text: His second book uses Indian market history and Indian companies to show these mistakes at work.

t4n3.text: It gives chapters to IPOs and to the growth trap: paying too much for exciting growth.

t5n1.text: Value investing, he said, is boring: you have to wait for years.

t5n2.text: You cannot sow today and reap tomorrow. He called this a law made by God, not by men.

t5n3.text: He kept a watchlist of sound companies and bought when they became cheap. Fortune favours the prepared mind.

t5n4.text: Buy a business, not a piece of paper whose price you hope will rise.

t6n1.text: Credible management that is fair to minority shareholders, a business you can understand, strong competitive moats, and pricing power.

t6n2.text: He separated a thing's value in use, what it does for you, from its value in exchange, what someone will pay for it.

t6n3.text: Never pay more than intrinsic value; doing so means relying on a greater fool to buy from you.

t6n4.text: He believed Buffett's style of value investing, buying with a margin of safety, works best in India.

t7n1.text: He promised that his senior team, including himself, would invest alongside outside investors in the fund.

t7n2.text: He, his family and key employees put personal money into the fund.

t7n3.text: He shut his broking business and surrendered the licence to avoid conflicts of interest with the mutual fund.

t7n4.text: He rejected quick-gain tactics such as futures and options trading, and upfront commissions to attract clients.

t8n1.text: PPFAS launched just one fund, managed in a go-anywhere style, so as not to confuse investors.

t8n2.text: There is only one right way of investing, he said; you can't have twenty.

t8n3.text: His fund could also buy shares overseas, including in the US.

t8n4.text: He saw a fund's dividend as just your own money handed back, and his fund was the first to hold unitholder meetings like company AGMs.

t9n1.text: His firm's tribute page calls him an iconoclast.

t9n2.text: When a SEBI committee proposed sharply raising the money needed to run a mutual fund, he argued it would shut out new, smaller competitors.

t9n3.text: A mutual fund, he insisted, merely passes investors' money through; it is not a bank. The proposal was shelved.

t10n1.text: He died in a road accident on 3 May 2015, travelling with colleagues after the Berkshire Hathaway annual meeting.

t10n2.text: He set out to build an organisation and a team able to run without him.

t10n3.text: His fund asked investors to think in terms of at least five years, holding quality through market cycles.

t10n4.text: Business Standard described his life as a journey from a childhood with polio to one of India's best-regarded value investors.

sp.title: Which bias is this? Tap your answer

items.q: A WhatsApp group says a small company will double. Everyone you know is buying, so you buy too.
items.why: Buying because others are buying. His books warn that the crowd is usually late.

items.q: You bought at ₹500. It is ₹300 and the business has got worse, but you won't sell until it's back to ₹500.
items.why: Refusing to take a loss. The market doesn't know or care what you paid.

items.q: Your Diwali bonus feels like free money, so you gamble it on options instead of investing it.
items.why: A rupee is a rupee, wherever it came from. Treat a bonus like any other savings.

items.q: You keep shares your father left you, though you would never buy them at today's price.
items.why: Valuing something more because you own it. Ask: would I buy this today?

items.q: You paid ₹50,000 for a trading course, so you keep trading to make it worthwhile, though you keep losing.
items.why: Money already spent is gone. Only future costs and benefits should decide.

items.q: There are so many mutual fund schemes that you can't choose, so your savings sit idle for years.
items.why: Too many choices freeze you. One reason he launched only one fund.

start.lede: Radhakishan Damani was a famous bear, or short seller, on Dalal Street in the Harshad Mehta years, then a patient long-term investor, and then, from 2000, the founder of DMart, one of India's most successful retailers. He almost never speaks in public. His lessons are in what he did: own quality, keep costs lower than anyone, pay suppliers fast, own the shop, and grow slowly until the model is proven.

themes.title: Leave the small pond
themes.idea: He did not start in the market. He ran a ball-bearings business until an uncle asked him: how rich is the top ball-bearings trader, next to Dalal Street's biggest names?
ask: Are you a big fish in a small pond?
What would it take to move to a bigger one?
themes.caption: The biggest fish in a small pond is still small. He chose the sea.

themes.title: The bear in the Harshad Mehta years
themes.idea: In the early 1990s, while Harshad Mehta drove prices to dizzying heights with borrowed money, Damani bet on a fall. He was right, but it hurt before it paid.
ask: Have you ever been right too early? What did it cost?
Could you hold a position while it went badly against you?

themes.title: From trader to owner
themes.idea: Influenced by Chandrakant Sampat, he moved from trading to owning quality businesses for years. Fund managers said they could never tell which hat he was wearing.
ask: Do you know, for each holding, whether you are trading or investing?
Would you pay more for quality? How much more?

themes.title: Listen more than you talk
themes.idea: He rarely speaks in public and has never appeared on television. Friends say he says little and listens a lot, asking people what they see.
ask: How much of your investing talk is listening?
Who do you ask about what customers really want?

themes.title: Why a shop?
themes.idea: In 2000, at the height of his market success, he turned to retailing, after studying how Indians shop.
ask: Is your money-making something you could grow, or hand on?
What business do you understand well enough to build?

themes.title: Everyday low cost, everyday low price
themes.idea: DMart's model is simple to say and hard to copy: keep costs lower than anyone, so prices can be lower than anyone's, every day, without flashy discounts.
ask: What could a company you know do to be the lowest-cost player in its field?
Who wins when a supplier is paid in a week?
themes.caption: Low costs pay for low prices; low prices bring shoppers; volume brings lower costs again.

themes.title: Own the shop
themes.idea: Most retailers rent. DMart prefers to buy land and build its own stores, which keeps costs stable and avoids rent shocks.
ask: Which costs in your life rise every year that you could fix once?
What does owning, rather than renting, cost up front?
themes.caption: Rent rises every year; an owned store's cost is paid once.

themes.title: Slow, then fast
themes.idea: He grew DMart slowly for years, proving the model in a few regions before expanding. Then it grew quickly, cluster by cluster.
ask: What are you trying to grow faster than it is ready to grow?
Where would you open the next shop, and why there?

themes.title: Frugal at the top
themes.idea: The man who became one of India's richest kept DMart's head office in a corner of an early store and worked without hierarchy.
ask: Where could you cut cost without cutting quality?
What do your habits tell the people around you?

t1n1.text: He grew up in Mumbai, where his father worked on Dalal Street, and left college after a year of commerce.

t1n2.text: He first ran a ball-bearings business and had no interest in the stock market.

t1n3.text: After his father died, an uncle reportedly persuaded him that real wealth meant leaving a small pond, even as its biggest fish.

t1n4.text: On Dalal Street he became skilled at both kinds of bet: on rises and on falls.

t2n1.text: He was a known bear, and twice took the other side of Harshad Mehta's rallies, winning both times.

t2n2.text: He sold ACC shares at about ₹3,000 and kept selling as they rose towards ₹10,000. Losses mounted until the prices finally cracked.

t2n3.text: He was a keen follower of Manu Manek, a famous short seller of his early years.

t3n1.text: He has often said he was inspired by Chandrakant Sampat, whom he met in the early 1990s.

t3n2.text: By market folklore he was the largest individual shareholder of HDFC Bank at its 1995 listing, and kept buying.

t3n3.text: He was willing to pay up for HDFC Bank; in his view, quality commands a premium.

t3n4.text: A fund manager said it was impossible to follow him, never knowing whether he was investing or trading in a share.

t4n1.text: He rarely speaks publicly, has never appeared on television, and keeps his views to himself.

t4n2.text: People who know him say he listens far more than he speaks.

t4n3.text: When a friend complained that DMart staff hovered around him while he shopped, Damani told them never to do it again.

t4n4.text: He did not respond to Business Standard's interview request for its 2020 profile.

t5n1.text: The company says he spent a couple of years in research and reflection, testing his ideas about the Indian consumer, before starting.

t5n2.text: In the late 1990s he ran a franchise of Apna Bazaar, a cooperative store chain, in Navi Mumbai. DMart refined the idea.

t5n3.text: DMart's own annual report says he conceived the chain in 2000.

t5n4.text: He was reportedly inspired by reading about Walmart.

t6n1.text: The company offers value retailing using its Everyday Low Cost, Everyday Low Price principle.

t6n2.text: It buys directly from manufacturers and pays vendors early, which earns better purchase prices.

t6n3.text: It reportedly pays suppliers within about a week, against the usual three months.

t6n4.text: It focuses on items that sell quickly, and on high sales from every square foot.

t7n1.text: Its chief executive has said the company typically prefers to buy land and then construct the buildings.

t7n2.text: In 2017 an analyst counted about 85% of its 131 stores as owned.

t7n3.text: Store ownership is part of the low-cost model that lets it keep prices low.

t8n1.text: DMart took eight years to open its first ten stores. The company says he wanted to prove the model both profitable and scalable first.

t8n2.text: It had about 25 stores by 2010, then sped up.

t8n3.text: The company deepens its presence where it already operates before moving to new regions.

t8n4.text: It had 176 stores in 11 states and a union territory in 2019, and 365 by March 2024.

t9n1.text: For years DMart's corporate office was a small space carved out of one of its early stores.

t9n2.text: He and his early team worked as one unit, without hierarchy or barriers.

t9n3.text: After the IPO he reportedly shared a budget hotel room with his buying team on a trip to China.

t9n4.text: The company credits its success to the values and way of thinking he instilled.

t10n1.text: Avenue Supermarts' ₹1,870 crore IPO, priced at ₹299 a share, was subscribed more than 104 times.

t10n2.text: The shares listed on 21 March 2017 at more than double the issue price.

t10n3.text: SEBI examined trading by three broking firms of the R.S. Damani group in 2001. It found no evidence of manipulation, but censured the firms for delays in moving shares to clients.

t10n4.text: Damani appeared at the hearing as a director of one firm; the order was against the three companies, not him personally.

sp.title: Tap each step of the DMart flywheel
items: DMart buys from manufacturers and pays vendors early, often within about a week.
Suppliers give better prices to a buyer who pays quickly and in bulk.
It prefers to buy land and build, rather than rent.
No rent increases; occupancy costs stay low and predictable.
Simple stores, fast-moving products, a frugal head office.
Every rupee saved can be passed on in prices.
Low prices every day, not flashy discounts.
Shoppers trust the price, so they keep coming back.
Busy stores sell more per square foot and turn their stock fast.
Stock sells before it has to be paid for again.
Higher volumes, store clusters and quick payment mean better terms from suppliers.
Which brings the wheel back to step one, a little faster each time.

sp.text: SEBI's order of 2 January 2007 concerned three broking firms of the R.S. Damani group: Damani Shares & Stock Brokers, Maheshwari Equity Brokers and Avenue Stock Brokers. SEBI examined their sales of Infosys shares on 23 February and 2 March 2001, and other dealings. It found no evidence of price manipulation, held that alleged links to two other market groups were not established, and found the firms had broadly complied with short-sale rules. The one violation upheld was that the firms had moved securities from their pool accounts to clients' accounts later than the 15-day limit. SEBI treated this as a technical violation with no bad intent, and imposed censure, a minor penalty. Radhakishan Damani appeared at the hearing as a director of one firm; he was not a party to the order. We include it because this library puts integrity first and tells readers what is on the public record.

honda.name: Seiroku Honda
honda.what: His book on money, and the record of the forester who saved a quarter of every pay cheque
honda.scope: His book is in Japanese and has no official English edition, so this page relies on Japanese summaries of it and translates short lines ourselves. Modern-money estimates of his wealth vary and are only rough.
honda.readHow: If you read Japanese, start with 私の財産告白 (My Confession of Wealth, 1950). If not, start with the stock exchange's education article and the Saitama Prefecture story of his gifts.
honda.sourcesNote: Sources: his book 私の財産告白 (1950) as published and as quoted by Japanese financial firms; articles by Japan Exchange Group's education site, MUFG Bank, Daiwa Securities, Rakuten Securities and President; and Saitama Prefecture's official materials on his life, gifts and scholarship. Lessons are in our own words; translations are ours.

start.lede: Seiroku Honda was born poor in 1866, became Japan's first doctor of forestry, and designed the forest of Meiji Shrine and parks across Japan. From the age of 25 he saved a quarter of every pay cheque before spending a yen, invested the savings in shares and forest land, and by 40 earned more from interest and dividends than from his salary. When he retired he gave almost all of it away. His 1950 book, My Confession of Wealth, is still read by Japanese savers today.
start.para: This page draws on his book as reported by Japanese banks, brokers and the stock exchange's own education site, and on Saitama Prefecture's account of his life and gifts. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

themes.title: A poor farmer's son
themes.idea: He was born poor in 1866, studied his way up, and became Japan's first doctor of forestry and the designer of famous parks and forests.
ask: What did your family teach you about money?
Could your day job also teach you about an investment?

themes.title: The quarter rule
themes.idea: Every time pay arrived, he set aside a quarter before spending anything, and saved every bonus and windfall in full.
ask: What share of your income do you save before spending?
Where does your last bonus sit today?
themes.caption: A quarter goes to savings first; the rest is what you live on.

themes.title: Hard years by choice
themes.idea: The rule hurt. With a large household, money ran out each month. He held firm, choosing hardship early rather than being forced into it later.
ask: Would you accept a few lean years for a lifetime of security?
Who in your home would need persuading?

themes.title: Vanity is the enemy
themes.idea: He saw the wish to look well-off as the biggest obstacle to saving, and believed early hardship makes for a better life later.
ask: Which of your spending is for show?
What would you stop buying if nobody could see it?

themes.title: The snowball
themes.idea: Savings, once they form a core, grow by themselves. By 40 his interest and dividends earned more than his salary.
ask: How many years until your investments could pay you as much as your job?
What is the core of your snowball today?
themes.caption: A small core, rolled for years, grows on its own.

themes.title: Own good businesses, widely
themes.idea: He put his savings into the sound companies of his day, starting with railways and spreading across more than thirty industries.
ask: Are your savings spread across businesses that will still matter in 20 years?
Who gave you your first investing tip, and was it good?

themes.title: Invest in what you know: his forest
themes.idea: As a forester, he understood land and trees. He bought natural forest in the Chichibu mountains, and it became part of his fortune, and later his gift.
ask: What do you understand better than most investors?
Would you sell part of something that rose seventy-fold, or all of it?

themes.title: Take a modest profit, protect the principal
themes.idea: He followed a simple selling rule: take a 20% gain when it comes, and if a holding doubles, sell half so the original money is safe.
ask: Do you have a rule for taking profits, or do you decide in the moment?
How would you feel holding a double with your original money already back?

themes.title: Patience, and no shame about money
themes.idea: He waited patiently for good chances, invested boldly when times were bad, and rejected the old samurai pose of looking down on money.
ask: Does your family treat money as something shameful to discuss?
What would you buy in the next downturn?

themes.title: Give it back
themes.idea: At 60 he retired and gave almost everything away, mostly anonymously. His forest still pays for students' education in Saitama.
ask: What would you give away, and when?
What would you want your money to keep doing after you?

t1n1.text: He was born in 1866 into a poor farming family in what is now Kuki, Saitama, and studied through hardship.

t1n2.text: He became Japan's first doctor of forestry and a professor at the Imperial University in Tokyo.

t1n3.text: He designed parks across Japan, including Hibiya Park in Tokyo, and the forest of Meiji Shrine.

t1n4.text: Today he is remembered at least as much for how he saved and invested as for his parks.

t2n1.text: He saved a quarter of each pay cheque the day it arrived, treating it as money he had never received.

t2n2.text: Bonuses and other one-off income went entirely into savings.

t2n3.text: In his words, if you earn 40 yen, think you received 30 and put 10 away.

t2n4.text: He insisted that saving is a matter of doing it, not of finding the right method.

t3n1.text: At the end of some months the family ate rice with only salt and sesame, and the children cried.

t3n2.text: He persuaded his family that the rule was right and would not let feeling override it.

t3n3.text: He argued that you should not cut back because poverty forces you to, but save on purpose to overpower poverty.

t4n1.text: Wanting to live better than others, or just to look as if you do, is what wrecks saving.

t4n2.text: He wrote that those raised in luxury tend to become poor, while those who meet poverty early do better later.

t4n3.text: Since everyone goes through a poor stretch at some point, he thought it best to get it over with young.

t5n1.text: He wrote that money is like a snowball: tiny at first, but once a core forms it grows remarkably.

t5n2.text: His first monthly saving was 14 yen and 50 sen.

t5n3.text: After two or three years, interest began to arrive, so life slowly became easier.

t5n4.text: Fifteen years in, at 40, his interest and dividends were far larger than his salary.

t6n1.text: His first purchase was 30 shares of Nippon Railway at 12.50 yen each, on a professor's advice that railways had a future.

t6n2.text: When the railways were nationalised, his shares were bought at about 2.5 times what he paid.

t6n3.text: As railway prospects dimmed he moved on, owning good shares across more than 30 industries, from gas and power to beer and cement.

t6n4.text: He kept away from speculation and stuck to sound investment.

t7n1.text: He bought natural forest in the Chichibu mountains, close to his expertise.

t7n2.text: After the Russo-Japanese War timber prices soared, and he sold part of his forest at about 70 times its cost.

t7n3.text: His forest holdings near Nakatsugawa in Chichibu covered about 2,600 hectares.

t8n1.text: On some positions, if he reached a 20% gain, he took it in full and put the money on deposit, without chasing more.

t8n2.text: If a holding more than doubled, he sold half at once, getting his original money back.

t8n3.text: With the principal safe, a later crash could not hurt him, and further gains were a bonus.

t9n1.text: Save a quarter; invest once a little has built up; wait patiently for good chances without forcing anything.

t9n2.text: Downturns pushed share prices down, and he invested actively when they did.

t9n3.text: He criticised the feudal habit of pretending to scorn money, calling money useful and worth having.

t10n1.text: He concluded that great wealth and fame do not guarantee happiness.

t10n2.text: On retiring in 1927 he gave nearly all his assets to public causes, mostly without his name.

t10n3.text: Saitama's scholarship in his name, funded by income from his donated forest, has lent to students since 1954.

t10n4.text: In 2024 it still offered interest-free loans of up to 30,000 yen a month to Saitama students.

takeda.name: Wahei Takeda
takeda.what: His interviews and the books about him, on being a patient patron of the companies you own
takeda.scope: Takeda published no investment returns, and estimates of his holdings vary by source and year. Most sources are in Japanese; summaries and translations are ours. Companies are named for history only.
takeda.readHow: If you read Japanese, start with 花のタネは真夏に播くな (Don't Sow Flower Seeds in Midsummer), a book of long interviews with him. If not, start with the MUFG Securities profile.
takeda.sourcesNote: Sources: his 2015 interview in Gendai Business, a 2024 profile by MUFG Securities, Jun Mizusawa's book of interviews (2008), his own first book (2005), reports of his 2011 talk and a 2015 investor profile, and his 2016 obituary in J-CAST News. Lessons are in our own words; translations are ours.

start.lede: Wahei Takeda built Takeda Seika into Japan's biggest maker of tamago boro, the little egg biscuits Japanese babies grow up on. From 1956 he invested the company's spare cash, and after a painful lesson moved to small and mid-sized companies, becoming a large shareholder in more than a hundred of them. Japan called him its Warren Buffett. He called being a shareholder being the company's danna, its patron.
start.para: This page draws on his 2015 magazine interview, an MUFG Securities profile, a book of interviews with him, reports of his talks, and his obituary. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

Small egg biscuits that melt in the mouth, a classic Japanese baby snack.

The share of after-tax profit a company pays out as dividends.
Shareholders' equity as a share of total assets; higher means sturdier.

Profits kept in the company rather than paid out (naibu ryūho).

themes.title: The biscuit maker
themes.idea: He was a confectioner first. He turned a sweet sold loose by weight into a bagged, machine-made product, and built Japan's biggest tamago boro maker.
ask: What simple improvement in your own work could others copy too late?
Does running a business make someone a better investor?

themes.title: From speculator to investor
themes.idea: He began by trading famous shares for quick profit. Later he called that speculation, and drew a sharp line between betting on prices and owning a business to support it.
ask: Which of your holdings are investments, and which are bets?
What was your first share, and why did you buy it?

themes.title: The lesson of a collapse
themes.idea: In the 1990s a large company in which he was the top individual shareholder went bankrupt, its managers insisting all was well to the end. He sold his large companies and turned to smaller ones he could understand.
ask: Do you know the people running the companies you own?
Could you read your largest holding's accounts in an evening?

themes.title: Be the danna
themes.idea: In old Japan a danna was a patron who stood behind a business or an artist. He said that becoming a shareholder means becoming the company's danna.
ask: How would you behave differently as a patron rather than a punter?
What would you say to the manager of a company you own?
themes.caption: The patron backs the company; the company shares its harvest.

themes.title: Fields and harvests
themes.idea: He saw investing as farming. Shares are the field and dividends the harvest. A good farmer watches the harvest, not the price of the land.
ask: Do you check your dividends as often as your prices?
What would you plant now, and what would you wait to plant?
themes.caption: The land's price swings; the harvest comes in year after year.

themes.title: Cheap, sound and generous
themes.idea: He wanted shares that were cheap against earnings, companies with strong balance sheets, and managers who shared profits with shareholders.
ask: What does a company you own pay out of each yen of profit?
What price would you pay for ten yen of yearly earnings?

themes.title: Dividends first
themes.idea: Dividends, not price gains, were the core of his returns. He noted that dividends hold up far better than prices in bad times.
ask: How much of your return comes from dividends?
Which company's success would make you genuinely glad?

themes.title: Calm in storms
themes.idea: He used only spare money, never borrowed to the limit, and refused to panic. A share price, he said, may go up or down; either is fine.
ask: Is any of your investing money needed in the next few years?
How do you behave when your portfolio is down a third?

themes.title: When to sell
themes.idea: He held for the long run, but sold when a share looked overvalued, and lost patience with companies that hoarded cash instead of rewarding owners.
ask: Which of your companies keeps cash it cannot use?
When did you last sell because a price was too high?

themes.title: Sincerity, and giving back
themes.idea: He believed sincerity passed from person to person brings success and happiness, ran a circle to develop young people, and gave back much of what he gained.
ask: Who passed sincerity on to you?
What would you build to develop the next generation?

t1n1.text: Born in Aichi in 1933 to a family of sweet makers, he was his father's right hand while still a teenager after the war.

t1n2.text: Tamago boro was sold loose by weight in sweet shops. He saw it could be sold in bags, and automated production before rivals did.

t1n3.text: He founded the company in 1952; it became Japan's largest tamago boro maker, also known for the Mugi Fah wafer.

t1n4.text: His interviewer described him as a once-poor confectioner who became Japan's biggest individual investor.

t2n1.text: In 1956, at 23, once the company was stable, he began investing its surplus cash.

t2n2.text: A friendship with a securities branch manager led to his first purchase, which rose quickly.

t2n3.text: He started with big blue chips and traded for quick gains, which he later called speculation, not investment.

t2n4.text: Gambling-style speculation and investing to support a company look alike, he said, but are different things.

t3n1.text: Management kept saying the business was fine right up to the bankruptcy.

t3n2.text: He sold all his large-company shares and moved to small and mid-sized listed companies.

t3n3.text: He came to prefer companies where you can see the manager's face over big, impressive ones.

t3n4.text: He valued simple, easy-to-read financial statements and knowing the management directly.

t4n1.text: To be a shareholder is to be the company's danna, its patron.

t4n2.text: He held with a nurturing attitude, waiting for the price to rise; if it didn't, he was content with dividends from a cheap purchase.

t4n3.text: He encouraged struggling managers to run their business joyfully and recover, so dividends would follow.

t4n4.text: To thank companies for their dividends he sent them pure gold medals, a habit he kept all his life.

t5n1.text: Stocks are the field and dividends the harvest; watch the yearly harvest, not the price of the land.

t5n2.text: Plant seeds in companies likely to bloom, take your share of the fruit, then plant again.

t5n3.text: He reinvested his dividends again and again, and his holdings grew past 10 billion yen.

t5n4.text: His interviewer titled the book with a gardener's rule: don't sow flower seeds in midsummer.

t6n1.text: Ideally he paid about ten times earnings, which he linked to a roughly 10% earnings yield.

t6n2.text: He watched the payout ratio, how much profit goes to dividends, and the equity ratio, a sign of financial strength.

t6n3.text: He used return on equity to find companies that were both profitable and cheap.

t6n4.text: He warned that buying overpriced shares always loses money in the end.

t7n1.text: Dividends were his main return; in 2015 he expected about 350 million yen of tax on them.

t7n2.text: Even if a share price halved, he said, dividends usually fell by no more than about 10%.

t7n3.text: He aimed for companies with steady future growth that would pay good dividends.

t7n4.text: He chose companies whose rising profits he could be truly happy about.

t8n1.text: He shrugged off falls with a short verse: a share price is fine going down and fine going up.

t8n2.text: In the 2008 crash his holdings showed large paper losses, and he held on.

t8n3.text: He invested only surplus funds and warned never to use margin to the limit.

t8n4.text: He said his only information source was the Shikiho company handbook, with no special inside sources.

t9n1.text: He held for the long term and did not sell quickly to lock in small profits.

t9n2.text: Sell when a share looks overvalued; don't wait for the top.

t9n3.text: Profitable companies that keep piling up retained earnings show poor prospects and little respect for shareholders, he said.

t9n4.text: At 82 he had cut from over 130 holdings to about 25, citing a proposed tax on large holders, the need for global reach, and the time research takes.

t10n1.text: His philosophy: a chain of sincerity brings success and happiness.

t10n2.text: He led a group called Marowa-ko to develop people, and returned his experience and wealth to society.

t10n3.text: He had gold coins struck of a hundred figures from Japanese history, displayed in a hall he planned in Nagoya.

t10n4.text: He died on 21 July 2016, aged 83; fans thanked him for the biscuits and investors called him a model.

sawakami.sourcesNote: Sources: Institutional Investor (2001), The Japan Times (2001 and 2016), Bloomberg (2018), Toyo Keizai (2014), Oricon's report of his 2015 talk, President Online (2024), and a Financial Services Agency notice (2006). Lessons are in our own words; translations are ours.

start.lede: Atsuto Sawakami ran the Japanese arm of the Swiss private bank Pictet, then in 1999 founded Japan's first fund company with no ties to a big financial group. He sold one fund, directly, with no up-front commission, and preached long-term investing through decades when few in Japan wanted to hear it. He refused pension money as too short-term. Bloomberg called him Japan's first evangelist of long-term investing.
start.para: This page draws on interviews and reports in Institutional Investor, The Japan Times, Bloomberg, Toyo Keizai and President, a report of his 2015 talk, and a 2006 notice from Japan's Financial Services Agency. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

Japan's best-known share index; it peaked at the end of 1989 and took decades to recover.

themes.title: The outsider from Pictet
themes.idea: He spent sixteen years at the head of a Swiss private bank's Japanese business, then left to build a fund company for ordinary savers, owned by no big group.
ask: Would you leave a secure job to do it your own way?
Who owns the firm that manages your money, and does it matter?

themes.title: Investing, not money-rolling
themes.idea: He divides the market in two: real long-term investing, and what he calls money-rolling, buying and selling on price moves.
ask: Did you last buy because the price had fallen or because it had risen?
How much of your activity is money-rolling?

themes.title: Buy when they sell
themes.idea: His fund adds to holdings when others sell and trims when others buy. Most people, he says, do the reverse and pay for it.
ask: What did you do in the last market fall?
Which unloved industry might people need in ten years?
themes.caption: The crowd buys on the way up; the long-term investor buys on the way down.

themes.title: Proof in a bad year, and the long record
themes.idea: In 2001, as Japanese shares crashed, his fund rose and gained customers. Over the long run its returns were steady rather than spectacular.
ask: Would 5% a year, steadily, satisfy you?
How did your investments do in the worst year you remember?

themes.title: Why even pensions turned short-term
themes.idea: He argues that pension funds, which should be the most patient money, became short-termist once they began judging managers every year. So he would not take their money.
ask: Who judges your investing, and how often?
How would you invest if nobody checked for ten years?

themes.title: Sell direct, charge little
themes.idea: He sold his fund straight to savers, with no up-front commission, a low fee, no advertising and no sales force.
ask: What do you pay, every year, for the funds you own?
Who earns a commission when you buy?

themes.title: Tell investors everything
themes.idea: He believed savers should be told more, not less, and reported on every move every month.
ask: When did your fund last tell you why it bought something?
Would you rather have a report or a sales call?

themes.title: Think in decades
themes.idea: Look at least ten years ahead, he says, and ask how a company helps people live now and will help them in future.
ask: Which companies you know will matter more in ten years?
What would you own if you could not sell for a decade?

themes.title: Letting go
themes.idea: He hired a former part-time actor, handed him the fund, and promised to judge him only over years, even when investors left and the style changed.
ask: Who will run your money when you can't?
How long would you give a new manager?

themes.title: NISA, Japan, and an honest note
themes.idea: He welcomed Japan's tax-free NISA accounts but warned about timing, and this library also sets out the one regulatory action on record against his firm.

t1n1.text: Born in Nagoya in 1947, he studied international economics in Geneva and led Pictet's Japan business from 1980 to 1996.

t1n2.text: He set up an advisory firm in 1996 and the Sawakami Fund in 1999.

t1n3.text: It was Japan's first fund company with no ties to a major financial institution.

t1n4.text: Bloomberg later called him Japan's first evangelist of long-term investing, and an old rebel.

t2n1.text: What most institutions, and many individuals, do is not investing but rolling money around, he told a 2015 audience.

t2n2.text: Ordinary investors buy more as prices rise; long-term investors buy more as prices fall.

t2n3.text: Buying low and selling high, he said, is the ideal and the whole of investing.

t3n1.text: In a crash most people fear further falls and don't buy; in a rally they keep buying, then panic-sell when prices collapse.

t3n2.text: The fund buys companies making what consumers will need in future, adds when others sell, and trims when others buy.

t3n3.text: In 2001 he bought restructuring 'failed' old-industry companies, then beaten-down technology names.

t4n1.text: In the 12 months to early March 2001 his fund gained 9% while the Nikkei fell 36%, with much of it in cash.

t4n2.text: While other Japanese funds faced withdrawals, his kept attracting new money.

t4n3.text: In 2015 he said the fund had returned about 5% a year over its 16 years.

t4n4.text: By 2016 Bloomberg put its total return since 1999 at 95%.

t5n1.text: From the mid-1970s pensions were managed for safety and checked every year, so short-term results came to matter most.

t5n2.text: Managers who sell too early are blamed, so they keep buying in rallies and get caught by the crash.

t5n3.text: He has refused to manage pension money, saying it doesn't give managers enough time.

t5n4.text: He told Bloomberg he has basically no dealings with institutional investors, whom he calls short-termist.

t6n1.text: No up-front commission and a 1% management fee, which meant he needed far more money to break even.

t6n2.text: He did not advertise; visitors to the office were offered wine and snacks.

t6n3.text: He relied on no sales staff.

t6n4.text: He told a younger founder that selling through brokerages was a mistake; the only way was to sell directly.

t7n1.text: His fund issued monthly information on its movements and investment decisions.

t7n2.text: He criticised fund managers who put the sales side before the customers they serve.

t7n3.text: The fund had about 27,000 customers in 2001 and more than 118,000 by 2016.

t8n1.text: Investors should look at least ten years ahead, and hold for about that long.

t8n2.text: Ask how a company supports people's lives today and how it will tomorrow; avoid businesses built on chasing money.

t8n3.text: With the world's population growing by about 185,000 people a day, demand for energy, food, materials and water must rise.

t8n4.text: He argued that 'Japan pessimism' was nothing to fear, and that it was the time for long-term investing.

t9n1.text: In 2007 a 28-year-old part-time actor came to his seminar; he later gave him a job and watched him grow.

t9n2.text: In 2013 the young man became chief investment officer and Sawakami's son became president.

t9n3.text: Investors withdrew ¥126.5 billion over three years after the handover.

t9n4.text: He said he would not judge his successor until five to ten years into the job.

t10n1.text: He said the new NISA, launched in January 2024, was a great system started at the worst possible time.

t10n2.text: He expected the trend to turn over the following decade and found that exciting.

t10n3.text: In 2006 Japan's regulator found his firm had placed share trades for overseas advisory clients, which the law then barred, and had kept incomplete records.

t10n4.text: It ordered a one-month halt to new advisory contracts and a plan to improve compliance.

items.why: Buying more as prices fall is exactly his description of the long-term investor.

items.why: Buying because the price has risen is the habit he says most people fall into.

sp.text: On 30 March 2006 Japan's Financial Services Agency took action against Sawakami Investment Trust. It found that the firm had placed securities orders many times for overseas clients with whom it had investment advisory contracts, which the investment advisory law of the time prohibited, and that it had not kept or delivered certain required documents for that business. The agency ordered the firm not to take on new investment advisory contracts for one month, from 3 April to 2 May 2006, and to set up a proper compliance system, strengthen internal controls and report on its measures. We include it because this library puts integrity first and tells readers what is on the public record.

watsa.what: His letters to Fairfax shareholders since 1985, on value, protection and patience
watsa.scope: Fairfax is a large, listed company and its results depend on many people, not one. Book value growth is the company's own measure, reported in US dollars and including dividends; it is not a fund return. Figures change every year: check the latest letter.
watsa.readHow: Start with his latest letter to shareholders, then the 2008 credit default swap update and the 2016 letter, where he explains the hedges that cost Fairfax dearly.
watsa.sourcesNote: Sources: Fairfax's 2024 and 2025 letters to shareholders, the 2025 annual report's guiding principles, Fairfax press releases of September 2008 and November 2016, the Canadian Encyclopedia, Horatio Alger Association, Canadian Underwriter, Investment Executive, Nasdaq and the Globe and Mail. Lessons are in our own words.

start.lede: Prem Watsa grew up in Hyderabad, studied chemical engineering at IIT Madras, and reached Canada in the early 1970s with almost no money. In 1985 he took control of a small, struggling trucking insurer and renamed it Fairfax Financial. He ran it on Ben Graham's value principles and wrote to its owners every year. Since 1985 Fairfax's book value per share has grown about 18.7% a year, and people call him Canada's Warren Buffett.
start.para: This page draws on his yearly letters to Fairfax shareholders, Fairfax's own press releases and guiding principles, the Canadian Encyclopedia, and press reports of his best and worst calls. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

Money an insurer holds from premiums before it pays claims, which it can invest meanwhile.
A contract that pays out if a borrower fails to repay its debts; a kind of insurance.
A position that gains when your main holdings fall, to cushion losses.
Prices falling across an economy, which makes debts heavier and profits harder.
A kind of reinsurance that transfers little real risk; its accounting drew scrutiny in the mid-2000s.
Run by the managers of each business, not from head office.

t1n1.text: He was born in Hyderabad in 1950; his father taught English and maths and later ran a boys' school.

t1n2.text: He graduated in chemical engineering from IIT Madras in 1971.

t1n3.text: He reached Canada with only a few dollars and paid for his MBA by selling furnaces in winter and air conditioners in summer.

t1n4.text: His father had lost both his own parents at the age of three.

t2n1.text: In 1984 he started an investment firm, Hamblin Watsa, with his former boss.

t2n2.text: In 1985 they took control of Markel Financial, a struggling Canadian trucking insurer, and renamed it Fairfax.

t2n3.text: Like Berkshire, Fairfax invests the money it holds for future claims, called float.

t2n4.text: By 2025 Fairfax earned a record $4.8 billion in a year.

t3n1.text: Buy securities below what they are worth, with a margin of safety, and wait.

t3n2.text: His record and his insurance-plus-investing model earned him the nickname.

t3n3.text: He has quoted Graham that only 1 in 100 survived the 1929–32 crash unless bearish in 1925.

t4n1.text: The goal is to compound book value per share by 15% a year over the long term.

t4n2.text: The focus is long-term growth in book value, not quarterly earnings.

t4n3.text: Since 1985 book value per share has grown 18.7% a year with dividends, and the share price 19.5%.

t4n4.text: Over the same forty years the S&P 500 returned 11.5% a year with dividends.

t5n1.text: Fairfax began buying credit default swaps, a kind of insurance against companies failing to pay debts.

t5n2.text: He described the swaps as steps to protect the balance sheet from investment risks.

t5n3.text: By September 2008 the swaps had produced about $2.1 billion of gains as the credit crisis broke.

t5n4.text: The Globe and Mail's business magazine named him CEO of the year, partly for holding on to the swaps.

t6n1.text: Between mid-2003 and mid-2006 Fairfax's share price fell about 50% as the swaps held back profits.

t6n2.text: In 2012 he wrote that Fairfax continued to be early, and bearish, citing Graham.

t6n3.text: Staying soundly financed is what lets an early investor survive until the market comes round.

t7n1.text: From 2010 Fairfax hedged about 100% of its shares; by September 2016 the hedges were 112.7% of its holdings.

t7n2.text: When removed in late 2016, the index shorts had cost about $1.2 billion that year alone.

t7n3.text: After the 2016 US election he judged the hedges no longer needed and took them off.

t7n4.text: Protection that works once can be too expensive the next time; the cost must be weighed.

t8n1.text: In his letters he accepts the blame for disappointments and shares the credit for successes.

t8n2.text: In 2009 he told shareholders Fairfax should have been far more careful with three failed value investments.

t8n3.text: Fairfax was BlackBerry's top shareholder through its decline; he later wrote of it as a mistake.

t9n1.text: A subsidiary, Odyssey Re, restated results for errors in accounting for finite reinsurance.

t9n2.text: Fairfax and Watsa received SEC subpoenas in 2006 over an answer he gave on an investor call.

t9n3.text: In June 2009 the SEC said it did not intend to recommend any enforcement action.

t10n1.text: Fairfax's companies are run by their own leaders, with the head office judging them over the long term.

t10n2.text: Always being soundly financed is one of the company's core principles.

t10n3.text: He was appointed a Member of the Order of Canada in 2015.

items.q: You buy cheap insurance that pays if credit markets freeze, because a freeze would badly hurt your business.

start.lede: Francisco García Paramés taught himself value investing from Peter Lynch's book and a letter he requested from Warren Buffett. From 1993 to 2014 his Spanish fund at Bestinver returned about 15.7% a year, more than five times its benchmark in total. He left over a disagreement with the owners, started Cobas in 2017, lived through years of painful losses, and stuck to his method. Spain calls him its Warren Buffett.
start.para: This page draws on his book Investing for the Long Term, his fund letters at Cobas, interviews, and profiles by MOI Global, the CFA Institute and MoneyWeek. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

themes.idea: Ten years into his career he discovered the Austrian school of economics. It became his compass: markets work, are never in balance, and growth comes from saving.
ask: Do you try to forecast the economy before investing?
Where does growth come from, in your view?

themes.title: Risk is losing money
themes.idea: He defines risk not as how much a price swings, but as the chance of losing money.
ask: Is a 30% fall a risk to you if you never need to sell?
What would make a loss permanent?

themes.title: Quality at a low price
themes.idea: He looks for strong businesses with high returns on capital, growth and little debt, bought when they are cheap.
ask: Do you know your holdings' returns on capital?
Would you buy a great business that is not cheap?

themes.title: Leaving, and starting again
themes.idea: In 2014 he left Bestinver over differences with its owners. After a two-year wait he launched Cobas in 2017.
ask: What would make you walk away from a successful job?
How would you use two forced years off?

themes.title: The hard years
themes.idea: Cobas had a brutal start: losses in 2018, then the worst period for value investing on record, and the Covid crash. He wrote honestly to his investors.
ask: Would you stay with a manager after three bad years?
How would you write to people who trusted you, after losing their money?

themes.title: The rebound
themes.idea: By mid-2026 his international fund had returned about 20% a year over five years, and Madrid had become Europe's value-investing capital.
ask: Which of your bad years later looked like a good time to buy?
What makes a method survive its worst decade?

themes.title: We are qualified to wait
themes.idea: His last lesson is patience: the best returns come to those who can wait, and to managers whose clients let them.
ask: What in your life makes it hard to wait?
Are your savings in a place that lets you be patient?

t1n1.text: He was born in 1963 in El Ferrol, in north-western Spain, one of five children.

t1n2.text: He spent 15 months as a graduate trainee at the retailer El Corte Inglés, then took an MBA.

t1n3.text: After reading a review in Business Week he picked up One Up on Wall Street, and then the other masters.

t1n4.text: He wrote to Buffett's company to get a copy of the shareholder letter.

t2n1.text: He joined Bestinver, part of the Acciona group, as a young analyst.

t2n2.text: When his first tasks slowed down he began analysing Spanish shares to keep busy.

t2n3.text: His approach meant being fully in shares, not timing the market.

t3n1.text: Bestinfond gained 2,279% from 1993 to 2014, about 15.7% a year, against 410% for its index.

t3n2.text: That turned each euro into about thirty.

t3n3.text: His global fund beat the world index even when the index went nowhere.

t3n4.text: When he left Bestinver in 2014, its assets fell by about 30%.

t4n1.text: Finding the Austrian economists ten years in was, he says, a major turning point.

t4n2.text: He starts from the idea that markets work, by definition, and are never in equilibrium.

t4n3.text: Economic growth comes from rising productivity, financed by savings.

t4n4.text: He sees trying to guess the economy's next move as close to a stab in the dark.

t5n1.text: Risk is the probability of losing money by holding an asset, not how much its price moves.

t5n2.text: His book sets out long-run data on shares against other assets to argue for a long view.

t5n3.text: Even his best decades held hard stretches, such as a 22% fall in six months in 2011.

t6n1.text: Bestinver judged business quality by return on capital employed.

t6n2.text: The managers paid special attention to how companies were governed.

t6n3.text: Cobas described its holdings as businesses with strong competitive positions, average returns on capital of about 25%, growth, and little debt.

t7n1.text: He left Bestinver in September 2014 after disagreements with its owners.

t7n2.text: A non-compete agreement kept him out of fund management for two years.

t7n3.text: He later said he saw an extraordinary opportunity in a beaten-down miner in late 2015.

t8n1.text: His funds fell sharply, hit by holdings such as shipping companies.

t8n2.text: He reminded investors that his first global year, 1998, lost 14.1% while markets rose 16.5%.

t8n3.text: In the Covid crash he acknowledged that most of his investors were suffering big losses in hard-earned savings.

t9n1.text: Bloomberg reported his international fund up about 20% a year over the five years to July 2026.

t9n2.text: He describes it simply: buy assets below their intrinsic value, and be patient.

t9n3.text: Former colleagues and students run their own value funds, making Madrid a hub.

t10n1.text: He calls waiting the most important thing, and says his team is qualified to do it.

t10n2.text: He does not try to predict markets or economies, only to understand companies.

t10n3.text: In the 2020 crash he thanked unitholders who kept their trust, some of whom invested more.

kostolany.name: André Kostolany
kostolany.what: His books and columns on speculation, crowd psychology and patience
kostolany.scope: Kostolany published no audited record; his fortune and trades are known from his own books and later accounts, and figures vary. He speculated, often with borrowed money in his youth. Most sources are in German; translations are ours.
kostolany.readHow: If you read German, start with Die Kunst über Geld nachzudenken (The Art of Thinking about Money, 2000). If not, start with justETF's collection of his sayings, then the comdirect profile.
kostolany.sourcesNote: Sources: comdirect magazine, extraETF, etf.capital, justETF, HSBC's investor-guru series, FinanzBuch Verlag's guide to his ideas, Kagels Trading, and the record of the 1953 London Debt Agreement. Lessons are in our own words; translations are ours.

start.lede: André Kostolany was born in Budapest in 1906, learned the stock market in Paris, fled to America in 1940, and spent his last decades explaining markets to Germans in books, columns and on television. He was not a value investor but a speculator, and he said so. He grew rich twice, lost nearly everything in between, and claimed to be right only 51% of the time. His thirteen books sold about three million copies, yet the English-speaking world barely knows him.
start.para: This page draws on German and English accounts of his life and ideas: his publisher's guide, bank and broker profiles, and collections of his sayings. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

glossary: Someone who buys or sells expecting to profit from price moves, often over shorter periods.
French and German words for a rising market and a falling one.
Investors who buy in euphoria and sell in panic.
Investors who act against the crowd and hold through falls.
A loan to a government or company that pays interest and is repaid at the end.
