themes.title: From Budapest to the Paris bourse
themes.idea: A wealthy boy who wanted to be an art critic, he was sent by his father to learn broking in Paris in the 1920s.
ask: What would you have been, if not what you are?
Do economists' forecasts change what you buy?

themes.title: Rich twice, broke in between
themes.idea: He made a fortune betting on falling prices around 1929, lost it, and came close to bankruptcy more than once.
ask: Could you live with being wrong half the time?
What does that say about sizing each bet?

themes.title: The German bond coup
themes.idea: After the war he bought old German bonds that almost no one wanted, betting that Germany would want its good name back. It did.
ask: Which unloved asset might a government or company want to make good on?
What would you need to believe to buy it?

themes.title: Money plus psychology
themes.idea: He said market trends come from two things: how much money is available, and the mood of the crowd.
ask: Is money easy or tight right now?
Is the crowd fearful or greedy?

themes.title: The egg
themes.idea: He drew the market cycle as an egg. Rises and falls each have three phases: correction, accompanying, exaggeration.
ask: Which phase of the egg do you think the market is in now?
What would panic look like in your market?
themes.caption: Each rise and each fall has three phases; he bought in panic and sold in euphoria.

themes.title: The dog and its owner
themes.idea: Prices relate to the economy like a dog to its owner on a walk: running ahead, falling behind, but always coming back.
ask: Is the dog ahead of its owner today, or behind?
How far can it run before it turns back?
themes.caption: The dog runs ahead and lags behind, but always comes back.

themes.title: The four Gs
themes.idea: He said a successful investor needs four Gs: Geld, Gedanken, Geduld and Glück. Money, thoughts, patience and luck.
ask: Which of the four Gs are you shortest of?
Is any of your investing done with borrowed money?

themes.title: Shaky hands and hard-boiled ones
themes.idea: He split investors into the shaky, who buy in euphoria and sell in panic, and the hard-boiled, who do the opposite.
ask: Were your hands shaky in the last crash?
What would make them steadier?

themes.title: Sleeping pills and trams
themes.idea: His most famous advice: buy good shares, take sleeping pills, and stop looking. And never chase a share, any more than a tram.
ask: How often do you check prices?
When did you last chase a share, and how did it end?

themes.title: Teacher of a nation
themes.idea: In later life he explained markets to millions of Germans in columns, seminars and television, and co-founded an early asset manager.
ask: Who explained money to you when you were young?
What would you warn the next generation about?

t1n1.text: He studied philosophy and art history and hoped to become an art critic.

t1n2.text: His father sent him to Paris in the mid-1920s to train under the broker Adrien Perquel.

t1n3.text: He never studied classical economics and mocked economists' forecasts all his life.

t2n1.text: He grew rich betting that share prices would fall around the 1929 crash.

t2n2.text: Big bets that went wrong wiped him out more than once.

t2n3.text: He admitted being right on 51% of his trades and wrong on 49%.

t3n1.text: He bought pre-war German bonds in Paris for about 250 francs each.

t3n2.text: He reasoned that the new West Germany would repay to regain its creditworthiness.

t3n3.text: The London Debt Agreement settled Germany's old foreign debts.

t3n4.text: He later sold the bonds for about 35,000 francs each: his stake grew more than a hundred times.

t4n1.text: Trend equals money plus psychology.

t4n2.text: Don't assume people buying in a frenzy know more than you.

t4n3.text: He argued that in a crisis governments and central banks act, which is why to buy then.

t5n1.text: Every rise and every fall moves through correction, an accompanying phase, and exaggeration.

t5n2.text: He bought in the exaggeration of a fall, when heavy selling signals panic, and added at the start of the rise.

t5n3.text: He sold in the euphoric last phase of a rise, at the latest early in the fall.

t5n4.text: In the middle phases he advised doing nothing.

t6n1.text: The share price runs ahead of the economy or lags behind, but returns to it.

t6n2.text: Over time prices follow the economy, even when short swings are wild.

t6n3.text: On the stock market anything is possible, even the opposite.

t7n1.text: Your own money, never borrowed.

t7n2.text: A considered plan: goals, time span and how much risk you can take.

t7n3.text: The most important of the four.

t7n4.text: It cannot be forced, but without it you lose confidence, and then patience.

t8n1.text: They buy when prices are high and the mood is euphoric, and sell at a loss in panic.

t8n2.text: They hold when others get nervous, and buy when sentiment is at its lowest.

t8n3.text: Anyone lacking one of the first three Gs ends up among the shaky.

t9n1.text: Buy shares, take sleeping pills, don't look for years, and you will be rich.

t9n2.text: Stock market profits are payment for pain: first comes the pain, then the money.

t9n3.text: Never run after a tram or a share; another one always comes.

t9n4.text: He liked to quote old Frankfurt brokers: money is made by sitting still, not with the head.

t10n1.text: He wrote over 400 columns for the business magazine Capital.

t10n2.text: His 13 books sold about three million copies.

t10n3.text: In 1971 he co-founded Fiduka, one of Germany's first asset managers, with Gottfried Heller.

t10n4.text: Shortly before his death in 1999 he warned against the dot-com mania.

sp.title: Shaky hands or hard-boiled? Tap your answer

items.q: Prices have doubled, everyone at dinner talks about shares, and you buy for the first time.
items.why: Buying in euphoria, when the crowd is already in, is his picture of shaky hands.

items.q: The market has fallen 35% on panic headlines. You buy more with spare money.
items.why: Buying in the exaggeration of a fall, with your own money, is what the hard-boiled do.

items.q: You borrowed to buy, prices drop, and the lender forces you to sell.

items.q: You bought a year ago, nothing has happened, and you are still waiting calmly.

sp.text: Kostolany was a speculator, not a value investor, and he did not hide it. In his early years he made and lost fortunes with large, sometimes borrowed bets, and he came close to bankruptcy more than once. He published no audited record, so his wealth and many trades are known only from his own books and later accounts. We include him for his lessons on crowd psychology and patience, which have lasted, and we recommend none of his speculative methods.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security or fund. Companies and funds are named for history and education only. Some sources are in Spanish or German; summaries and translations are our own.

cundill.name: Peter Cundill
cundill.what: His approach, his best and worst investments, and his last interview
cundill.scope: Fund returns are as reported in books and the press; figures differ by period and by source. He died in 2011, and his later record was earned with a team. Companies are named for history only.
cundill.readHow: Start with There's Always Something to Do (Christopher Risso-Gill, McGill-Queen's University Press, 2011), then his last interview with the Globe and Mail.
cundill.sourcesNote: Sources: There's Always Something to Do (2011) and Routines and Orgies (2014), both by Christopher Risso-Gill; The Globe and Mail's last interview (2011); ThinkAdvisor's 2004 interview; Morningstar Canada; McGill University; Investment Executive; GuruFocus. Lessons are in our own words.

start.lede: Peter Cundill was a Canadian accountant who read Ben Graham's Security Analysis on a flight home in December 1973 and changed his life. He took over a small fund that had lost two-thirds of its value and turned it into the Cundill Value Fund. He hunted the world for shares selling below their liquidation value, from Japan to Europe, and compounded about 22% a year for his first fifteen years without a losing year. They called him the Indiana Jones of Canadian money managers.
start.para: This page draws on the book of his approach, There's Always Something to Do, his last interview with the Globe and Mail, a 2004 interview, McGill University's tributes, and Morningstar's account of his favourite trades. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

glossary: What a company would fetch if it stopped trading and sold everything, after paying its debts.
A share priced below current assets minus all liabilities: Graham's deepest bargain.
Current assets, such as cash, stock and money owed by customers, minus current liabilities.
Assets minus liabilities, as shown in the accounts.
Price to earnings: the share price divided by yearly earnings per share.
The gap between price and value that protects you if you are wrong.

themes.title: A $500 lesson
themes.idea: His first investment, as a summer office boy, was a mining tip. He lost all $500 in under two days, and never forgot it.
ask: What was your first investing loss?
What did it teach you?

themes.title: The eureka moment
themes.idea: On a flight home in December 1973 he read Graham's Security Analysis. It gave him the method he had been missing.
ask: Which book gave you your method?
Would you take over something that had lost two-thirds of its value?

themes.title: A dollar for forty cents
themes.idea: He bought shares priced below the company's liquidation value: what it would be worth if it closed and sold everything.
ask: What would your largest holding fetch if it closed tomorrow?
How big a gap would you want?
themes.caption: Buy below what the company would fetch if it closed: the gap is the margin of safety.

themes.title: His six tests
themes.idea: He wrote down his criteria: cheap against value and book, profitable, paying dividends, well off its high, and on a low P/E.
ask: Which of the six tests do your holdings fail?
Which test would you drop, and why?

themes.title: Hidden assets
themes.idea: He read accounts for what they hid: buildings at old costs, valuable leases, power plants. JWT was his textbook case.
ask: What might your company own that its accounts undervalue?
When did you last read a balance sheet line by line?

themes.title: Buy more as it falls
themes.idea: His best investment, Cleveland-Cliffs, fell by more than half after he bought. He kept buying.
ask: Would you buy more of a sound business after it halves?
How do you tell a bargain from a trap?

themes.title: Indiana Jones
themes.idea: He searched the world for bargains, often starting with the country whose market had done worst that year.
ask: Which market is most hated this year?
Would you go there?

themes.title: Cash is a position
themes.idea: When few shares met his tests he simply held cash, sometimes up to 40%, and waited.
ask: How much cash do you keep for bargains?
What would you buy first in a crash?

themes.title: The one that went wrong
themes.idea: His worst investment, Cable and Wireless, met every Graham test and still failed. Careful analysis guarantees nothing.
ask: What is your Cable and Wireless?
What would you do differently next time?

themes.title: Patience, history and giving back
themes.idea: He ended advising patience, picking good managers, and studying history, and left a large prize for history writing.
ask: What can history teach you about today's market?
Who would you trust to manage your money for twenty years?

t1n1.text: He was born in Montreal in 1938 and studied commerce at McGill, graduating in 1960.

t1n2.text: As an office boy in 1959 he put $500 into a speculative mining share and lost it all within 48 hours.

t1n3.text: He qualified as a chartered accountant before moving into investment work.

t2n1.text: Flying from Toronto to Vancouver for Christmas in 1973, he read Graham and found his road.

t2n2.text: In 1975 he took control of a small fund whose shares had fallen from $6 to $2.

t2n3.text: He renamed it the Cundill Value Fund and ran it on Graham's rules.

t3n1.text: A share is cheap when its price is below what the business would fetch if wound up.

t3n2.text: That gap was the margin of safety he swore by.

t3n3.text: He popularised the idea of buying a dollar of value for 40 cents.

t3n4.text: His favourite was a share below working capital minus all debts, Graham's net-net.

t4n1.text: The price must be below intrinsic value and book value, ideally below net working capital less long-term debt.

t4n2.text: Ideally five years of growing earnings.

t4n3.text: Ideally a regularly rising dividend.

t4n4.text: A price under half its former high, preferably near its all-time low, and a P/E under ten.

t5n1.text: The advertising agency J. Walter Thompson listed above $20 in 1972 and fell to about $4.

t5n2.text: Its book value of $18 a share left out freehold buildings in Tokyo and Paris and a London lease.

t5n3.text: He bought at about $8 on average and sold a year later above $20.

t5n4.text: Very few investors do the homework, which is the edge.

t6n1.text: An iron-ore pellet maker with a large market share, it fell from his first price of $15 to $6.

t6n2.text: He bought and bought as the price dropped, though the supply seemed endless.

t6n3.text: He sold much of it in the 1986–87 rally and bought back after the October 1987 crash.

t6n4.text: When he finally sold in 1991 he had compounded at over 30% a year.

t7n1.text: He was nicknamed the Indiana Jones of Canadian money managers.

t7n2.text: He would look at the country with the year's worst stock market and put some money there.

t7n3.text: After the 1997 crash he found hundreds of Japanese shares selling below net cash, with strong balance sheets.

t7n4.text: In 2004 over a third of his fund was in Japan.

t8n1.text: In 2004 he held about 33% in cash because he was finding few bargains.

t8n2.text: In the past his cash had been as high as 40%.

t8n3.text: Cash kept him free to buy when the next crisis came.

t9n1.text: He bought after the dot-com bust: a low price, no debt, lots of cash, profitable networks.

t9n2.text: He called it the investment where he had his head handed to him.

t9n3.text: Even strict adherence to Graham's rules is no guarantee.

t10n1.text: His mantra was patience, patience and more patience; the big rewards come from compounding.

t10n2.text: After selling his firm to Mackenzie in 2006 he picked few shares himself and backed managers who used his value approach.

t10n3.text: He saw history and investing as alike: both study the past to understand the present.

t10n4.text: His foundation created the Cundill History Prize at McGill in 2008, the largest of its kind.

start.lede: Luiz Barsi Filho lost his father at one and grew up in a São Paulo tenement, shining shoes and selling sweets. At 14 he found work at a stockbroker. Worried that Brazil's state pension would fail him, he began in the early 1970s to buy shares in one durable company a month and reinvest every dividend. Half a century later he is Brazil's biggest individual investor, said to receive more than a million reais a day in dividends, and he still rides the metro.
start.para: This page draws on Brazilian business press profiles, his 2022 autobiography as excerpted by InfoMoney, investor-education sites, and Brazil's securities regulator. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

t1n1.text: He was born in São Paulo in 1939 and raised by his mother in a tenement in the Brás district.

t1n2.text: His father, an immigrant, died when he was a year old.

t1n3.text: From about seven he shined shoes, sold sweets at a cinema and helped his mother as a tailor's apprentice.

t1n4.text: His stated aim was never to be poor again.

t2n1.text: At 14 he started at a stockbroker, where he became fascinated by balance sheets.

t2n2.text: He trained as an accounting technician, then studied law and economics.

t2n3.text: He taught balance-sheet analysis, worked as an auditor and analyst, and was a newspaper's economics editor for 18 years.

t3n1.text: He concluded that Brazil's social security system could not be relied on.

t3n2.text: In 1970 he ranked sectors by how long they would last: food, sanitation, energy, mining and finance.

t3n3.text: The study's title, Shares Guarantee the Future, now names an education company run by his daughter.

t4n1.text: His first pick, a food company, was dropped because of succession worries; he chose the power company CESP instead.

t4n2.text: He aimed for 100,000 shares and bought about 1,000 a month.

t4n3.text: He bought from his salary and reinvested the dividends.

t4n4.text: Within about ten years his dividends exceeded a state pension.

t5n1.text: He looks for companies in durable sectors that pay good dividends and trade below book value.

t5n2.text: He judges product longevity, governance, management, finances, profits and how regularly dividends come.

t5n3.text: He saw himself as owning part of profitable businesses, not trading in and out.

t5n4.text: Several of his holdings have been owned for more than 30 years.

t6n1.text: Banks, energy, sanitation, insurance and telecoms are the starting filter taught by his followers.

t6n2.text: The sector is where the analysis begins, not where it ends.

t6n3.text: He has excluded the state oil company, airlines, tourism and appliance retail.

t7n1.text: Never invest money you might need.

t7n2.text: Never sell out of necessity.

t7n3.text: He avoids leverage, futures and options.

t7n4.text: He jokes that fixed income, renda fixa, is really perda fixa: a fixed loss.

t8n1.text: He bought Santander Brasil preferred shares for about R$0.50; in 2020 they traded above R$25.

t8n2.text: In 2019 one power company alone paid him about R$4 million in dividends.

t8n3.text: His portfolio, near US$2 billion, is reported to pay him over R$1 million a day.

t9n1.text: He counts investments in banks that collapsed, including Banco Nacional, among his mistakes.

t9n2.text: The regulator examined Unipar shares he bought in May 2021 while on its board.

t9n3.text: In March 2024 it acquitted him unanimously.

t9n4.text: He said the purchase was made to collect dividends, in line with his strategy.

t10n1.text: He commutes by metro with a free pass for older people.

t10n2.text: Asked if he is rich, he turns the question back: what does wealth mean to you?

t10n3.text: Two of his children work in investing, and one teaches his method.

t10n4.text: In 2026 he became vice-chairman of Unipar's board.

sp.text: Brazil's securities regulator, the CVM, brought a case alleging that Luiz Barsi Filho traded on inside information when he bought Unipar shares worth about R$1.1 million on 28 May 2021, while he sat on the company's board, days before it announced a deal. On 26 March 2024 the CVM's board acquitted him unanimously. His defence was that the purchase was made to collect dividends, in line with his long-standing strategy. He has also lost money on banks that failed in the 1990s. We include this because the library puts integrity first and tells readers what is on the public record.

start.lede: Allan Gray grew up in South Africa, studied at Harvard, and made his name at Fidelity in Boston in 1962, when the market fell 21.7% in a month and his portfolio rose. In 1973 he went home to Cape Town and started a firm that became South Africa's largest private investment manager, then founded Orbis to invest worldwide. He shunned publicity, asked more questions than he answered, and gave his controlling stake in both firms to a charitable foundation.
start.para: This page draws on his 2015 letter to clients, his firm's collection of colleagues' memories of his thinking, Orbis's own accounts of its philosophy, the firm's fund factsheets, and his obituaries. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

A fee that rises when a fund beats its benchmark and falls when it lags.

themes.title: Butterworth to Harvard
themes.idea: He came from a pioneering family in the Eastern Cape, overcame dyslexia, and studied at Rhodes, the LSE and Harvard.
ask: What difficulty shaped how you learn?
Who in your family broke new ground?

themes.idea: At Fidelity in Boston, the market fell 21.7% in January 1962 and stayed weak until October. His portfolio rose 10%.
ask: How did your portfolio do in the last crash?
What would make it rise when others fall?

themes.title: Chosen, not sold
themes.idea: In 1973 he started his own firm in Cape Town, believing clients should choose its services rather than be sold them.
ask: Would your work grow if nobody sold it?
Do you prefer advisers who sell or who are chosen?

themes.title: Contrarian by nature
themes.idea: He looked for cheap, neglected companies others overlooked, and trusted his own judgment over the crowd's mood.
ask: Which unloved company do you understand well?
When did you last disagree with the crowd and act on it?
themes.caption: The crowd moves one way; the bargains are where it is leaving.

themes.title: Cycles
themes.idea: He believed in cycles: good times breed bad times, and strong businesses bought near a cyclical low offer a discount and improving results.
ask: Where is your industry in its cycle?
Which company could you hold for twenty years?

themes.title: Value, then dream a little
themes.idea: He stood firmly on what a business was worth, then looked for the upside the market was not pricing.
ask: What is the floor under your best idea?
And what could go right that nobody expects?

themes.title: Wrong, and changing your mind
themes.idea: He accepted being wrong sometimes, because good calls would more than pay for bad ones, and he changed his mind when the facts changed.
ask: When did you last change your mind about a holding?
What evidence would make you sell your favourite?

themes.title: The price of being different
themes.idea: He warned that a long-term contrarian approach pays only for those who can bear long, uncomfortable spells of underperformance.
ask: How long could you lag before giving up?
Who around you would lose patience first?

themes.title: Fees that serve clients
themes.idea: His firms tied their fees to results, so they earned more only when clients did, an idea Orbis took further with refundable fees.
ask: Do your fund's fees fall when it does badly?
How are the people who manage your money paid?

themes.title: Giving it all back
themes.idea: He funded students' education for years, then gave his family's controlling stakes in both firms to a charitable foundation.
ask: What would you want your work to fund after you?
Who should own a firm built for the long term?

t1n1.text: His family came from Aberdeen in the 1890s; his grandmother became South Africa's first woman mayor.

t1n2.text: He was dyslexic, and still went on to study accounting at Rhodes University.

t1n3.text: He studied at the London School of Economics and took an MBA at Harvard.

t2n1.text: He spent eight years at Fidelity in Boston.

t2n2.text: In 1962 the market fell 21.7% in January; his portfolio ended up 10%.

t2n3.text: The experience made contrarian thinking the base of his philosophy for life.

t3n1.text: He founded Allan Gray Investment Counsel in Cape Town.

t3n2.text: He wanted services clients chose, so the firm's growth would prove it was helping them.

t3n3.text: So private was he that he was called the 'ghost of Cape Town'.

t4n1.text: He hunted for cheap companies the market had forgotten.

t4n2.text: When a share was beaten down he pushed colleagues to make the case for it.

t4n3.text: Being contrarian does not make you right more often; it finds prices where bad news is already in.

t5n1.text: He often said that good times, by their nature, produce the tough times.

t5n2.text: Strong businesses near a cyclical low give both a discount and better results ahead.

t5n3.text: He also liked businesses that could compound for a very long time.

t6n1.text: Investments rested on business value.

t6n2.text: He looked for undervalued potential the market had not priced.

t6n3.text: He encouraged younger colleagues to imagine what could go right.

t7n1.text: He accepted some mistakes because the right decisions could more than offset smaller losses.

t7n2.text: He sought out contrary evidence and reversed positions when the facts changed.

t7n3.text: He taught that a good investment idea loses its value quickly if not acted on.

t8n1.text: Superior results come only if you can withstand uncomfortably long periods of lagging.

t8n2.text: Owners and decision-makers must share the conviction to stay the course.

t8n3.text: The firm's flagship equity fund has returned about 19.2% a year since 1998, against 14.4% for its benchmark.

t9n1.text: The flagship fund's fee rises and falls with its result against the benchmark.

t9n2.text: Orbis is known for client-aligned, refundable fees.

t9n3.text: Colleagues recall that he insisted good returns must turn into real wealth for clients.

t10n1.text: In 2005 he created a foundation for school and university scholarships across southern Africa.

t10n2.text: In 2015 the family gave its controlling stakes in Allan Gray and Orbis to a foundation.

t10n3.text: He said free enterprise had done much for many, and those it rewards should help others.

t10n4.text: He wanted the firms free from short-term pressure from outside owners.

start.lede: Cheah Cheng Hye grew up poor in Penang, sold pineapples by the road after his father died, and never went to university. He became a financial journalist in Hong Kong, taught himself accounting, and in 1993 co-founded Value Partners with less than US$5 million. Its Classic Fund rose about 3,588% over the next 32 years, against 722% for the Hang Seng Index. Asia calls him its Warren Buffett.

t1n1.text: He was born in Penang in 1954 to a poor family and often went hungry.

t1n2.text: His father died when he was nine; as the eldest he supported the family.

t1n3.text: He sold pineapples by the road, folded newspapers, and sold joss sticks at a temple.

t2n1.text: He joined The Star at 17 folding newspapers, then became a reporter.

t2n2.text: He moved to Hong Kong in 1974 and worked for the Asian Wall Street Journal and Asiaweek.

t2n3.text: He was first to report that the Hong Kong dollar would be pegged to the US dollar in 1983.

t2n4.text: He has said being an ex-journalist helps in investing.

t3n1.text: He never went to university.

t3n2.text: He set himself a course in accountancy, law and statistics.

t3n3.text: He read companies' reports from cover to cover and worked long hours.

t3n4.text: In 1989 he became head of research and a trader at Morgan Grenfell in Hong Kong.

t4n1.text: He co-founded Value Partners with V-Nee Yeh, with less than US$5 million.

t4n2.text: Its 2007 share offer drew demand for more than 300 times the shares available.

t4n3.text: The Classic Fund rose about 3,588% from April 1993 to January 2025, against 722% for the Hang Seng.

t5n1.text: He describes himself as a value investor in the Graham-and-Dodd tradition.

t5n2.text: He weighs cash flow more heavily than Graham did.

t5n3.text: In emerging markets he gives corporate governance special weight.

t6n1.text: Value Partners makes about 2,500 company visits a year.

t6n2.text: Staff are encouraged to spend little time at their desks.

t6n3.text: After BYD's shares fell sharply he visited, judged it unfairly marked down, and became its second-largest shareholder.

t7n1.text: We buy when people sell and sell when people buy, he says.

t7n2.text: He prefers dull stocks when others chase exciting ones.

t7n3.text: He bought no dot-com shares while the market chased them.

t7n4.text: When Buffett invested in BYD in 2008 and the market followed, Value Partners sold for a large profit.

t8n1.text: He urges a 'stupid-clever' mindset that takes the self out of investment decisions.

t8n2.text: He reckons about a third of his decisions are mistakes, mainly from misjudging managers.

t8n3.text: He admits his trusting nature can be a weakness in a fund manager.

t8n4.text: He put US$30 million into a Hong Kong airline that went bust within six months.

t9n1.text: Value investing is not always in favour: the Classic Fund was in the red in seven of 25 years.

t9n2.text: Hong Kong's regulator reprimanded him and the firm over buy orders near the close in late December 1998.

t9n3.text: It found the effect unintentional, but said he should have known it could affect prices.

t9n4.text: The firm was fined HK$4 million when two funds issued more shares than allowed; no investor losses were apparent.

t10n1.text: He says the unlucky boy was very lucky, but did not know it then.

t10n2.text: He believes working harder can make up for a rival's cleverness.

t10n3.text: In January 2025, as a Chinese broker took control of the firm, he stepped down as co-chairman.

sp.text: On 5 October 2000 Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission publicly reprimanded Value Partners Limited and Cheah Cheng Hye, the person responsible for its investment decisions. It found that on 28, 29 and 31 December 1998 the firm had placed buy orders near the close of trading in five stocks, which left their closing prices higher than they might otherwise have been. The SFC found this unintentional but said he should have known it could affect prices, and cited inadequate controls. In January 2017 the SFC reprimanded two Value Partners companies and fined them HK$4 million in total because two funds had issued more shares than their constitutions allowed, and the firm reported this six months late; the SFC found no apparent investor losses, and he was not named. We include this because the library puts integrity first and tells readers what is on the public record.

start.lede: Paul Tudor Jones learned to trade in the cotton pits of the 1970s, nearly wiped himself out in 1979, and decided never again to risk everything on one trade. He founded Tudor Investment in 1980, expected the 1987 crash, and his main fund is reported to have made 125.9% after fees that year, the year the market fell 22.6% in a single day. His rules are about defence first: cut losses, never add to losers, and look for trades that could pay five times what they risk.
start.para: This page draws on SEC filings for a fund he managed alone, his interviews in Market Wizards and with Tony Robbins, press reports of his career, and his 2020 letter on inflation. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

themes.title: From Memphis to the cotton pit
themes.idea: After university a relative in the cotton business sent him to the great cotton trader Eli Tullis, who hired him and taught him on the floor of the New York Cotton Exchange.

Could you stay calm while losing money in public?

themes.idea: In 1979 a cotton trade went badly wrong and he lost 60 to 70% of his clients' money. It nearly ended his career and shaped every rule he made afterwards.

What rule would have saved you from your worst loss?

themes.idea: In 1980 he started his own firm. Dunavant and Tullis were among his first clients, and Commodities Corporation gave him $30,000 to manage.

How long did you practise before managing others' money?

themes.title: 1987: the crash he expected
themes.idea: In 1987 his deputy Peter Borish mapped that year's market against the run-up to the 1929 crash, and the two expected a collapse. In October the Dow fell 22.6% in a day. His main fund is reported to have made 125.9% that year.
ask: What would make you sure enough to bet against everyone?
Why might he have wanted the film taken off the air?

themes.title: Defence first
themes.idea: His most repeated lesson: protect what you have before trying to make more. Never add to a losing position.
ask: Have you ever added to a loser to 'average down'? How did it end?
What do you do when you are on a losing streak?

themes.title: Five to one
themes.idea: He looks for trades that could make five times what they risk. That means he can be wrong most of the time and still come out ahead.
ask: Do you know your reward-to-risk before you buy?
How often are you right, honestly?
themes.caption: Risk one to make five: you can be wrong four times in five and still come out a little ahead.

themes.title: The 200-day line
themes.idea: He watches the 200-day moving average of closing prices. If something falls below it, he gets out and plays defence.
ask: Where are your holdings against their 200-day average?
Would a simple rule have kept you out of your worst loss?
themes.caption: Above the long-term average, play offence; below it, play defence.

themes.title: Everything is connected

themes.title: Two eras
themes.idea: His flagship fund averaged about 26% a year from 1987 to 2007, then about 4.7% a year from 2008 to 2016. Even legends have long flat stretches.

t1n1.text: He was born in Memphis, Tennessee, in 1954 and graduated from the University of Virginia in 1976.

t1n2.text: Billy Dunavant, a cotton merchant in his family (he calls him his uncle; Wikipedia says cousin), sent him to Eli Tullis in New Orleans.

t1n3.text: Tullis offered him a job on the floor of the New York Cotton Exchange.

t1n4.text: Tullis later fired him for falling asleep at his desk after a night out in New Orleans.

t2n1.text: He traded too many cotton contracts; the market went against him, costing 60 to 70% of the accounts he managed.

t2n2.text: He said the trade nearly broke him, and asked himself why he would risk everything on one trade.

t2n3.text: He decided to make trading a pursuit of happiness rather than pain, and to learn discipline and money management.

t3n1.text: He founded Tudor Investment Corporation at 26.

t3n2.text: Dunavant and Tullis were among his first clients; Commodities Corporation gave him $30,000 to manage.

t3n3.text: SEC filings say he traded for his own account from 1977 and for customers from 1981.

t3n4.text: For the employee fund on this page he was the only person making trading decisions.

t4n1.text: The 1987 PBS documentary Trader showed him, at 32, managing $125 million; he later persuaded PBS to stop showing it.

t4n2.text: Peter Borish laid the 1987 market over the market before the 1929 crash.

t4n3.text: He told Tony Robbins that prices had fallen below his long-term trend line, and he was out at the top.

t4n4.text: On 19 October 1987 the Dow fell 22.6% to 1,738.74, its worst day ever.

t4n5.text: Market Wizards reported 62% for his Tudor Futures Fund in October alone; his main fund reportedly made 125.9% after fees in 1987.

t5n1.text: Never add to a position that is losing money.

t5n2.text: Cut your trading when you are trading badly; increase it when you are trading well.

t5n3.text: Avoid trades where you cannot control your risk.

t5n4.text: In nearly 14 years of SEC-filed monthly results, the employee fund's worst month was a fall of 9.62%, in July 1990.

t6n1.text: He risks one dollar to make five.

t6n2.text: At five to one, he says, you can win just 20% of the time; one win pays for four losses, with a little left over.

t6n3.text: The rule assumes you will often be wrong, and plans for it.

t7n1.text: The 200-day moving average of closing prices is his metric for everything.

t7n2.text: He has seen too many stocks and commodities go to zero.

t7n3.text: Get out of anything that falls below it.

t8n1.text: SEC filings describe his approach as directional, short-term and discretionary, guided by strict risk control.

t8n2.text: He bought put options on Japan's stock market in February 1990; his main fund reportedly made 87.4% that year as the market collapsed.

t8n3.text: He chaired the New York Cotton Exchange from 1992 to 1995.

t8n4.text: In May 2020 he argued that money printing could bring inflation, and said his main fund might trade bitcoin futures as a hedge.

t9n1.text: Investor documents showed about 26% a year from 1987 through 2007.

t9n2.text: From 2008 through 2016 the average fell to about 4.7% a year, and clients withdrew money.

t9n3.text: In the financial crisis his fund lost nearly 5%, about 32 points better than the S&P 500.

t10n1.text: After the crash, which hurt so many others, he and friends set up the Robin Hood Foundation, in 1988.

t10n2.text: He pleaded guilty after protected wetlands on his Maryland hunting estate were filled without a permit, paying a $1 million fine and $1 million to a wildlife foundation.

t10n3.text: In 1996 Tudor paid $800,000 to settle SEC claims about short sales in 1994, without admitting or denying them.

sp.text: In 1990 he pleaded guilty in a federal case after 86 acres of protected wetlands on his Maryland hunting estate were filled without a permit; he paid a $1 million fine and $1 million to the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation. In September 1996 Tudor Investment Corporation settled an SEC proceeding about alleged breaches of the 'uptick rule' in short sales over two days in March 1994, paying $800,000 without admitting or denying the findings. In April 2002 a private lawsuit claiming 'short-swing' profits under Section 16(b) was settled, with the Tudor defendants paying $1.45 million. In 2013 he apologised for saying that motherhood keeps women from being great traders, and in 2017, after a supportive email he had sent Harvey Weinstein was reported, he told staff he had believed and defended Weinstein too long. We include this because the library puts integrity first and tells readers what is on the public record.

Nothing on this page is a recommendation to buy, sell or trade anything, and none of it is a trading system. Figures for funds other than the SEC-registered employee fund are as reported by the press and are not audited by us.

rec.intro: Hedge funds rarely publish their results. But from 1990 Tudor ran a small fund for its own employees that was registered with the SEC, so its monthly returns sit in public filings. Paul Tudor Jones was its only manager. These charts use those figures, after fees, from July 1990 to April 2004.
rec.barsNote: From 1991 to 2003 the fund compounded about 18.9% a year, against about 12.1% for the S&P 500 with dividends. It lagged the index in strong bull years such as 1995 and 1997, but it made money in 2000, 2001 and 2002, when the index fell three years running. It had no losing calendar year in this record.
rec.crashNote: Each dot is a Dow closing level; the dashed line jumps almost two years, to August 1989. The Dow closed at a record 2,722 on 25 August 1987. On Monday 19 October it lost 22.6% in one day, from 2,246.73 to 1,738.74, then bounced back above 2,000 within two days. It did not pass the old high until 24 August 1989. Market Wizards reported that his Tudor Futures Fund gained 62% in October 1987 alone, and his main fund is reported to have made 125.9% after fees that year.
rec.erasNote: Average yearly gains of the flagship Tudor BVI Global Fund as reported by Bloomberg from investor documents in August 2017. These are press-reported figures for a different, much larger fund, not audited by us. From the mid-2000s he made fewer of the fund's trading decisions himself: by 2014, investors told CNBC he accounted for about 20% of its positions.
sources: Monthly returns and annual rates of return, July 1990 to April 2004: Tudor Fund For Employees L.P., prospectus filed with the SEC in 2004.
S&P 500 total returns: published yearly figures (Slickcharts and US500 agree); other datasets differ by a few tenths of a point.
Statistics such as compound growth and the deepest fall from a high are our own calculations from the monthly figures.
Dow closing levels: CNBC (August 1987 high), 24/7 Wall St (16 and 19 October), Benzinga (20 October), The Motley Fool (21 October), AP via Lincoln Daily News (24 August 1989).
Flagship fund figures: CNBC (2014), Bloomberg via Yahoo Finance (August 2017), GuruFocus (2017); the 62% October figure is from Market Wizards as quoted by GuruFocus.

Lessons are in our own words.

start.lede: Mark Minervini left school early, played music, bought his first stock in 1983 and made a quick profit on it. Then, for about six years, he kept losing money until his capital was gone. After that he studied the biggest winning stocks in history, built a method he calls SEPA, and won the U.S. Investing Championship twice, in 1997 and 2021. His trademark is a strict checklist: buy only leading stocks in strong uptrends, at a precise point, and cut every loss small.
start.para: This page draws on his books, his interviews, Jack Schwager's Stock Market Wizards and the contest's own published results. About an hour a week for ten weeks: one idea here, then the source it comes from.

themes.title: A musician who lost it all
themes.idea: He wanted to be a musician, bought his first stock in 1983, and made money at once. Then he lost money for about six years, until his capital was gone.
ask: What did your first lucky win teach you, rightly or wrongly?
How long would you keep going while losing money?

themes.title: Study the winners
themes.idea: Instead of guessing, he studied what the biggest winning stocks in history looked like before their big moves, and built a 'leadership profile' to copy.
ask: Do you buy what looks cheap, or what looks strong?
What did your best past winners have in common?

themes.title: SEPA: a specific entry point
themes.idea: In 1993 he founded Quantech Research Group, selling research based on his method, Specific Entry Point Analysis, or SEPA.
ask: Do you know exactly why, and exactly when, you buy?
Which matters more to you: the company or the price trend?

themes.title: Stage 2 only
themes.idea: Borrowing Stan Weinstein's idea that stocks move through four stages, he buys only in Stage 2: when a stock is already in a strong, rising trend.
ask: Do you buy shares while they are falling, hoping for a bottom?
What would a Stage 2 chart of a stock you own look like?
themes.caption: Stan Weinstein's four stages. Minervini buys only in Stage 2, when a stock is already rising.

themes.title: The Trend Template
themes.idea: His trademark filter: eight tests on price, moving averages and the yearly high and low. A stock that fails any of them is not a candidate.
ask: How many of your holdings would pass all eight tests today?
Why might a rule-based filter beat your gut?

themes.title: The VCP
themes.idea: His favourite setup is the Volatility Contraction Pattern: a rising stock pauses, and each pullback is smaller than the one before, until the price breaks out.
ask: Why would shrinking swings mean fewer sellers?
Where would your stop go if you bought at a breakout?
themes.caption: Each pullback is smaller than the last, and volume dries up. The buy point is the breakout above the final tight range.

themes.title: Cut losses small
themes.idea: After losing everything once, he made one rule above all: cut losses while they are small. He says no loss should ever reach 10%, and the average should be far smaller.
ask: What is the biggest loss you have let a single stock reach?
How much would you need to gain to recover a 50% loss?
themes.caption: The bigger the loss, the bigger the gain needed just to get back to where you started.

themes.title: 220% a year
themes.idea: Jack Schwager reported that from mid-1994 to 1999 he averaged about 220% a year, with only one small losing quarter. These are his own figures, not an audited fund.
ask: Why do reported returns need independent checking?
What would 220% a year do to $10,000 in five years?

themes.title: Two championships
themes.idea: To prove his method with real money, he entered the U.S. Investing Championship twice and won both times: +155% in 1997 and a record +334.8% in 2021.
ask: Is one great year proof of skill, or could it be luck?
Why does real-money verification matter?

themes.title: Teacher, critics and the CNBC moment
themes.idea: He now writes books and sells trading education. His record has fans and critics, and a 2021 TV interview showed the limits of trading charts without knowing the business.
ask: How should you weigh advice from someone who sells courses?
Should a trader understand the business behind a stock?

t2n1.text: Richard Love's Superperformance Stocks and William Jiler's work became the backbone of his method.

t2n2.text: After meeting Stan Weinstein in 1990 he added trend analysis to his work.

t2n3.text: He reversed his old habits and copied what winning stocks looked like before they ran.

t2n4.text: Looking back, he found he let small losses grow and had no clear rules for buying.

t3n1.text: Quantech Research Group, founded in 1993, sold his research to professional investors.

t3n2.text: He called the method Specific Entry Point Analysis: SEPA for short.

t3n3.text: SEPA combines a stock's price trend with its earnings growth.

t3n4.text: In 2000 he started a hedge fund, also called Quantech.

t4n1.text: Resting, rising, topping, falling: he wants only the rising stage.

t4n2.text: He avoids shares that have fallen far from their highs, however cheap they look.

t4n3.text: A stock must prove itself by rising before he will look at it.

t5n1.text: Price above its 50-, 150- and 200-day averages, stacked in that order, with the 200-day rising.

t5n2.text: Within 25% of its 52-week high, and well above its 52-week low.

t5n3.text: His first book asks for 30% above the low; his second says 25%.

t5n4.text: It should be beating at least 70% of other stocks.

t6n1.text: Pullbacks of, say, 25%, then 15%, then 8%, each one tighter.

t6n2.text: Trading volume dries up as the pattern tightens: sellers are running out.

t6n3.text: He buys as the price breaks above the final tight range, with a stop just below it.

t7n1.text: If the market is to beat him, he says, it must do it one small loss at a time.

t7n2.text: He sets a firm maximum loss of 10%, with an average loss much lower.

t7n3.text: He may split a position, with half stopped out at 6% and half at 10%.

t7n4.text: He expects to be right only about half the time, so losses must stay smaller than gains.

t8n1.text: About 220% a year compounded over five and a half years from mid-1994.

t8n2.text: His worst year in that stretch was a gain of 128%.

t8n3.text: Only one quarter lost money, by less than 1%.

t8n4.text: His books describe this as five years of triple-digit returns, about 33,500% in total.

t9n1.text: He won with a 155% return, trading only shares.

t9n2.text: He won the $1 million-plus stock division with +334.8%, then a contest record.

lines: This page is about a professional trader who buys and sells fast-moving shares, often in large positions, and sells quickly when they fall. It is for education, not a trading course or a recommendation.
Most individuals who trade lose money. In India, SEBI found that 93% of individual equity F&O traders lost money between FY22 and FY24.
Contest wins are single years. Past results, his or anyone's, do not predict future ones. Never trade with money you cannot afford to lose.

rec.intro: There is no public, audited year-by-year record of his trading to chart. What can be checked are his two entries in the U.S. Investing Championship, a real-money contest whose organiser verifies each entrant's brokerage account. His earlier five-year run comes from his own published figures, as reported by Jack Schwager.

rec.duelNote: Each bar is one calendar year. The contest years are his best-known, so this is the best side of his record, not a typical year. In 2024 another trader, J Law of Hong Kong, set a new record of 353.9%.
rec.claimNote: This is only arithmetic: what 220% a year would do to $10,000 over five years. It is not his actual year-by-year record, which he has not published. His book describes five years at 220% (33,500% in total); Jack Schwager describes about five and a half years from mid-1994. The sources differ slightly, so treat these as his own approximate figures, not audited by us.

1994 to 1999 figures: Jack Schwager, Stock Market Wizards (2001), as summarised by TradingMarkets and The 7 Circles; the 33,500% total is from his book's description.
S&P 500 total returns: 1997 from Slickcharts and US500; 2021 from S&P Dow Jones Indices, FactSet via Fisher Investments, and Bloomberg via a market update.
The 2024 record: the contest's 2025 first-half release, via Webull.

checklistSeed: Has anything changed in the business, or only in the price?
Would I make this trade if the market were closed for the next three years?
Is this inside my circle? Can I state the moat in two sentences?
What is my range of value, and where is today's price within it?
What will tax and costs take out of this trade, in money terms?
What will I own instead, and is it clearly better after those costs?
Am I acting because I am bored, anxious, or reacting to someone else's gain?
Have I slept on it for at least a week?

hero.title: Thirteen years, two teachers
hero.sub: I built this library. This is my own record as an investor, shown only in percentages: where I followed Buffett and Munger, where I didn't, and what each choice cost or earned.
stats: full years I beat my yardstick fund
of all I earned went on living costs

story: In 2015 I left my job. Since then this portfolio has paid my living costs.
For ten years, 2015 to 2024, I earned 10.6% a year. The diversified fund I use as my yardstick earned 18.3%. Berkshire's share price earned 11.7%, in dollars.
By my own rule, I should have handed my money to that fund in 2020. I didn't.
From the 2021 high my portfolio fell 40% on returns alone, and took almost four years to recover.
Then one winner I let run changed the picture: up 64% in 2025 and 100% so far in 2026.
Today one stock is about 69% of my portfolio. That breaks my own rules, and it is my biggest risk.
journey.fallsNote: Berkshire's falls are in its share price, from Buffett's 2017 letter. Munger's partnership fell 31.9% in 1973 and 31.5% in 1974, about 53% over the two years. Mine is the fall in my returns, leaving out money I took out; counting withdrawals, the portfolio's value fell 48%.
caveats: Not a fair race. The currencies, sizes, eras and lengths differ. Munger's record runs 14 years and Berkshire's 60; mine is 13.
My figures are worked out from my own records. They are unaudited and before tax. Years before 2020 rest on year-end values, so they are rougher.
My whole-career figure counts the timing of money in and out (XIRR). The yearly figures are time-weighted, so money I took out does not count against them.
Over 2015 to 2024 even Berkshire's share price trailed the S&P 500. Most of my lead today comes from one stock, in 2025 and 2026.

lessons.title: Four years that went nowhere
facts: In three of those years my living costs took more out than the portfolio made.
My own rule says: if my three-year return trails the fund three times in a row, hand the money to the fund. That happened at the end of 2020, and the run lasted seven windows. I didn't hand over.

rule.text: Most investors do better in a low-cost index fund than by picking stocks, and fees and activity eat returns.

lessons.now: I check the rule every year, and I publish it here so I can't quietly forget it.

lessons.title: Buying when others froze
facts: I had sold down as the market fell in February and March 2020. Straight after the crash, I put almost all of the portfolio back into stocks over three days, 7 to 9 April.
2020 ended +46.6% against the fund's +33.3% (my figure is rough: there is a gap in my records from January to March).

rule.text: Be greedy when others are fearful.

lessons.now: The decision my whole record rests on. When everyone freezes, I look harder, not away.

lessons.title: Trading far too much
facts: From April 2020 to March 2023 I traded five to seven times the portfolio's value every year. My own limit is twice.
Brokerage and trading taxes since 2020 have cost about 4% of everything the portfolio earned.

rule.text: For investors as a whole, the more they move, the less they keep.

lessons.now: Trading at most twice the portfolio's value a year.

lessons.title: Buying a story outside my circle
facts: In 2021 I bought a basket of hyped new listings. It was a story, not my lane of small, clean, little-followed companies.
Two of them lost money while I held them, at −19% and −83% a year.

rule.text: Stay inside your circle of competence; the edge matters more than the size.

lessons.now: Only companies in my lane, and a written reason for each one.

lessons.title: Selling into the frenzy
facts: In December 2021 I sold a big winner near the peak of the excitement. It had earned about 65% a year while I held it.

rule.text: A price that makes sense at one level stops making sense at another.

lessons.now: I write my selling zone down before I buy, so the crowd can't set it for me.

lessons.title: Holding on, and adding, while it stalled
facts: For four years one stock was often more than half of my portfolio, at times 76%.
I kept adding as it fell. Over its whole life it earned about 4% a year. The fund earned about 15% a year over 2022 to 2025.

rule.text: Our minds hate to change a conclusion once made, and we deny what hurts. He named these tendencies so we can catch them.

lessons.now: A big position that stalls gets 18 months, then I change boats. I never average down on a falling thesis.

lessons.title: No cash cushion in a bad market
facts: My living costs took about 7% of the portfolio in 2022 and 11% in 2023, sold near the lows.
The portfolio's value fell 48% from its September 2021 high, counting withdrawals; 40% on returns alone.

rule.text: Never put yourself where you can be forced to sell.

lessons.now: Keep two years of spending outside stocks, so I am never a forced seller.

lessons.title: Not giving up at the bottom
facts: Down almost half from the high, I did not sell out.
I also stopped churning: trading fell from 5.5 times the portfolio a year to about 0.5 times.
It took 47 months on returns alone to get back above the old high.

rule.text: Setbacks will come, some of them unfair; what you do next decides the result.

lessons.now: When I'm down, I read more and trade less.

lessons.title: Letting a winner run
facts: 2025: +64.2% against the fund's +8.2%. 2026 so far: +99.8% against −0.6%.
One stock earned about 250% a year while I held it, and made about 44% of everything the portfolio earned since 2020.

rule.text: Mistakes fade; a few winners can keep growing for a very long time.

lessons.now: Sit when the thesis holds. The money is made by waiting.

lessons.title: The old trading habit came back
facts: In the year to March 2026 I traded 3.1 times the portfolio, and this year is on pace for 2.8 times. My limit is twice.

rule.text: Activity is a cost, even when it feels like work.

lessons.title: Borrowing to buy more
facts: From September 2025 I borrowed money to add to stocks.
So far the borrowed money has grown about 63%, against interest of about 6% of it. But at one point it was 11% under water, and the repayments can only come from selling stock.
In a fall like 2022 I would be a forced seller.

rule.text: Credit is easy to get until the day it vanishes, and that is the day you need it.

lessons.now: Pay it down. No new borrowing to buy stocks.

lessons.title: One stock is 69% of my portfolio
facts: My top holding is about 69% of the portfolio and the top two about 98%.
My own rules say at most 30 to 35% in one idea and 60 to 65% in the top two.

rule.text: Munger argued that a few great holdings can be rational. Buffett's first rule is never to risk a permanent loss. Both apply here, and they pull in opposite directions.

lessons.now: Bring it back inside my limits, in steps, without selling in a panic.

lessons.title: Cutting losers early
facts: Of 101 stocks I owned since 2020, 74 made money. Gains were 8.6 times the losses.

rule.text: Cut a loser within 45 days. This one is mine, not theirs.

lessons.now: Keep cutting losers fast, and let the winners do the work.

rulesNow: Own 4 to 7 stocks, only in my lane: small, governance-clean, little-followed companies.
An unproven idea gets at most 30 to 35% of the portfolio; the top two at most 60 to 65%.
Trade at most twice the portfolio's value in a year.
Cut losers within 45 days. Nothing stuck for more than 18 months.
Sell at a price zone written down in advance, based on how big the business can get, never on the P/E alone.
Add when the thesis is confirmed. Never average down on a falling thesis.
Before every buy, check that the company's market value makes sense.
At results, try to prove the thesis wrong, not just judge the quarter.
Before every buy, a pre-mortem: if this halves in 18 months, what broke?
No new buying in a year when I'm in a big drawdown. Big decisions get a second opinion.
Check every number that matters, including the ones a computer gives me.
If my three-year return trails my yardstick fund three times in a row, hand the money to the fund.
Never be a forced seller: keep two years of spending outside stocks.
journey.rulesNote: Two of these I am breaking right now: the size limits and the trading limit.
method: Source: my own records up to the 13 Nov 2026 close. Percentages only, by choice: no amounts, no stock names.
Yearly returns are time-weighted (Modified Dietz, monthly from April 2020; yearly before that). The whole-career figure is cash-flow based (XIRR).
Yardstick: a widely held diversified equity fund, direct plan, growth option, calendar-year returns from two public sources.
Berkshire and the S&P 500: Buffett's 2024 letter. Berkshire's falls: his 2017 letter. Munger's partnership: Buffett's 1984 essay “The Superinvestors of Graham-and-Doddsville”.
disclaimer: This is a personal record, shared only for education. It is not investment, financial, legal or tax advice, and not a recommendation to buy, sell or hold anything.
The figures are self-reported, unaudited and before tax, and may contain errors. Past returns do not predict future ones.
Concentration and borrowing, both shown here, can cause large and permanent losses. They are described as risks, not suggestions.
