M.d: Grows up in Omaha, the son of a lawyer and grandson of a federal judge. As a teenager he works at Buffett & Son, the grocery owned by Warren Buffett's grandfather.
Studies mathematics at the University of Michigan, then leaves a few days after his 19th birthday to join the war effort.
Trains as a weather forecaster, including at Caltech in Pasadena, and serves in Nome, Alaska.
Admitted without a college degree; graduates magna cum laude, one of 12 in a class of 335.
Practises law in Los Angeles. A hard decade at home: a divorce in 1953 and the death of his young son.
Founds the law firm now called Munger, Tolles & Olson and runs his partnership, Wheeler, Munger & Co. (1962-75). Stops practising law in 1965.
Buffett's partner for 45 years. Also chairs Wesco Financial (1984-2011) and Daily Journal (1977-2022) and sits on Costco's board from 1997.

B.d: Grows up in Omaha in the Depression, selling gum, Coke and magazines and reading every money book he can find.
His father is in Congress, so the family lives in Washington. Paper routes, a pinball business and a small farm.
Two years at Wharton, then a business degree from the University of Nebraska at 19.
Studies under Benjamin Graham and David Dodd at Columbia Business School.
Sells securities at his father's firm, Buffett-Falk & Co.
Works for Graham in New York until Graham retires.
Runs the Buffett partnerships from Omaha: 29.5% a year before fees, against 7.4% for the Dow.
Chairman from 1970 (in control since 1965) and chief executive until the end of 2025.
Chairman while Greg Abel is CEO; chairman emeritus from September 2026.

L.d: Grows up near Boston. His father dies when he is 10; from 11 he caddies at Brae Burn Country Club.
On a caddie scholarship. Studies history, psychology and philosophy rather than business.
Fidelity summer intern (1966), Wharton MBA (1968), then two years in the Army, in Texas and Korea.
Covers textiles, metals, mining and chemicals; director of research from 1974.
Runs Fidelity Magellan from May 1977 to May 1990: about 29% a year, $18 million to $14 billion.
Vice chairman of Fidelity Management & Research, author of three books and a major giver in Boston.

timeline.sp2026: Up about 10% this year to mid-November (price only, before dividends).

eras.title: The Roaring Twenties
eras.tag: A boom, a baby, a crash
eras.intro: Radio, cars and easy credit. Ordinary Americans discover the stock market, the first modern mutual fund opens in Boston, and Charlie Munger is born in Omaha. It ends in the crash of 1929.

where.M: A small boy in Omaha.
where.B: Not yet born.
where.L: Not yet born.

eras.title: Depression childhoods
eras.intro: Banks fail, a quarter of workers lose their jobs and stocks lose most of their value. Washington answers with the New Deal and the SEC. Warren Buffett is born ten months after the crash. The decade ends with a world at war.

where.M: An Omaha schoolboy, then a maths student in Michigan.
where.B: An Omaha boy already selling things for profit.
where.L: Not yet born.

eras.title: War and first trades
eras.intro: America fights and wins a world war, then builds the post-war order. Buffett buys his first stock at 11, Munger forecasts weather for the Army and talks his way into Harvard Law, and Peter Lynch is born near Boston.

where.M: Army weatherman, Harvard Law, then a young Los Angeles lawyer.
where.B: A teenage businessman in Washington, then Wharton.
where.L: A baby, then a small boy in Newton, Massachusetts.

eras.title: Students of Graham
eras.tag: A teacher, a stock, a meeting
eras.intro: A booming, confident America; the Dow finally regains its 1929 peak in 1954. Buffett learns from Benjamin Graham, works for him, then starts his own partnership. Lynch loses his father and starts caddying. In 1959 Buffett and Munger meet.

where.M: A Los Angeles lawyer through a hard decade at home.
where.B: Columbia, Omaha broker, Graham-Newman, then his own partnership.
where.L: A boy caddying at a Boston-area golf club.

eras.title: The go-go years
eras.intro: Kennedy, Vietnam, civil rights and the Moon. Wall Street falls for fast-trading 'go-go' funds. Buffett buys a struggling textile mill called Berkshire Hathaway; Munger starts his own firm and fund; Lynch goes from college to Fidelity.

where.M: Founds his law firm and runs his own investment partnership.
where.B: Runs his partnership; takes control of Berkshire in 1965; closes the partnership in 1969.
where.L: Boston College, a Fidelity internship, Wharton and the Army.

eras.title: The lost decade
eras.intro: Watergate, oil shocks and inflation. Stocks go nowhere for a decade and crash in 1973-74. Buffett buys See's Candies, the Washington Post and GEICO at bargain prices; Munger's fund is battered, then recovers; Lynch takes over a tiny fund called Magellan.

where.M: Rides out a brutal 1973-74, winds up his fund and joins Berkshire as vice chairman in 1978.
where.B: Runs Berkshire and buys great businesses cheaply.
where.L: Fidelity analyst, research director, then Magellan's manager from 1977.

eras.title: The great bull begins
eras.intro: Paul Volcker breaks inflation with sky-high rates, and a great bull market begins in 1982. Magellan becomes the most famous fund in America. Berkshire buys Nebraska Furniture Mart and Coca-Cola. Black Monday tests everyone in 1987.

where.M: Berkshire's vice chairman; also runs Wesco from 1984.
where.B: Turns Berkshire into a conglomerate of great businesses.
where.L: Builds Magellan from about $100 million to about $10 billion.

eras.title: The bubble decade
eras.intro: The Cold War ends, the web arrives and tech stocks soar. Lynch quits at the top at 46. Buffett rescues Salomon and buys GEICO and General Re. Munger gives his most famous talks. By 1999 critics call Buffett out of touch.

where.M: Gives his landmark talks on worldly wisdom and human misjudgment.
where.B: Builds Berkshire's insurance empire and refuses to chase tech.
where.L: Retires from Magellan, writes two more books and turns to giving.

eras.title: Bust, war and crisis
eras.intro: The dot-com bubble bursts, terrorists strike on 9/11, and in 2008 the financial system nearly collapses. Buffett warns about derivatives, pledges his fortune to charity and invests boldly in the panic, with Munger's China idea in the mix.

where.M: Vice chairman and sage; his sayings become a best-selling book.
where.B: Warns early, then invests heavily in the 2008 panic.
where.L: Vice chairman at Fidelity and a full-time philanthropist.

eras.title: The long recovery
eras.intro: A slow recovery, then a long bull market led by technology. Buffett launches the Giving Pledge, receives the Medal of Freedom, buys Apple and wins his famous bet against hedge funds. Berkshire starts preparing for life after its founders.

where.M: In his 80s and 90s, still at Buffett's side and still giving big gifts.
where.B: Buys huge businesses and Apple; names vice chairmen.
where.L: Gives away money through the Lynch Foundation; loses his wife in 2015.

eras.title: Pandemic, AI and farewells
eras.intro: A pandemic crash, artificial intelligence, war and new tariffs. Munger dies in 2023, 34 days short of 100. Buffett hands the CEO job to Greg Abel and then the chair to his son Howard. Lynch, in his 80s, is still at Fidelity.

where.M: Works into his late 90s; dies in November 2023.
where.B: Steps back: CEO until 2025, chairman until September 2026.
where.L: In his 80s, still meeting Fidelity's young analysts.

M.t: Born in Omaha, Nebraska. His father is a lawyer; his grandfather is a federal judge.

W.t: The first modern American mutual fund, Massachusetts Investors Trust, opens in Boston.
Calvin Coolidge wins the presidential election.
F. Scott Fitzgerald publishes The Great Gatsby.
The Scopes trial in Tennessee puts the teaching of evolution on trial.
NBC, the first national radio network, goes on the air.
Charles Lindbergh flies solo and non-stop from New York to Paris.
The Jazz Singer brings talking pictures to cinemas.
Alexander Fleming discovers penicillin in London.
Herbert Hoover is elected president. The same month, Mickey Mouse appears in Steamboat Willie.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average peaks at about 381.
Wall Street crashes: Black Thursday, Black Monday and Black Tuesday (Oct 24-29). The Great Depression begins.

B.t: Born in Omaha, Nebraska, ten months after the crash.

W.t: The Smoot-Hawley Act raises tariffs on thousands of imports; other countries hit back.
The Bank of United States fails as bank runs spread.

B.t: The bank where his father works fails. Howard Buffett starts his own small brokerage.

W.t: The Empire State Building opens in New York.
Stocks lose about 44% in the year, the worst calendar year on record.
The Dow bottoms at 41, down 89% from its 1929 peak.
Franklin D. Roosevelt wins the presidency in a landslide.
Adolf Hitler becomes chancellor of Germany.
Roosevelt takes office, closes the banks for a 'bank holiday' and launches the New Deal.
The Securities Act and the Glass-Steagall Act pass; bank deposits become federally insured.
The Securities Exchange Act creates the SEC to police Wall Street. Joseph Kennedy is its first chairman.
Benjamin Graham and David Dodd publish Security Analysis, the founding text of value investing.
The Social Security Act becomes law.

B.t: At six, buys six-packs of Coca-Cola and resells the bottles one by one at a profit.

W.t: Jesse Owens wins four gold medals at the Berlin Olympics.
Roosevelt wins a second term.
The Golden Gate Bridge opens in San Francisco.
A sharp new recession: stocks lose about 35% in the year.
Disney's Snow White, the first full-length cel-animated feature, premieres.
The Fair Labor Standards Act sets the first federal minimum wage.
Orson Welles's War of the Worlds radio drama alarms listeners.
Germany invades Poland. World War II begins in Europe.
Gone with the Wind and The Wizard of Oz reach cinemas.

B.t: At 10, visits New York with his father and tours the New York Stock Exchange.
As a boy he often chalks stock prices onto the blackboard at his father's brokerage office.

W.t: The Investment Company Act sets the rules for mutual funds.
Roosevelt wins a third term.

M.t: Leaves Omaha for the University of Michigan to study mathematics.

W.t: Citizen Kane premieres.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor. The United States enters World War II.

B.t: At 11, buys his first stock: three shares of Cities Service preferred at $38 (and three for his sister). They fall to $27; he sells at $40, then watches them climb past $200.
His father, Howard Buffett, is elected to Congress.

W.t: The Manhattan Project to build an atomic bomb begins.
Casablanca premieres.

M.t: A few days after turning 19, leaves college for the Army Air Corps. He trains as a weather forecaster and later serves in Nome, Alaska.

B.t: The family moves to Washington, D.C. He takes on several newspaper routes.

W.t: Oklahoma! opens on Broadway.

B.t: At 13, files his first tax return and deducts his bicycle and watch as business expenses: $35.

L.t: Peter Spencer Lynch is born in Newton, Massachusetts, near Boston.

W.t: D-Day: Allied troops land in Normandy.
The Bretton Woods conference designs the post-war money system and creates the IMF and World Bank.

M.t: Marries Nancy Huggins while training in California.

B.t: At 14, buys a 40-acre Nebraska farm with $1,200 of savings. With a friend, puts a $25 used pinball machine in a barbershop.

W.t: Roosevelt dies. Harry Truman becomes president.
Germany surrenders in May. After atomic bombs fall on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan surrenders and World War II ends.
The United Nations is founded.

M.t: Out of the Army, talks his way into Harvard Law School without a college degree, helped by family friend Roscoe Pound, the former dean.

B.t: At 15, earns more than $175 a month from his paper routes.

W.t: ENIAC, an early electronic computer, is unveiled.
It's a Wonderful Life premieres.

B.t: Graduates from high school at 16, sells the pinball business for $1,200 and enters Wharton.

W.t: Jackie Robinson breaks baseball's colour line with the Brooklyn Dodgers.
The Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe is announced.
Bell Labs invents the transistor.

M.t: Graduates from Harvard Law magna cum laude, one of 12 in a class of 335, and moves to Los Angeles to practise law.

W.t: Truman upsets Thomas Dewey in the presidential election.

B.t: Leaves Wharton after two years for the University of Nebraska.

W.t: Benjamin Graham publishes The Intelligent Investor.
NATO is founded.
Mao Zedong proclaims the People's Republic of China.

B.t: At 19, reads The Intelligent Investor, which he later calls by far the best investing book ever written.
Graduates from Nebraska. Turned down by Harvard Business School, he enrols at Columbia to learn from Graham and Dodd.

W.t: North Korea invades the South. The Korean War begins.

B.t: Knocks on GEICO's door in Washington on a Saturday. Lorimer Davidson spends hours explaining insurance to him, and Buffett buys GEICO shares.
Earns his master's degree at Columbia, then sells securities at his father's Omaha firm, Buffett-Falk & Co.

W.t: William McChesney Martin becomes Fed chairman; he will serve almost 19 years.
I Love Lucy debuts on television.

B.t: Marries Susan Thompson.

W.t: Dwight Eisenhower is elected president.

M.t: His first marriage ends in divorce.

W.t: Watson and Crick publish the double-helix structure of DNA.
An armistice ends the fighting in Korea.

B.t: Joins Graham's firm, Graham-Newman, in New York at $12,000 a year.

L.t: His father, a former Boston College maths professor, dies of brain cancer. Peter is 10.

W.t: Brown v. Board of Education outlaws segregated public schools.
The Dow closes above its 1929 peak for the first time, 25 years later.

M.t: His son Teddy dies of leukemia, aged nine.

L.t: At 11, starts caddying at Brae Burn Country Club, where he hears golfers talk about their stocks.

W.t: Disneyland opens in California.
Rosa Parks refuses to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama.

M.t: Marries Nancy Barry Borthwick.

B.t: Graham retires. Buffett returns to Omaha and, at 25, starts a partnership with $105,100 from seven family members and friends. His own stake: $100.

W.t: The Interstate Highway Act funds a national road network.
Eisenhower is re-elected.

B.t: An Omaha doctor, Edwin Davis, invests $100,000 with him because Buffett reminds him of someone named Charlie Munger.

W.t: Standard & Poor's launches the S&P 500 index.
The Soviet Union launches Sputnik. The space race begins.

B.t: Buys a house on Farnam Street in Omaha for $31,500. He still lives there decades later.

W.t: NASA is created.
American Express launches its charge card.

M.t: Back in Omaha after his father's death, he meets Warren Buffett at a dinner arranged by the Davis family. They hit it off at once.

B.t: Meets Charlie Munger. He knows straight away that this is someone he will learn from.

W.t: Alaska and Hawaii become the 49th and 50th states.
Ben-Hur premieres; it wins a record 11 Oscars.

M.t: Around now Buffett tells him that law is fine as a hobby, but he could do better.

B.t: Takes a large stake in Sanborn Map, whose investments are worth more than its share price, and joins its board.

W.t: Kennedy and Nixon hold the first televised presidential debate.
John F. Kennedy is elected president.

B.t: Takes control of Dempster Mill, a Nebraska windmill and pump maker.

L.t: Enters Boston College on a caddie scholarship.

W.t: Yuri Gagarin becomes the first human in space; the Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba fails.

M.t: Founds the law firm now called Munger, Tolles & Olson and starts his own fund, Wheeler, Munger & Co. First year: +30.1% while the Dow falls 7.6%.

B.t: Merges his funds into Buffett Partnership, Ltd. and becomes a millionaire. Starts buying a struggling New England textile maker: Berkshire Hathaway.

W.t: The 'Kennedy Slide': a one-day crash caps a sharp fall in stocks.
Sam Walton opens the first Walmart, in Arkansas.
The Cuban Missile Crisis brings the superpowers to the brink of nuclear war.

B.t: The 'salad oil' fraud hammers American Express shares. Buffett checks Omaha restaurants and shops, finds people still using the card, and buys heavily.

L.t: As a sophomore, buys Flying Tiger, an air-freight company, at about $7 a share. He sells in stages as it climbs, the last near $80, and the profits help pay for graduate school.

W.t: Martin Luther King Jr. gives his 'I Have a Dream' speech.
President Kennedy is assassinated in Dallas. Lyndon Johnson takes over.

B.t: Berkshire's boss, Seabury Stanton, offers slightly less for Buffett's shares than they had agreed. Angry, Buffett decides to buy control instead.

W.t: The Beatles appear on The Ed Sullivan Show.
The Civil Rights Act becomes law.

M.t: Stops practising law to concentrate on investing.

B.t: Takes control of Berkshire Hathaway. Ken Chace runs the mills; Buffett runs the money.

L.t: Graduates from Boston College, having studied history, psychology and philosophy rather than business.

W.t: US combat troops land in Vietnam.
Medicare and Medicaid are created.

M.t: With Buffett and Sandy Gottesman, buys a Baltimore department store, Hochschild, Kohn, through a new company, Diversified Retailing. Buffett later calls it a mistake.

B.t: Closes the partnership to new money. Buys about 5% of Walt Disney Productions and meets Walt Disney himself.

L.t: Wins a summer job at Fidelity, one of three picked from about 75 applicants. He had caddied for Fidelity's president, D. George Sullivan.

W.t: The Dow nears 1,000, then stalls. It will not stay above 1,000 until 1982.

B.t: Berkshire buys National Indemnity, an Omaha insurer, for $8.6 million. Its 'float' becomes the engine of Berkshire's investing.

W.t: The first Super Bowl is played.
Muriel Siebert becomes the first woman to own a seat on the New York Stock Exchange.

B.t: The partnership's best year ever: +58.8% against +7.7% for the Dow.

L.t: Earns his MBA at Wharton and marries Carolyn Hoff. Then two years in the Army, in Texas and Korea.

W.t: Martin Luther King Jr. is assassinated. Robert Kennedy is killed in June.
A paperwork crisis closes the New York Stock Exchange on Wednesdays.
Richard Nixon is elected president.

B.t: Tells partners he will close the partnership: the market is too speculative and bargains too scarce. They can take cash or Berkshire shares.

L.t: Joins Fidelity full time as an analyst covering textiles, metals, mining and chemicals.

W.t: Apollo 11: Neil Armstrong walks on the Moon.
The Woodstock festival.
The first message travels over ARPANET, the internet's ancestor.

B.t: Becomes chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, at a salary of $50,000 a year.

W.t: Arthur Burns becomes Fed chairman.
The Penn Central railroad goes bankrupt, the biggest US bankruptcy to that date.
The first Earth Day.
The Nasdaq stock market opens, the first electronic exchange.
Nixon ends the dollar's convertibility into gold.
Intel introduces the first commercial microprocessor, the 4004.

M.t: Pushes Buffett to pay up for a great business: through Blue Chip Stamps they buy See's Candies for $25 million. It changes how both of them invest.

B.t: Buys See's Candies for $25 million, about three times its book value: a big break from Graham's bargain-hunting.

W.t: The Godfather premieres.
Burglars break into the Watergate building.
The Dow closes above 1,000 for the first time.

M.t: His partnership loses 31.9% while the Dow falls 13.1%.

B.t: Buys about a tenth of The Washington Post Company for about $10.6 million and befriends its publisher, Katharine Graham.

W.t: The 1973-74 bear market begins.
The Arab oil embargo roughly quadruples the price of oil.
The Chicago Board Options Exchange opens.

M.t: His partnership loses another 31.5%. His investors' money is down by about half in two years.

B.t: Berkshire's shares fall 48.7% this year. In Forbes he says bargains are everywhere: "Now is the time to invest and get rich."

L.t: Becomes Fidelity's director of research.

W.t: Nixon resigns over Watergate. Gerald Ford becomes president.
The Dow bottoms near 578, down about 45% from its 1973 peak.
ERISA sets rules for private pension plans.

M.t: His partnership rebounds 73.2%. Over 1962-75 it compounded 19.8% a year, against 5.0% for the Dow.

W.t: 'May Day': fixed brokerage commissions end and trading costs fall.
John Bogle founds Vanguard.
Bill Gates and Paul Allen found Microsoft. Saigon falls on April 30.
Jaws invents the summer blockbuster.

M.t: Winds up Wheeler, Munger & Co.

B.t: GEICO nears collapse. Buffett backs its new boss, Jack Byrne, and Berkshire buys a big stake, helping to rescue it.

W.t: Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak found Apple.
America celebrates its 200th birthday.
Vanguard launches the first index fund for ordinary investors.
Jimmy Carter is elected president.

M.t: Begins 45 years as chairman of Daily Journal Corp., the Los Angeles legal newspaper he bought into.

B.t: Berkshire buys the Buffalo Evening News for $32.5 million. His 1977 letter is the first in Berkshire's online archive.

L.t: At 33, takes over Fidelity's small Magellan Fund, then about $18 million.

W.t: Star Wars premieres.
The Apple II goes on sale.

M.t: Becomes vice chairman of Berkshire Hathaway: the start of 45 years at Buffett's side.
In his 50s, a failed cataract operation costs him the sight of his left eye; the eye is later removed.

W.t: The Revenue Act of 1978 creates the 401(k) retirement plan.
The Camp David Accords between Egypt and Israel.

B.t: Writes in Forbes that pension funds shunning stocks are paying a very high price for a cheery consensus. Berkshire's shares more than double this year.

W.t: Paul Volcker becomes Fed chairman to fight inflation.
BusinessWeek's cover declares 'The Death of Equities'.
The Three Mile Island nuclear accident.
The Iran hostage crisis begins.
Inflation peaks near 15%. By December the prime rate reaches 21.5%.
CNN launches 24-hour news.
Ronald Reagan is elected president.

L.t: Magellan opens to the public for the first time since 1965. Money starts to pour in.

W.t: Reagan takes office; the Iran hostages are freed.
IBM launches its personal computer.
MTV launches.

B.t: Appears on the first Forbes 400 list of the richest Americans.

L.t: Magellan has the best five-year record of any fund, and the press takes notice.

W.t: The great bull market begins, with the Dow near 777.
E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial premieres.

B.t: On his 53rd birthday, buys 90% of Nebraska Furniture Mart from Rose 'Mrs. B' Blumkin, 89, for about $55 million, on a handshake and a one-page contract.
Blue Chip Stamps merges into Berkshire.

L.t: Magellan passes $1 billion.

W.t: ARPANET switches to TCP/IP, often called the internet's birthday.
Return of the Jedi premieres.

M.t: Becomes chairman of Wesco Financial, a post he holds until 2011.

B.t: At Columbia, gives 'The Superinvestors of Graham-and-Doddsville': Graham's students beat the market again and again. Munger's record is one of his examples.

W.t: Apple launches the Macintosh.
AT&T is broken up.
Los Angeles hosts the Olympics.

B.t: Agrees to put up $517 million to help Capital Cities buy ABC. Later in the year, closes Berkshire's last textile mills.

W.t: New Coke flops, and Coca-Cola brings back the original formula.
Back to the Future premieres.
The Plaza Accord pushes the dollar down.

M.t: At a Los Angeles school graduation, explains how to guarantee a miserable life: turn the question upside down.

B.t: Berkshire buys Scott Fetzer, maker of Kirby vacuums and World Book, for about $315 million.

L.t: Magellan takes in $2.3 billion of new money in one year, more than half its size at the start of the year.

W.t: The space shuttle Challenger explodes.
Microsoft goes public.
Ivan Boesky is charged with insider trading.

B.t: Berkshire invests $700 million in Salomon Inc. preferred stock.
In the crash, Berkshire's shares fall from about $3,890 to $3,170 within days. Berkshire still ends the year up 4.6%.

L.t: On Black Monday he is in Ireland, on his first trip there. Magellan loses about a third of its value in two days, and he cuts the trip short.

W.t: Black Monday: the Dow falls 22.6% in a single day, still its worst day ever.
Alan Greenspan becomes Fed chairman, two months before the crash.
The film Wall Street premieres.

B.t: Begins buying Coca-Cola: about $1 billion of shares by early 1989. Berkshire lists on the New York Stock Exchange.

W.t: George H. W. Bush is elected president.
KKR wins RJR Nabisco for $25 billion, the 'Barbarians at the Gate' buyout.

B.t: Quotes Lynch's line about selling winners being like pulling out the flowers and watering the weeds. Reveals Berkshire owns about 7% of Coca-Cola.

L.t: Publishes One Up on Wall Street with John Rothchild: ordinary people can beat the professionals by investing in what they know. It sells more than a million copies.
Warren Buffett calls him at home, out of the blue, to ask if he may quote a line from the book in Berkshire's annual letter.

W.t: The Exxon Valdez oil spill.
The Berlin Wall falls.
Japan's Nikkei peaks. It will take 34 years to regain that level.

B.t: Buys about 10% of Wells Fargo during a banking scare.

L.t: Quits Magellan at 46, at the top, to spend more time with his family. The fund has grown from $18 million to about $14 billion; $1,000 invested in 1977 is worth about $28,000.

W.t: Drexel Burnham Lambert, the junk-bond firm, goes bankrupt.
Iraq invades Kuwait.
The Hubble Space Telescope is launched.

B.t: A trading scandal threatens Salomon. Buffett steps in as interim chairman and tells Congress: "lose a shred of reputation for the firm, and I will be ruthless."

L.t: Elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

W.t: Operation Desert Storm drives Iraq out of Kuwait.
The World Wide Web goes public.
The Soviet Union dissolves.
'Black Wednesday': George Soros profits as Britain is forced out of Europe's exchange-rate system.
Bill Clinton is elected president.

B.t: Buys Dexter Shoe with Berkshire shares, a deal he later ranks among his worst. Forbes names him the richest American.

L.t: Publishes Beating the Street, telling how he picked stocks at Magellan.

W.t: The first US exchange-traded fund, the S&P 500 'Spider' (SPY), launches.
A truck bomb explodes under the World Trade Center.
Jurassic Park premieres; Schindler's List follows in December.

M.t: At USC's business school, gives 'A Lesson on Elementary Worldly Wisdom': think with a latticework of models from many fields.

L.t: Writes the foreword to Robert Hagstrom's The Warren Buffett Way.

W.t: The Fed starts a run of surprise rate rises; bond prices tumble.
Jeff Bezos founds Amazon.
Forrest Gump and The Shawshank Redemption reach cinemas.

M.t: At Harvard, gives 'The Psychology of Human Misjudgment', his list of the mental tendencies that trip people up.

B.t: Agrees to buy the half of GEICO that Berkshire does not already own, for $2.3 billion.

L.t: Publishes Learn to Earn, a first investing book for teenagers and beginners.

W.t: Netscape's stock-market debut kicks off the internet boom.
The Oklahoma City bombing.
Toy Story, the first fully computer-animated feature film.

B.t: Creates cheaper Class B shares so small investors can buy Berkshire directly instead of through costly copycat funds.

L.t: Tells PBS Frontline that time spent forecasting the economy is mostly wasted.

W.t: Greenspan asks whether 'irrational exuberance' has pushed prices too high.
Clinton is re-elected.

M.t: Joins the board of Costco, a company he admires deeply.

B.t: Quietly buys about 130 million ounces of silver; the purchase is revealed in early 1998.

W.t: The Asian financial crisis starts in Thailand.
Amazon goes public; IBM's Deep Blue beats chess champion Garry Kasparov.
The Dow drops 554 points and trading is halted early.
Titanic premieres and becomes the highest-grossing film yet.

B.t: Agrees to buy General Re for about $22 billion in Berkshire stock, his biggest deal so far. Also buys Executive Jet, now NetJets.
With AIG and Goldman Sachs, offers to buy the collapsing hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management. The offer is turned down.

W.t: Russia defaults on its debt.
The Fed brokers a bank rescue of Long-Term Capital Management.
Google is founded.
Saving Private Ryan premieres.
Clinton is impeached by the House; the Senate acquits him in 1999.

B.t: At Sun Valley, warns tech-loving executives that stock returns ahead will disappoint. Berkshire's shares fall 19.9% as the tech boom roars.

W.t: The Dow closes above 10,000 for the first time.
The euro is launched.
The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act tears down the Glass-Steagall wall.
The Matrix premieres.

M.t: Janet Lowe's biography of him, Damn Right!, is published.

B.t: Proved right: Berkshire's shares rise 26.6% while the S&P 500 falls 9.1%. Buys MidAmerican Energy and Benjamin Moore and agrees to buy Johns Manville.

L.t: A new edition of One Up on Wall Street warns that very few dot-com investors "benefit from the full ride."

W.t: The Nasdaq peaks above 5,000. It will fall 78% by 2002.
Vanguard's S&P 500 index fund overtakes Magellan as the world's largest mutual fund.
The Supreme Court settles the Bush-Gore election.

B.t: Buys Shaw Industries, the carpet maker.

W.t: Terrorists attack New York and Washington. The stock exchange stays shut until September 17.
Enron files for bankruptcy.
Apple launches the iPod.

B.t: Begins buying shares of PetroChina.

W.t: WorldCom collapses; Congress passes the Sarbanes-Oxley Act to tighten corporate accounting.
The bear market hits bottom: the S&P 500 is down about half from its 2000 peak.
Euro notes and coins go into circulation.

M.t: At UC Santa Barbara, takes academic economics to task for ignoring psychology and other fields.

B.t: In his letter for 2002, calls derivatives "financial weapons of mass destruction." Buys Clayton Homes and McLane.

W.t: The Iraq War begins.
The space shuttle Columbia breaks up on re-entry.
The Human Genome Project is completed.

M.t: Gives Stanford Berkshire shares worth $43.5 million for graduate housing.

B.t: His wife, Susan Thompson Buffett, dies.

W.t: Facebook is founded at Harvard.
Google goes public.
The Indian Ocean tsunami kills about 230,000 people.

M.t: Peter Kaufman publishes Poor Charlie's Almanack, a collection of his talks and wit.

W.t: Hurricane Katrina devastates New Orleans.
YouTube is founded.

B.t: Pledges most of his fortune to charity, mainly to the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the biggest gift in history at the time.
Marries Astrid Menks on his 76th birthday. Earlier, buys 80% of Israeli toolmaker Iscar for $4 billion.

W.t: Ben Bernanke becomes Fed chairman.
US house prices peak.
Twitter is launched.

B.t: Sells PetroChina for about $4 billion, builds a stake in the railroad Burlington Northern and agrees to buy Marmon. Takes up a $1 million bet that an S&P 500 index fund will beat a group of hedge funds over the 10 years from 2008.

W.t: Steve Jobs unveils the iPhone.
A French bank freezes funds holding US subprime loans; the credit crunch begins.
The Dow peaks above 14,000.

M.t: His idea: Berkshire buys about 10% of Chinese carmaker and battery maker BYD for about $230 million.

B.t: As Wall Street panics, invests $5 billion in Goldman Sachs and $3 billion in General Electric, then writes in The New York Times: "Buy American. I Am."
Forbes ranks him the richest person in the world.

W.t: JPMorgan rescues Bear Stearns.
Lehman Brothers goes bankrupt; the government rescues AIG.
Congress passes the $700 billion TARP bailout.
Barack Obama is elected president.
Bernie Madoff is arrested.

M.t: Near the market bottom, Daily Journal, which he chairs, buys shares in big US banks.

B.t: Agrees to buy the rest of Burlington Northern Santa Fe, calling it an all-in bet on the US economy. The deal values the railroad at about $44 billion including debt.

W.t: The S&P 500 bottoms at 677, down about 57% from its 2007 peak.
General Motors goes bankrupt.
Avatar premieres; it becomes the highest-grossing film ever.

M.t: His wife, Nancy, dies at 86.

B.t: With Bill and Melinda Gates, launches the Giving Pledge, asking the very rich to give away most of their wealth.
The Burlington Northern purchase closes; hires investment manager Todd Combs.

L.t: The Lynch Foundation gives $20 million to create a leadership academy at Boston College.

W.t: The 'Flash Crash' knocks nearly 1,000 points off the Dow in minutes.
The Dodd-Frank Act reshapes financial regulation.
The Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico.

M.t: Wesco merges into Berkshire, ending his annual Wesco meetings in Pasadena.

B.t: Receives the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Obama.
Buys Lubrizol for about $9 billion and invests $5 billion in Bank of America. In The New York Times, argues that the super-rich should pay more tax.

W.t: An earthquake and tsunami in Japan cause the Fukushima nuclear disaster.
S&P strips the United States of its AAA credit rating.
Steve Jobs dies.

B.t: Announces he has early-stage prostate cancer; he finishes radiation treatment that year.

W.t: Facebook goes public.
A software glitch costs Knight Capital $440 million in 45 minutes.
Hurricane Sandy shuts the stock market for two days.
Obama is re-elected.

M.t: Announces a $110 million gift to the University of Michigan.

B.t: Teams up with 3G Capital to buy Heinz for about $23 billion.

L.t: The New York Times profiles him: once a money manager, now a full-time giver.

W.t: The S&P 500 closes at a record, finally above its 2007 peak.
The Wolf of Wall Street premieres.

M.t: Pledges $65 million to UC Santa Barbara's Kavli Institute for physics.

B.t: Swaps Berkshire's Procter & Gamble shares for the Duracell battery business.

W.t: Janet Yellen becomes the first woman to chair the Fed.
Alibaba raises $25 billion in the biggest share sale yet.

M.t: For Berkshire's 50th anniversary, writes his own letter to shareholders for the first time, next to Buffett's.

B.t: Looks back on 50 years in his anniversary letter. Later, Kraft merges with Heinz and Berkshire agrees to buy Precision Castparts, one of its biggest deals ever.

L.t: His wife, Carolyn, co-founder of the Lynch Foundation, dies at 69.

W.t: China's stock market crashes.
The Fed raises rates for the first time since 2006.
The Big Short brings the 2008 crisis to cinemas.

M.t: Pledges $200 million to UC Santa Barbara for a huge student dormitory he designs himself.

B.t: Berkshire reveals its first Apple shares. Apple later becomes its biggest stock holding.

W.t: Donald Trump is elected president.
Britain votes to leave the European Union.
Google's AlphaGo beats Go champion Lee Sedol.

B.t: Wins his 10-year, $1 million bet: the S&P 500 index fund beats the hand-picked hedge funds by a wide margin.

W.t: Bitcoin nears $20,000.
The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act cuts the corporate tax rate to 21%.

B.t: Makes Greg Abel and Ajit Jain vice chairmen, a clear step towards succession.

W.t: The Dow falls 1,175 points, its biggest point drop to that date.
Apple becomes the first US company worth $1 trillion.
A Christmas Eve sell-off caps the worst December since 1931.

B.t: Admits Berkshire overpaid for Kraft Heinz after a $15.4 billion write-down. Commits $10 billion to help Occidental Petroleum buy Anadarko.

W.t: Avengers: Endgame passes Avatar as the highest-grossing film.
Saudi Aramco's share sale is the largest ever.

B.t: Holds the annual meeting in an empty arena, with Greg Abel beside him; Munger stays home in Los Angeles. Reveals Berkshire has sold all its airline shares.
On his 90th birthday, reveals stakes of about 5% in each of five Japanese trading houses.

W.t: COVID-19: the S&P 500 falls 34% in 33 days, the fastest bear market ever. Trading halts four times in March.
The $2.2 trillion CARES Act.
Joe Biden is elected president.

M.t: At the annual meeting, lets slip that Greg Abel will keep Berkshire's culture. Days later Buffett confirms Abel as his successor.
His windowless design for the Munger Hall dormitory sparks a public row.

L.t: At an MIT conference, calls Buffett the greatest investor of all time.

W.t: Rioters storm the US Capitol.
The GameStop short squeeze.

M.t: Steps down as chairman of Daily Journal after 45 years, at 98.

B.t: Buys big stakes in Occidental and Chevron and agrees to buy Alleghany for $11.6 billion. Berkshire's shares rise 4.0% while the S&P 500 falls 18.1%.

W.t: Russia invades Ukraine.
The Fed starts its fastest rate rises since the 1980s.
The FTX crypto exchange collapses.
ChatGPT is released.

M.t: Dies at 99 in a Santa Barbara hospital, 34 days before his 100th birthday. Buffett says Berkshire could not have been built without him.

B.t: Visits Japan and raises Berkshire's stakes in the trading houses.

L.t: In interviews, talks about his biggest misses, like Apple, and says of rapid trading: "That's not investing. That's gambling."

W.t: Silicon Valley Bank fails.
Nvidia passes $1 trillion in market value.
Oppenheimer and Barbie open on the same day.

B.t: Opens his annual letter with a tribute: 'Charlie Munger - The Architect of Berkshire Hathaway'.
Berkshire becomes the first US company outside technology worth $1 trillion. During the year it sells much of its Apple stake.

L.t: Turns 80.

W.t: US regulators approve spot bitcoin ETFs.
Japan's Nikkei finally passes its 1989 peak.
Donald Trump wins a second term.

B.t: At his 60th annual meeting as CEO, warns that trade should not be used as a weapon, then surprises everyone: Greg Abel will become CEO at year-end. The board agrees the next day.
Berkshire agrees to buy OxyChem for $9.7 billion, probably his last big deal as CEO.
In a Thanksgiving letter, says he is "going quiet" and will no longer write the annual letter.

L.t: The Museum of American Finance gives him its Lifetime Achievement Award.

W.t: Trump begins his second term.
A cheap Chinese AI model, DeepSeek, knocks about $590 billion off Nvidia in a day.
'Liberation Day' tariffs: the S&P 500 drops 10.5% in two days and nearly 20% from its peak before most tariffs are paused.
Leo XIV becomes the first American pope.
Nvidia becomes the first company worth $5 trillion.
The longest government shutdown in US history: 43 days.

M.t: At the meeting, Berkshire retires a jersey for him too, with the number 45: his years as vice chairman.

B.t: Greg Abel becomes CEO. Buffett, 95, stays chairman and still comes to the office five days a week.
For the first time in 60 years, the annual letter is not his: Abel writes it.
Watches the annual meeting from the front row while Abel runs it. Berkshire retires a jersey for him with the number 60, his years as CEO.
At 96, steps down as chairman and becomes chairman emeritus. His son Howard, a director since 1993, becomes chairman.
In his Thanksgiving letter, gives about $5.5 billion of Berkshire shares to four family foundations and writes that kindness compounds.

L.t: Turns 82. Still vice chairman of Fidelity Management & Research, meeting its young analysts several times a year.

W.t: The United States and Israel strike Iran. Oil heads towards $120 as the Strait of Hormuz closes.
After a wobble, the S&P 500 hits new records, led by AI companies.
Kevin Warsh succeeds Jerome Powell as Fed chairman.
America turns 250.
The United States, Canada and Mexico host the FIFA World Cup.
Americans vote in the midterm elections.

threads.1924: The mutual fund is born in Boston the year Munger is born. Twenty years later Lynch is born near Boston; one day he will run the biggest fund of its kind.
threads.1930: Tariffs then and now: Smoot-Hawley deepened the slump. In 2025, new tariffs sent stocks down nearly 20%, and Buffett, born in 1930, warned against using trade as a weapon.
threads.1934: Graham and Dodd's book appears when Buffett is four. Sixteen years later he enrols at Columbia to learn from them in person.
threads.1949: The Intelligent Investor comes out. Within a year it changes Buffett's life.
threads.1957: The S&P 500 is born in the first full year of Buffett's partnership.
threads.1959: Lynch, 15, is carrying golf bags near Boston the year Buffett and Munger meet in Omaha.
threads.1966: Lynch walks into Fidelity as a summer intern the year Buffett closes his partnership to new money.
threads.1972: See's Candies is bought in January; in November the Dow passes 1,000. Lynch is a 28-year-old analyst.
threads.1977: Lynch takes over Magellan; Munger starts chairing Daily Journal; Buffett writes the first letter in Berkshire's online archive. All in one year.
threads.1987: All three in one storm: Buffett had just bought into Salomon, Munger was his vice chairman, and Lynch was on a golf trip in Ireland.
threads.1990: Lynch retires at 46. At 46, Buffett was rescuing GEICO and Munger was running his own fund.
threads.2000: The index fund overtakes Magellan, the fund Lynch built, just as the dot-com bubble bursts.
threads.2008: Munger's idea (BYD) and Buffett's nerve (Goldman Sachs, GE) in the same autumn.
threads.2023: Munger dies 34 days short of 100, after 64 years of friendship with Buffett.
threads.2026: For the first time since 1970, Buffett is neither CEO nor chairman of Berkshire.

crossings.d: As a teenager Munger worked at Buffett & Son, the Omaha grocery owned by Warren's grandfather. Warren worked there too, later. They did not meet.
Dr. Edwin Davis invests $100,000 with Buffett because he reminds him of Charlie Munger. The Davises are determined to introduce them.
Back in Omaha after his father's death, Munger meets Buffett at a dinner arranged by the Davis family. Buffett knows at once he has found someone to learn from.
Buffett tells Munger that law is fine as a hobby, but he could do better. Two years later Munger starts his own fund.
With Sandy Gottesman they buy the Baltimore department store Hochschild, Kohn. It is a mistake, and an early lesson for both.
Munger persuades Buffett to pay up for a great business. See's becomes the model for Berkshire's later buys.
Munger formally joins Berkshire as vice chairman: the start of 45 years side by side.
Buffett's famous Columbia talk uses Munger's partnership record as proof that Graham's way works.
Buffett phones Lynch at home to ask if he may quote One Up on Wall Street in his annual letter. Lynch's daughter takes the call.
Lynch writes the foreword to The Warren Buffett Way.
Munger champions the Chinese carmaker BYD, and Berkshire buys about 10% of it.
For Berkshire's 50th anniversary each writes his own letter to shareholders, side by side.
Lynch calls Buffett the greatest investor of all time.
Munger lets slip at the annual meeting that Greg Abel will keep the culture. Buffett confirms Abel as his successor.
Munger dies at 99. Buffett says Berkshire could not have been built to what it is without him.
Berkshire retires a '60' jersey for Buffett and a '45' jersey for Munger at the first meeting run by Greg Abel.

storms.name: The Great Crash
storms.what: Wall Street crashes in October 1929 and keeps falling for almost three years. Banks fail and a quarter of workers lose their jobs.
storms.M: Aged 5 to 8 in Omaha.
storms.B: Born in August 1930, in the middle of it. In 1931 the bank where his father works fails.
storms.L: Not yet born.

storms.name: The 1937 relapse
storms.what: Just as the economy recovers, a new recession hits. Stocks lose about 35% in 1937 alone.
storms.M: A 13-year-old in Omaha.
storms.B: Six or seven, already selling things for a profit.
storms.L: Not yet born.

storms.name: The Kennedy Slide
storms.what: A sharp fall in the first half of 1962, with a one-day crash on May 28.
storms.M: Starts his own fund this year and makes +30.1% while the Dow falls 7.6%.
storms.B: His partnership makes +13.9% against -7.6% for the Dow.
storms.L: 18, at Boston College.

storms.name: The 1973-74 crash
storms.what: Oil shock, inflation and Watergate. The 'Nifty Fifty' favourites collapse and the S&P 500 loses nearly half its value.
storms.M: His fund loses 31.9% and then 31.5%. He holds on, and in 1975 it rebounds 73.2%.
storms.B: Buys a stake in the Washington Post in 1973. Berkshire's shares fall 48.7% in 1974, yet he tells Forbes: "Now is the time to invest and get rich."
storms.L: Becomes Fidelity's director of research in 1974.

storms.name: The Volcker squeeze
storms.what: The Fed pushes interest rates to record highs to kill inflation. Two recessions follow, then a great bull market starts in August 1982.
storms.M: Berkshire's vice chairman.
storms.B: Berkshire's shares rise 31.8% in 1981 while the S&P 500 falls 5%.
storms.L: Magellan opens to the public in 1981. Later he says: "Nobody called me to tell me about the recession in 1980 and 1981."

storms.name: Black Monday
storms.what: The Dow falls 22.6% in a single day, still its worst day ever. Yet the S&P 500 ends the year slightly up.
storms.M: Berkshire's vice chairman. Berkshire ends 1987 up 4.6%.
storms.B: Had just invested $700 million in Salomon. Berkshire's shares drop from about $3,890 to $3,170 within days.
storms.L: On a golf trip in Ireland. Magellan loses about a third in two days; he cuts the trip short.

storms.name: LTCM and Russia
storms.what: Russia defaults and the giant hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management nearly collapses. The Fed organises a rescue by Wall Street banks.
storms.M: Berkshire's vice chairman.
storms.B: Offers, with AIG and Goldman Sachs, to buy LTCM. The offer is turned down.
storms.L: Retired from fund management since 1990.

storms.name: The dot-com bust
storms.what: The internet bubble bursts. The Nasdaq loses 78% and the S&P 500 about half.
storms.M: With Buffett, refuses to buy tech stocks he cannot value.
storms.B: Mocked in 1999 when Berkshire falls 19.9%; proved right in 2000 when it rises 26.6% as the market falls.
storms.L: Warns in a new edition of his book that very few dot-com investors "benefit from the full ride."

storms.name: The financial crisis
storms.what: Subprime loans go bad, Lehman Brothers fails and the financial system nearly freezes.
storms.M: Champions BYD; near the bottom, Daily Journal buys big-bank shares.
storms.B: Invests in Goldman Sachs and GE, writes "Buy American. I Am." and agrees to buy Burlington Northern.
storms.L: Long retired from fund management; in his 60s, at Fidelity.

storms.name: The COVID crash
storms.what: A pandemic shuts the world. The fastest bear market ever, then a fast recovery.
storms.M: At 96, stays home from Berkshire's empty-arena meeting.
storms.B: Sells all of Berkshire's airline shares; later buys into five Japanese trading houses.
storms.L: In his 70s, at Fidelity.

storms.name: The inflation bear
storms.what: Inflation returns and the Fed raises rates faster than at any time since the 1980s.
storms.M: Steps down as Daily Journal chairman at 98.
storms.B: Buys Occidental, Chevron and Alleghany. Berkshire's shares rise 4.0% as the S&P 500 falls 18.1%.
storms.L: Still at Fidelity, in his late 70s.

storms.name: The tariff shock
storms.what: Sweeping new tariffs send stocks down 10.5% in two days. Most are paused on April 9 and the market recovers to new records.
storms.M: Died in 2023.
storms.B: At his last meeting as CEO, says trade can be an act of war, then announces he will step down.
storms.L: Receives a lifetime achievement award at 81.

agePresets: At 11, Buffett buys his first stock and Lynch starts carrying golf bags. Munger is an Omaha schoolboy.
At 19, Buffett reads The Intelligent Investor, Lynch buys Flying Tiger and Munger leaves college for the Army.
At 25, Buffett starts his partnership and Lynch joins Fidelity full time. Munger is a young Los Angeles lawyer.
At 33, Lynch takes over Magellan and Buffett buys into American Express after the salad-oil scandal.
At 35, Munger meets Buffett. In the year he turns 35, Buffett takes control of Berkshire.
At 38, Munger starts his own fund. In the year he turns 38, Buffett has his best partnership year.
At 46, Lynch retires. In the year he turns 46, Buffett rescues GEICO.
At 54, Munger becomes Berkshire's vice chairman. In the year he turns 54, Buffett gives his Superinvestors talk.
In the year he turns 78, Buffett invests through the 2008 panic.
In the year he turns 95, Buffett announces he will step down as CEO.
At 99, Munger dies, still working.

o: The first index fund for ordinary investors

about: A year-by-year record of three investors' lives, from Charlie Munger's birth in 1924 to today, set against what was happening in America and the world.
Each year shows how old each man was, where he was in life, what he decided, and the big events around him: presidents, wars, crashes, inventions and films.
Only the three of them. Nothing here is about the person who built the library.
method: Investor facts come from their own letters, books and talks, from biographies and from major news reports. Most were checked against at least two independent sources; each fact carries a short source tag.
Market numbers come from primary tables: Berkshire's annual letters, Buffett's partnership letters, his 1984 Columbia article and Aswath Damodaran's historical returns at NYU Stern.
World events are summarised from the standard historical record. Where sources give different dates or figures, we use the most widely cited and say 'about'.
Ages are the age each man reaches in that year. Munger was born on 1 January, Lynch on 19 January and Buffett on 30 August, so Buffett is a year younger than the label for most of each year.
All summaries are in our own words. Exact quotes are short, in quotation marks, and come from the named source.
disclaimer: For education and general information only. Nothing here is investment, financial, legal or tax advice, or a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.

This is a historical summary. It may contain errors or omissions and is provided as is, without any warranty of accuracy or completeness. Check the original sources before relying on any date or figure.
Past results, including every return quoted here, do not predict future results. Investing involves risk, including the loss of capital.
No liability is accepted for any loss or damage arising from use of this material.

Independent and unaffiliated: not endorsed by Berkshire Hathaway, Fidelity Investments, Daily Journal, any person named or any publisher. All names, trademarks and copyrights belong to their owners. No photographs of any person are used.

people.name: John Maynard Keynes
people.line: Economist who ran King's College's money from 1921 to 1946, and changed how he invested halfway through.

people.name: Anthony Bolton
people.line: Contrarian stock picker who ran Fidelity Special Situations for 28 years.

people.name: Terry Smith
people.line: Exposed creative accounting, built two brokers, then founded Fundsmith in 2010.

labels.title: Three British Lives
labels.hook: Keynes, Bolton and Smith on one line, from 1883 to today, against Britain's history, prime ministers and market crashes.
labels.legendNote: Each colour is one life: Keynes, Bolton and Smith. Gold is Britain and the world.
labels.pulseNote: UK shares: Cambridge Associates to 2017, FTSE All-Share total return since. Keynes's fund: Chambers and Dimson, years ending in August, against their UK index. Fundsmith: its factsheets, against the MSCI World in pounds. Bolton's year-by-year figures are not published in a source we could check.
labels.mktStart: The UK share series used here starts in 1900.
labels.stormNote: Peak-to-bottom falls are approximate and use the index named. Year chips: UK shares in that calendar year, with dividends.
labels.ageNote: Each row shows the year he turns that age, so for part of that year he is still a year younger.
labels.investLede: Put money in with Keynes's King's fund, Fundsmith or UK shares in any year, then live through it one year at a time. After each year you see what happened and choose: stay in, or get out.

M.d: Grows up at 6 Harvey Road, Cambridge, the eldest of three children of a Cambridge don and a writer and social reformer.
Wins a scholarship to Eton College.
An undergraduate at King's College, Cambridge, among the friends who later form the Bloomsbury Group.
A civil servant at the India Office in London, after coming second in the entrance examination.
Lecturer in economics, Fellow of King's from about 1909, and editor of the Economic Journal from 1912.
Works on Britain's wartime finance at the Treasury, heading its external-finance division from 1917, then goes to the peace conference in Paris.
Bursar of King's (first bursar from 1924), investor, journalist and the most famous economist of his day.
Treasury adviser, peer, and Britain's chief negotiator at Bretton Woods and in Washington.

B.d: Educated at Stowe School, then Trinity College, Cambridge, where he reads engineering and also studies composition.
Starts in 1971 at the merchant bank Keyser Ullman, then runs money for a year or two at Schlesinger Investment Management.
Runs Fidelity Special Situations from December 1979 to December 2007: about 19.5% a year.
Steps back from running money to mentor younger managers at Fidelity, and writes his own book.
Moves to Hong Kong in April 2010 to run Fidelity China Special Situations, which he manages until April 2014.
Retires from fund management and composes music, including an opera about Alexander Litvinenko, premiered in 2021.

L.d: Grows up in East London, goes to Stratford Grammar School, then reads history at University College Cardiff, graduating with a First in 1974.
Works for Barclays Bank, running a branch and then in its finance department. MBA from Henley in 1979.
Banking analyst at W. Greenwell and then BZW, rated the top bank analyst in London.
Head of UK company research, until he is sacked in 1992 over Accounting for Growth.
Collins Stewart (chief executive from 2000), then Tullett Prebon, one of the biggest brokers between banks.
Founds Fundsmith in 2010 and runs its Equity fund; leaves Tullett Prebon in 2014 to focus on it.

eras.title: Victorian sunset
eras.intro: Britain runs the largest empire in history and London is the world's money market. Keynes is born in Cambridge in 1883. Gold is found in South Africa, the vote widens, and the reign of Queen Victoria ends in 1901.

where.M: A Cambridge boy, then a scholar at Eton.
where.B: Not yet born.
where.L: Not yet born.

eras.title: The Edwardian years
eras.tag: Reforms, Dreadnoughts and a young don
eras.intro: Liberal governments bring old-age pensions and national insurance and curb the House of Lords. Keynes studies at King's, works at the India Office, and returns to Cambridge to teach economics.

where.M: King's College, the India Office, then a Cambridge lecturer and editor.
where.B: Not yet born.
where.L: Not yet born.

eras.title: The Great War
eras.tag: The exchange shuts, the Treasury calls
eras.intro: War closes the London Stock Exchange for five months. Britain borrows heavily to fight. Keynes joins the Treasury and helps run the country's wartime finance.

where.M: A senior Treasury official in his thirties.
where.B: Not yet born.
where.L: Not yet born.

eras.title: Peace, gold and speculation
eras.tag: A famous book, a fund and a crash
eras.intro: Keynes quits the peace talks in protest, and his book about them makes him famous. He speculates, is wiped out, recovers, and starts running money for King's. Britain goes back to gold in 1925; the decade ends in crashes in London and New York.

where.M: Bursar of King's, investor and famous critic of the peace.
where.B: Not yet born.
where.L: Not yet born.

eras.title: Slump and a new theory
eras.tag: Off gold, a new method, a war
eras.intro: The slump bites, Britain leaves the gold standard in 1931 and money becomes cheap. Keynes changes from forecasting the market to picking a few undervalued shares, writes The General Theory, survives a heart attack and a 1937-38 fall, and sets down his three principles.

where.M: At the peak of his fame and his fortune, then ill.
where.B: Not yet born.
where.L: Not yet born.

eras.title: War and a new order
eras.tag: Bretton Woods, a death, the NHS
eras.intro: Britain stands alone in 1940, then wins the war with its allies. Keynes, now a peer, designs much of the post-war money system and dies in 1946. Labour builds the welfare state; the pound is devalued in 1949.

where.M: Treasury adviser and negotiator; dies in April 1946.
where.B: Not yet born.
where.L: Not yet born.

eras.title: Never had it so good
eras.tag: Two births and a booming market
eras.intro: Rationing ends, a new queen is crowned and shares boom in the 1950s. The pound is devalued again in 1967. Anthony Bolton is born in 1950 and Terry Smith in 1953.

where.M: Died in 1946.
where.B: A boy, then a pupil at Stowe and a Cambridge student.
where.L: A boy in East London.

eras.title: The troubled seventies
eras.tag: Strikes, inflation and the worst crash
eras.intro: Decimal money, Europe, oil shocks, strikes and inflation above 25%. UK shares lose half their value in 1974, then more than double in 1975. The decade ends with Margaret Thatcher and the end of exchange controls.

where.M: Died in 1946.
where.B: Learns the trade at Keyser Ullman and Schlesinger; joins Fidelity in December 1979.
where.L: Cardiff, then Barclays and an MBA.

eras.title: Big Bang and the long boom
eras.intro: Privatisations, Big Bang in the City and a long bull market, interrupted by Black Monday in 1987 and the pound's exit from the ERM in 1992. The Bank of England becomes independent in 1997.

where.M: Died in 1946.
where.B: Builds Special Situations into the UK's best-known fund.
where.L: Top bank analyst, then sacked for Accounting for Growth; builds Collins Stewart.

eras.title: Bust and crisis
eras.intro: The dot-com bubble bursts, then the first British bank run in over a century and the financial crisis. The FTSE 100 halves twice.

where.M: Died in 1946.
where.B: Proved right on technology; hands over his fund at the end of 2007.
where.L: Floats Collins Stewart and builds Tullett Prebon.

eras.title: New funds, new shocks
eras.intro: Austerity, the Brexit vote, a pandemic, a gilt crisis and seven prime ministers in ten years. Smith founds Fundsmith; Bolton runs a China fund, then retires to compose. In January 2026 the FTSE 100 closes above 10,000 for the first time.

where.M: Died in 1946.
where.B: Runs a China fund until 2014, then composes music.
where.L: Runs Fundsmith: years well ahead of the market, then five behind.

M.t: Born at 6 Harvey Road, Cambridge. His father is a Cambridge don; his mother is a writer and social reformer.

W.t: The volcano Krakatoa erupts in the Dutch East Indies; its ash colours sunsets around the world.
An international conference chooses Greenwich as the prime meridian, the starting line for the world's time zones.
The Third Reform Act gives the vote to many more working men in the countryside.
Khartoum falls and General Gordon is killed.
Karl Benz builds his first motor car in Germany.
Gold is discovered on the Witwatersrand in South Africa. The gold mines become a big part of the London stock market.
Gladstone's first bill for Irish Home Rule is defeated.
Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee: fifty years on the throne.
The Football League plays its first season.
The Eiffel Tower opens in Paris.
The London dock strike wins dockers a pay rise and boosts the trade unions.
The Baring crisis: the Bank of England organises a rescue of Baring Brothers, one of the City's great banks.
The Forth Bridge opens in Scotland.
Elementary schooling in England becomes free.
Gladstone becomes prime minister for the fourth time, aged 82.
The Independent Labour Party is founded.
Tower Bridge opens in London.
Death duties on large estates are introduced.
The Lumière brothers show the first films to a paying audience in Paris.
The first modern Olympic Games are held in Athens.
The Daily Mail is launched.

M.t: Wins a scholarship to Eton College.

W.t: Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee.
The Battle of Omdurman in Sudan.
The Second Boer War begins in South Africa.
The Labour Representation Committee is founded: the start of the Labour Party.
Mafeking is relieved after a 217-day siege.
Queen Victoria dies after 63 years on the throne. Edward VII becomes king.

M.t: Goes up to King's College, Cambridge.

W.t: The Boer War ends.
Emmeline Pankhurst founds the Women's Social and Political Union to fight for votes for women.
The Wright brothers make the first powered flights in North Carolina.
The Entente Cordiale settles old quarrels between Britain and France.

M.t: Completes his degree at Cambridge.

W.t: Albert Einstein publishes his papers on relativity and the nature of light.

M.t: Joins the India Office in London, having come second in the civil service examination.

W.t: The Liberals win a landslide general election.
HMS Dreadnought is launched and starts a naval arms race with Germany.
A banking panic in New York; J. P. Morgan organises a rescue.

M.t: Returns to Cambridge as a lecturer in economics.

W.t: H. H. Asquith becomes prime minister.
Old-age pensions are introduced.
London hosts the Olympic Games.

M.t: Becomes a Fellow of King's and wins the Adam Smith Prize.

W.t: Lloyd George's 'People's Budget' raises taxes on the rich to pay for pensions; the Lords reject it.
Edward VII dies. George V becomes king.
The Parliament Act ends the House of Lords' power to block money bills.
The National Insurance Act brings in sickness and unemployment insurance.

M.t: Becomes editor of the Economic Journal, a post he holds for over thirty years.

W.t: The Titanic sinks on its first voyage.

M.t: Publishes his first book, Indian Currency and Finance, and joins the Royal Commission on Indian currency.

W.t: The United States creates the Federal Reserve.

M.t: Publishes an account of the City's crisis, 'The City of London and the Bank of England, August 1914'.

W.t: As war approaches, the London Stock Exchange closes. It does not reopen until 4 January 1915.
Britain declares war on Germany.

M.t: Joins the Treasury.

W.t: The Gallipoli campaign begins.
The liner Lusitania is sunk by a German submarine.

M.t: Granted exemption from conscription because of his Treasury work. He also applies as a conscientious objector, but does not attend the hearing.

W.t: The Battle of the Somme: about 420,000 British casualties.
The Easter Rising in Dublin.
David Lloyd George becomes prime minister.

M.t: Put in charge of the Treasury's new 'A' division, which handles Britain's external finance. Made a Companion of the Bath in May.

W.t: The United States enters the war.
The Bolsheviks seize power in Russia.
Women over 30 win the vote.
The Armistice ends the fighting.
Influenza kills millions around the world.

M.t: Goes to the Paris peace conference as the Treasury's chief representative.
Resigns in protest at the harsh terms for Germany and leaves Paris in June.
Becomes second bursar of King's College.
Publishes The Economic Consequences of the Peace. It makes him famous around the world.
Starts speculating in currencies with borrowed money.

W.t: The Treaty of Versailles is signed.

M.t: Wiped out by his currency bets.

W.t: The post-war boom collapses into a slump.
The League of Nations is founded.

M.t: Starts running a fund for King's College that he can invest freely, alongside the college's land and bonds.
Becomes chairman of the National Mutual Life Assurance Society.

W.t: The Anglo-Irish Treaty is signed.

M.t: By the end of the year he has cleared his debts and has net assets of over £20,000.

W.t: The BBC makes its first broadcasts.
The Irish Free State is founded.

M.t: Publishes A Tract on Monetary Reform.
Becomes chairman of the weekly Nation and Athenaeum.

W.t: Hyperinflation destroys the German mark.

M.t: Becomes first bursar of King's College, a post he holds until his death.

W.t: Ramsay MacDonald forms the first Labour government.

M.t: Marries the Russian ballerina Lydia Lopokova.
Attacks the return to gold in The Economic Consequences of Mr. Churchill.

W.t: Britain returns to the gold standard at the pre-war rate. Winston Churchill is Chancellor.
The General Strike.
John Logie Baird demonstrates television in London.
The BBC becomes a public corporation.
Charles Lindbergh flies solo from New York to Paris.
Women win the vote on the same terms as men, at 21.
Alexander Fleming discovers penicillin in London.

M.t: Heavy losses on commodities at the end of the 1920s cut his own net worth to under £8,000.
Appointed to the Macmillan committee on finance and industry.

W.t: Wall Street crashes. The slump spreads around the world.
Ramsay MacDonald forms his second Labour government.
The fraudulent business empire of Clarence Hatry collapses, shaking the London market.

M.t: Publishes A Treatise on Money.

W.t: The airship R101 crashes in France on its first long flight.
UK shares lose 15.4% in the year as the slump deepens.
Britain leaves the gold standard. The pound falls sharply against the dollar.
A financial crisis splits the Labour government; MacDonald leads a National Government.

M.t: From the early 1930s he stops trying to time the market and picks individual undervalued shares instead.

W.t: Britain brings in general tariffs on imports.
Bank Rate is cut to 2%, where it stays until the war: the start of 'cheap money'.

M.t: His King's fund gains 51.4% in the year to August 1933.

W.t: Adolf Hitler becomes chancellor of Germany.

M.t: Writes to F. C. Scott that it is better to put fairly large sums into a few businesses one understands.

W.t: Hitler makes himself Führer.
George V's Silver Jubilee.
Stanley Baldwin becomes prime minister for the third time.

M.t: Publishes The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money.
Opens the Arts Theatre in Cambridge, which he has largely paid for.
His own fortune peaks at over £500,000.
About two-thirds of his King's fund is in mining shares.

W.t: Edward VIII abdicates. George VI becomes king.
George V dies. Edward VIII becomes king.
The Jarrow March: 200 unemployed men walk to London.

M.t: Collapses with heart trouble and is ill for months.
Becomes a director of the Eugenics Society, until 1944. His eugenic views, shared by many in his time, are now widely condemned.

W.t: Neville Chamberlain becomes prime minister.
UK shares lose 15.7% in the year.

M.t: Writes his post-mortem memo for King's: timing the market failed; his three principles are careful selection, steadfast holding and balance.
His King's fund loses 22.6% in the year to August 1938.
In the slump his own fortune falls below £200,000.

W.t: The Munich Agreement.
Britain declares war on Germany.

M.t: Publishes How to Pay for the War.
Moves into an office at the Treasury as an adviser to the Chancellor.

W.t: Winston Churchill becomes prime minister.
The Battle of Britain, then the Blitz.
The evacuation from Dunkirk.

M.t: Elected a director of the Bank of England.
Becomes a trustee of the National Gallery.

W.t: Japan attacks Pearl Harbor; the United States enters the war.
The United States starts Lend-Lease aid to Britain.

M.t: Made a peer: Baron Keynes of Tilton.
Becomes chairman of the wartime council for music and the arts that later becomes the Arts Council.

W.t: The Beveridge Report plans a welfare state 'from the cradle to the grave'.
Victory at El Alamein.
Italy surrenders.

M.t: Leads Britain's team at the Bretton Woods conference, which creates the IMF and the World Bank. He has a mild heart attack during it.

W.t: D-Day.
The Education Act promises free secondary schooling for all.

M.t: The American loan he has negotiated in months of hard talks in Washington is signed.

W.t: Victory in Europe.
Labour wins a landslide. Clement Attlee becomes prime minister.

M.t: Attends the first meetings of the IMF and World Bank governors in Savannah, Georgia.
Dies at Tilton in Sussex after a heart attack, aged 62. His estate is valued at about £480,000.

W.t: The Bank of England is nationalised.
The Arts Council of Great Britain receives its charter.
India and Pakistan become independent.
A sterling crisis forces Britain to suspend the pound's convertibility after five weeks.
The National Health Service begins.
London hosts the 'austerity' Olympics.
The pound is devalued from $4.03 to $2.80.
NATO is founded.

B.t: Born on 7 March 1950.

W.t: The Korean War begins.
The Festival of Britain.
Winston Churchill returns as prime minister.
George VI dies. Elizabeth II becomes queen.
The Great Smog of London.

L.t: Born in London; he grows up in the East End.

W.t: Crick and Watson describe the structure of DNA in Cambridge.
Hillary and Tenzing reach the top of Everest.
The coronation of Elizabeth II.
Rationing finally ends.
UK shares gain 41.9% in the year.
Anthony Eden becomes prime minister.
ITV, the first commercial television channel, starts broadcasting.
The Suez crisis ends in humiliation for Britain.
Premium Bonds go on sale.
Harold Macmillan becomes prime minister; that summer he says most people have 'never had it so good'.
Six countries sign the Treaty of Rome and create the European Economic Community, without Britain.
The Munich air disaster kills eight Manchester United players.
Britain's first motorway, the Preston bypass, opens.
The Mini is launched.
The first section of the M1 opens.
UK shares gain 50.5% in the year.
Macmillan's 'wind of change' speech on African independence.
Britain applies to join the European Economic Community. The Berlin Wall goes up.
The Cuban missile crisis.
The Beatles release their first single.
France's President de Gaulle vetoes Britain's entry to the EEC.

B.t: Starts work in the City at the merchant bank Keyser Ullman.

W.t: Decimal Day: the pound is divided into 100 new pence.
Rolls-Royce goes bust and is nationalised.
Bloody Sunday in Derry, and a national miners' strike.
The pound is floated.
Britain joins the European Economic Community.
A secondary banking crisis: the Bank of England organises a 'lifeboat' to rescue failing lenders.
An oil embargo quadruples the price of oil within months.

L.t: Graduates from University College Cardiff with a First in history, and turns down a research fellowship to start a business career at Barclays.

W.t: UK shares lose 51.8% in the year, their worst year since at least 1900.
The three-day week: industry is rationed to three days' electricity a week.
Harold Wilson returns as prime minister after the first of two elections that year.
UK shares gain 152.1% in the year, more than doubling.
Two-thirds of voters choose to stay in the EEC in a referendum.
Inflation peaks above 25%.
Britain borrows from the International Monetary Fund to defend the pound.
James Callaghan becomes prime minister.
The Queen's Silver Jubilee.
The 'Winter of Discontent': strikes across the public sector.

B.t: Joins Fidelity, aged 29, on the day it launches its first four unit trusts for British investors, and starts running Special Situations.

L.t: Completes an MBA at Henley.

W.t: Margaret Thatcher becomes prime minister.
Exchange controls are abolished: Britons can invest abroad freely for the first time in forty years.
Unemployment passes 2 million.
UK shares gain 35.4% in the year.
364 economists write to The Times attacking the government's tight budget.
Prince Charles marries Lady Diana Spencer.
The Falklands War.
The £1 coin comes into use.
Margaret Thatcher wins a landslide.

L.t: Leaves Barclays to become a banking analyst at the stockbroker W. Greenwell; he is soon rated the top bank analyst in London.

W.t: The FTSE 100 index is launched at 1,000.
The miners' strike begins; it lasts a year.
British Telecom is privatised; millions of people buy shares for the first time.

B.t: Also starts running Fidelity's European fund, which he manages until 2002.

W.t: Live Aid.
Big Bang: fixed commissions end and the City's trading goes electronic.
British Gas is privatised: 'Tell Sid'.
Black Monday: the FTSE 100 falls more than a fifth in two days.
The Great Storm hits southern England.
Margaret Thatcher wins a third term.
The top rate of income tax is cut to 40%.
The Berlin Wall falls.
UK shares gain 36.1% in the year.

L.t: Becomes head of UK company research at UBS Phillips & Drew. His research on how companies dress up their profits begins as a note to clients.

W.t: Britain joins the European Exchange Rate Mechanism.
Polly Peck collapses, one of several companies that go bust while reporting profits.
John Major becomes prime minister.
The Gulf War.
Robert Maxwell dies; it emerges he has stolen from his companies' pension funds.

Joins the stockbroker Collins Stewart.

W.t: Black Wednesday: the pound is forced out of the Exchange Rate Mechanism.

The Maastricht Treaty comes into force, creating the European Union.

B.t: Starts managing the investment trust Fidelity Special Values, until 2007.

W.t: The Channel Tunnel opens.
The National Lottery starts.
Barings, Britain's oldest merchant bank, collapses after a trader's huge losses in Singapore.

L.t: Becomes a director of Collins Stewart.

W.t: England hosts the European football championship.

L.t: Stands as the Referendum Party candidate in West Chelmsford at the general election.

W.t: Labour wins a landslide. Tony Blair becomes prime minister.
The Bank of England is given control of interest rates.
Diana, Princess of Wales, dies in Paris.
The Good Friday Agreement.

W.t: The euro is launched; Britain stays out.

W.t: The dot-com bubble peaks and starts to burst.
Terrorist attacks on New York and Washington.
Foot-and-mouth disease hits British farms.

B.t: Resumes studying musical composition.

W.t: Euro notes and coins arrive in twelve countries.
UK shares lose 22.7%, their third losing year in a row.

L.t: Collins Stewart buys the broker Tullett Liberty.

W.t: The FTSE 100 hits bottom, about half its 1999 peak.
The Iraq war begins.

L.t: Collins Stewart buys Prebon, creating one of the world's biggest brokers between banks.

W.t: The European Union grows by ten countries.
London wins the 2012 Olympics; the next day, bombs on the Underground and a bus kill 52 people.

B.t: His fund, now about £6 billion and the UK's largest, is split into a UK fund and a global fund.
His Garland of Carols is premiered at St Paul's Cathedral.

L.t: Collins Stewart and Tullett Prebon split into two companies. He chairs Collins Stewart and runs Tullett Prebon.

W.t: UK shares gain 16.8% in the year.

B.t: Moves to a full-time role mentoring Fidelity's younger fund managers.

The government takes big stakes in the banks to stop the system collapsing.

B.t: Publishes his book, Investing Against the Tide.
Chooses his favourite music on BBC Radio 3's Private Passions.

W.t: The Bank of England cuts Bank Rate to 0.5% and starts buying bonds with new money.
The FTSE 100 hits bottom, down about half from its 2007 peak.

W.t: Riots in London and other cities.

Launches the Fundsmith Emerging Equities Trust.

The Conservatives win a majority.

L.t: Made an Honorary Fellow of Cardiff University.

Theresa May becomes prime minister.

L.t: Launches the Fundsmith Sustainable Equity Fund.

L.t: Smithson Investment Trust raises £822.5 million, the biggest launch of a UK investment trust ever.

W.t: The builder Carillion collapses.

Boris Johnson becomes prime minister.
